text: A 45-year-old patient undergoes complete ileal and partial jejunal resection due to Crohn's disease. Which of the following deficiencies is he most likely to develop in the long term?
expl: Explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) is absorbed primarily in the terminal ileum after binding to intrinsic factor (IF) secreted by gastric parietal cells. Complete ileal resection → impaired B12 absorption → megaloblastic anemia and neurological symptoms (paresthesia, memory impairment). Jejunal resection affects absorption of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, and some vitamins, but does not significantly impact B12 absorption , which occurs mainly in the ileum. Therefore, Vitamin B12 deficiency is the most immediate and predictable outcome. Ileum resection: B12, bile salts → fat malabsorption, steatorrhea Jejunum resection: Carbs, proteins, water-soluble vitamins → malnutrition, diarrhea Explanation of Other Options: Folic acid deficiency (Option A): Absorbed in proximal small intestine (duodenum, jejunum). Only a minor portion of the jejunum is resected → folate absorption may be partially affected, but B12 deficiency is more likely. Gastric ulcer (Option C) : Not directly caused by ileal or jejunal resection. Gastric acid secretion or IF may be affected indirectly by B12 deficiency but does not cause ulceration. Constipation (Option D) : May occur due to decreased bowel length or malabsorption, but not the most likely or direct consequence compared to B12 deficiency. Key Takeaway Points: Site of Vitamin Absorption in Small Intestine Clinical Correlation: Vitamin B12 deficiency signs: Megaloblastic anemia (macrocytosis) Neurological: peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord Management: Lifelong B12 supplementation (oral if some ileum remains; otherwise parenteral).

text: An 18-year-old was brought to the emergency department by her friends as she had turned blue. She was well otherwise. On examination she has central cyanosis; all other parameters are normal. What is the most likely cause?
expl: The question deals with cyanosis in an otherwise well patient. Cyanosis is seen in hypoxia. But the patient with hypoxia will be dyspnoeic. Here the patient is otherwise normal. Rare cause of cyanosis is due to abnormal hemoglobins like methemoglobin or Sulfhemoglobin. The causes of methemoglobinemia includes: Nitrates, nitric oxide or nitrobenzene Aniline dyes Propanil(a herbicide) Dapsone Pyridium So the accurate among the options are drinking water contaminated with nitrates. Lead poisoning will not lead to cyanosis but bluish lines in the gums. Carbon monoxide poisoning will cause cherry red discolouration. Anorexia nervosa is a disease of distorted perception of body image, where the patient restricts food intake and will be malnourished. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:459 Pg 3593

text: A 38 year old athlete has pain on abduction of her arm, particularly when resisted. Which tendon pathology is affected?

text: Myelophthisis is due to I. Marrow replaced by fibrous tissue by granulomatous process II. Marrow replaced by fibrous tissue by primary hematological process III. Marrow replaced by fibrous tissue by secondary to tumour
expl: Bone marrow can be replaced by fibrous tissue (composed of reticulin fibers and collagen) due to a variety of causes. When this fibrosis is due to a primary hematologic process, it is called myelofibrosis . When the fibrosis is secondary to a tumor or a granulomatous process, it is called myelophthisis . Bone marrow cavity replaced by fibrous tissue Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 103, Pg: 805

text: A 48-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding. Which of the following hormones is most commonly associated with shedding of the endometrium during menstruation?
expl: Involution of the corpus luteum results in a decrease in progesterone and estradiol secretion. This occurs around day 24 of a 28-day menstrual cycle. The loss of hormonal support causes endometrial shedding. LH, FSH, GnRH and estrogen are not involved in this process. Estradiol is primarily responsible for endometrial proliferation during the earlier phases of menstrual cycle. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3035

text: A 16-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhoea. General physical examination reveals no abnormality. Breast development appear to be normal with scanty pubic hair growth. On karyotyping, she is found to have XY genotype. What is the most probable cause for her condition?
expl: This girl has testicular feminisation, wherein testosterone is being produced in adequate amounts by the testes located in the abdomen. The majority of cases occur due to a mutation in androgen receptor rendering them non-functional to testosterone and dihydrotestosterone (DHT). DHT is formed from testosterone by 5a-reductase and is responsible for the development of male secondary sex characteristics. In the absence of androgen receptors, the cells are more receptive to estradiol, which is also produced from testosterone by the enzyme aromatase. Thus, although the genotype is XY, these girls will have well-developed feminine secondary sex characteristics. Primary amenorrhoea is often the only symptom that brings these girls to medical attention. These children also would have absent mullerian structures due to normal MIS production from testes during intrauterine period. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3003

text: Which is not correct regarding RA?

options.A: The incidence of RA increases between 25 and 55 years of age, after which it plateaus until the age of 75 and then decreases
options.B: The most common pattern of joint involvement is symmetrical and polyarticular.
options.C: Flexor tendon tenosynovitis is a frequent hallmark of RA
options.D: Macrocytic anemia is the most common hematologic abnormality in RA

ansText: Macrocytic anemia is the most common hematologic abnormality in RA
expl: A normochromic, normocytic anemia often develops in patients with RA and is the most common hematologic abnormality. Macrocytic anemia may occur in RA due to Methotrexate toxicity. Flexor tenosynovitis can occur in RA. It causes trigger fingers. The most common tendon involved is Flexor Pollicis Longus. The age of onset of RA is between 25 to 55 years of age, after which it plateaus until the age of 75 , after which it decreases. The most common pattern of involvement is symmetrical, polyarthritis. DIP is usually not involved, but if so, it is often due to OA. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:358 Pg:2753

text: Which of the following denotes normal cardiac axis?
expl: The cardiac axis represents the overall direction of electrical activity as it spreads through the cardiac conduction system The normal cardiac axis is directed downward and slightly to the left. It falls within the range of -30° to +90°. Left Axis Deviation (LAD): When the QRS axis is less than -30°. Right Axis Deviation (RAD): When the QRS axis is greater than +90°. Extreme Axis Deviation: Occurs when the QRS axis lies between -90° and 180° ("Northwest Axis") Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1870

text: Which of the following is caused by a lesion of the occipital lobe?
expl: Lesions of the frontal lobe include difficulties with task sequencing and executive skills: Expressive aphasia (receptive aphasias a temporal lobe lesion) Primitive reflexes Perseveration (repeatedly asking the same question or performing the same task) Anosmia Changes in personality. Lesions of the parietal lobe include : Apraxias Neglect Astereognosis (unable to recognise an object by feeling it) Visual field defects (typically homonymous inferior quadrantanopia). They may also cause acalculia (inability to perform mental arithmetic). Lesions of the temporal lobe cause: Visual field defects (typically homonymous superior quadrantanopia) Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia Auditory agnosia Memory impairment. Occipital lobe lesions include: Cortical blindness (blindness due to damage to the visual cortex and may present as Anton syndrome where there is blindness but the patient is unaware or denies blindness) Homonymous hemianopia Visual agnosia (seeing but not perceiving objects - it is different from neglect, since in agnosia the objects are seen and followed but cannot be named). text: In some individuals, peptic ulcers do not develop despite the presence of Helicobacter pylori. This is most likely due to:

options.A: NSAIDs causing ulceration independent of H. pylori
options.B: Variation in host and bacterial virulence factors
options.C: Colonization limited to the antrum in asymptomatic individuals
options.D: All strains of H. pylori being non-ulcerogenic in certain hosts

ansText: Variation in host and bacterial virulence factors
expl: Explanation: The development of peptic ulcer disease in a person infected with Helicobacter pylori is not inevitable; it reflects a complex interaction between the bacterium's properties, the host's response, and environmental cofactors. Some H. pylori strains carry virulence determinants (for example, the cag pathogenicity island including cagA , cytotoxin-associated vacA genotypes, adhesins such as babA ) that provoke a stronger inflammatory response, more mucosal damage and a higher risk of ulcers. At the same time, host factors - including genetic polymorphisms in cytokine genes (e.g., IL-1β , TNF-α, IL-10), patterns of gastric acid secretion, and the effectiveness of mucosal defence (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins) - alter how much damage a given bacterial insult produces. Thus, an infected person with a less virulent strain and/or a host genetic profile that limits inflammation or preserves mucosal defence may remain asymptomatic and ulcer-free, whereas another with a virulent strain and a pro-inflammatory host genotype may develop ulcers. Explanation for other Options: NSAIDs causing ulceration independent of H. pylori (Option A): This is true as a separate statement: NSAIDs can produce ulcers by inhibiting cyclooxygenase and lowering mucosal prostaglandins, so they can cause ulcers regardless of H. pylori status. However, this statement does not explain why some H. pylori-infected people do not develop ulcers; it only describes an alternate cause of ulcers. Colonization limited to the antrum in asymptomatic individuals (Option C): Antral infection can actually increase acid secretion and ulcer risk, so location alone is not protective. All strains of H. pylori being non-ulcerogenic in certain hosts (Option D): Many strains carry virulence genes; it is the interaction between host factors and bacterial virulence, not a universal lack of pathogenicity, that explains differing outcomes.

text: A 24-year-old patient is admitted after falling asleep drunk in a toilet cubicle. On examination his BP 130/70, pulse 98 bpm and there is no pericardial rub. There is 'boggy' tenderness of his right calf and both thigh muscles. Biochemistry reveals urea 125 mg/dl, creatinine 4.0 mg/dl, bicarbonate 15 mmol/l, pH 7.1, potassium 7.8 mmol/l and creatine kinase 17 000 IU/l. text: An 18-year-old girl presents with intermittent weakness and feelings of tiredness. Her family physician requested some blood tests and found her to have a potassium level of 2.8 mmol/l and a bicarbonate of 32 mmol/l. She is normotensive. You arrange a renin and aldosterone level, and both are elevated. Urinary calcium excretion is elevated. Urinary diuretic screen is negative. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
expl: The patient has increased urinary calcium excretion, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis and raised renin and angiotensin levels suggestive of Bartter syndrome. This is not Conn's syndrome because the patient is normotensive and both her renin and angiotensin levels are raised. Bartter's syndrome is due to a mutation in the Na+-K+-2Cl- co-transporter, the ATP-regulated potassium channel, or the kidney-specific basolateral chloride channel. This impairs sodium and chloride reabsorption, and causes an increase in the production of renal prostaglandin E2. Hyperplasia of the juxtaglomerular apparatus is seen on renal biopsy. Gitelman's syndrome is due to a different mutation, and produces a clinical picture similar to that seen with chronic thiazide administration. It also has hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis in the absence of hypercalciuria. Liddle's syndrome is characterised by potassium wasting and hypertension with suppresssed renin and aldosterone levels. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 350

text: A child is brought to the emergency department with a history of ingesting 10-20 ferrous sulfate tablets. Arterial blood gas analysis shows acidosis. Which of the following agents can be used in the management of this condition?
expl: Explanation: The presentation is consistent with acute iron poisoning , typically seen after ingestion of large amounts of ferrous sulfate. Clinical consequences include gastrointestinal upset (vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain), metabolic acidosis , and in severe cases, multi-organ failure and death. Deferoxamine (Desferrioxamine): Drug of choice for iron toxicity. Chelates free circulating iron to form ferrioxamine, which is then eliminated via urine. Administered IM or IV in severe cases. Side effects: Skin rash, urticaria, pruritus, wheals, and in rare situations, anaphylaxis. The urine may become reddish-brown due to ferrioxamine excretion. Explanation of Other Options: Activated Charcoal (Option B): While useful in binding many drugs/toxins (e.g., carbamazepine, dapsone, barbiturates, quinine), it does not bind iron effectively , and therefore has no role in iron poisoning . Dimercaprol (Option C): A chelating agent effective against arsenic, mercury, gold, and lead . It has no efficacy in iron overdose . Penicillamine (Option D): Used as a chelator in copper poisoning (e.g., Wilson's disease) and in some cases of lead or mercury toxicity , but ineffective for iron . Key Takeaways: Deferoxamine is the definitive antidote for severe iron poisoning. Activated charcoal is ineffective in iron toxicity. Dimercaprol and penicillamine are chelators for other heavy metals but not for iron . Early recognition and treatment are critical to prevent multi-organ failure .

text: A 52 year old lady complains of epigastric burning pains due to stress. She finally undergoes an UGI endoscopy which shows gastro-oesophageal reflux. Which medication is the most effective for her condition?
expl: The main pharmacological therapy for GERD is inhibition of gastric acid suppression . Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, lansoprazole and pantoprazole are more effective than H2 receptor blockers such as ranitidine, cimetidine or nizatidine. Healing in oesophagitis is better with a PPI. Bismuth is a mucosal protective agent used in the treatment of peptic ulcer disease. Magnesium hydroxide is an antacid. It is not as effective as PPI for GERD. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2429-2431

text: A patient with no comorbidities presents with serum K+ of 3.0 mmol/L and a normal ECG. What is the preferred treatment?
expl: Explanation: The patient has moderate, asymptomatic hypokalemia (K+ 3.0 mmol/L) with a normal ECG , indicating no immediate life-threatening conduction abnormalities. Oral potassium replacement (e.g., Potassium Chloride solution/powder) is safer than intravenous (IV) administration, carrying no risk of phlebitis or sudden hyperkalemia from infusion error. It is highly effective for correcting chronic deficits when the patient is stable and can tolerate oral intake. Standard management protocols recommend oral repletion for stable patients with moderate hypokalemia and no warning signs (e.g., ECG changes, muscle weakness, arrhythmias). Explanation of other options: Calcium gluconate (Option A): This is a cardioprotective agent used in the emergency treatment of severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes, to stabilize the cardiac membrane. It is contraindicated here. Sodium bicarbonate (Option B): This is used to correct metabolic acidosis and can also be used to shift potassium intracellularly in the treatment of hyperkalemia . Insulin with dextrose (Option D): This combination is used to drive potassium into cells as a temporizing measure for severe hyperkalemia . Key Takeaways: Oral potassium chloride is the first-line treatment for stable, asymptomatic hypokalemia. IV potassium is reserved for severe hypokalemia ( References: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482465/

text: Which of the following drugs is employed in the management of tumour lysis syndrome (TLS)?
expl: Explanation: Tumor lysis syndrome occurs due to massive breakdown of malignant cells during chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or immunotherapy. This leads to release of potassium, phosphate, and uric acid into circulation. High uric acid precipitates in the renal tubules causing renal failure . Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase enzyme that rapidly converts uric acid into the more soluble allantoin , easily excreted by kidneys, thereby preventing uric acid crystal deposition. Hence, it is the drug of choice in TLS management. Explanation of other options: Rituximab (Option B): Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody used in B-cell malignancies, not for TLS. Gemtuzumab (Option C): Anti-CD33 monoclonal antibody used in acute myeloid leukemia, not indicated in TLS. Alemtuzumab (Option D): Anti-CD52 monoclonal antibody for CLL and lymphomas, not effective in TLS. Key Takeaways: TLS is life-threatening due to renal complications. Rasburicase is the drug of choice in preventing uric acid nephropathy in TLS.

text: A 23-year-old man who lives with his male partner consults you for an opinion. He has suffered anal discharge and pruritus for the past 3 days. There are also some symptoms of dysuria. A urethral smear reveals intracellular diplococci. What is the most likely infectious agent to fit with this clinical picture?
expl: Gonorrhea, a sexually transmitted bacterial infection, may manifest with urethritis, cervicitis, salpingitis or anorectal symptoms. Symptoms in men may be severe and include purulent discharge from the anterior urethra and dysuria, with rectal discharge where anal intercourse has taken place. Symptoms in women are often mild, with urethritis and cervicitis occurring a few days after exposure. In around 20% of cases, uterine invasion may occur with signs and symptoms of endometritis or salpingitis. Inflamed Bartholin's glands may occur. The cause is the Gram-negative intracellular diplococci Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Their presence is diagnostic in male urethral smears, although there is a false-negative rate of 60- 70% in samples from women. Patients should of course also receive screening for other sexually transmitted diseases. Gonorrhoeae should be treated with ceftriaxone 500 mg in a single IM dose plus treatment for chlamydia if infection has not been excluded. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 156 Pg: 1234-1240

text: A 12-year-old girl presents with short stature, webbed neck and primary amenorrhoea.Given the likely clinical diagnosis, which hormone would be most appropriate to treat this condition?
expl: This girl most probably has Turner's syndrome , which is most commonly associated with absence of one X chromosome (XO pattern). Characteristic features in this condition include streak ovaries and absent internal genitalia. Estrogen administration will develop female secondary sex characters and life-long therapy will be required. Growth hormone may be useful for a limited period to increase her height. As the ovaries are absent, pulsatile GnRH and luteinising hormone would be of no use. Progesterone would be useful for inducing withdrawal bleed in females sufficiently treated with estrogen. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3000

text: A 23-year-old student presents for review. She is distressed by the fact that she is overweight and is embarrassed of excessive facial hair. She also notices that she appears to have more generalized body hair than other women. On further history, she can sometimes miss a couple of menses, but pregnancy testing is consistently negative. Her mother apparently had similar problems in her youth, took a while to conceive and now has type-2 diabetes. Testosterone is just above the upper limit of normal range, her LH:FSH ratio is increased and prolactin is normal. Which diagnosis fits best with this woman's clinical picture?
expl: PCOS is said to occur in 3% of adult women. Symptoms usually begin around the time of menarche and the diagnosis is often made in adolescence. Obesity is present in around 40% of sufferers and there is an increased association with type-2 diabetes due to insulin resistance. Biochemical abnormalities characteristically include a mildly raised testosterone level and an increased LH: FSH ratio. The cornerstone of management is life style modifications to achieve weigh reduction. The use of OCPs can reduce the androgen levels and help achieve regular menstrual cycles. The anovulation associated with PCOS is treated with ovulation induction agents like Clomiphene citrate and Letrozole Hyperprolactinemia is unlikely as her prolactin is normal. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3036

text: A 24-year-old woman visits her doctor complaining of feeling tired all the time for the last few months. She has amenorrhea for 6 months, and has been feeling dizzy while getting up in the morning. Which of the following clinical signs would the family doctor most likely find if the diagnosis was thought to be Addison's disease?

options.D: Hypertension in supine position with postural hypotension

expl: Hypoadrenalism has many causes including Addison's disease, granulomatous disorders, TB, tumour (particularly lung) or infections (meningococcal septicaemia). Secondary hypoadrenalism is caused by hypopituitarism or hypothalamic disorders. Pallor is present in hypopituitarism due to normochromic, normocytic anemia and a lack of melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH; cleaved from the precursor of ACTH). Secondary AI differs from Addison disease in that it lacks the hyperpigmentation, and aldosterone production is spared as it is regulated by RAAS rather than ACTH. Buccal pigmentation is also associated with glucocorticoid deficiency, most commonly from Addison's disease. ACTH is elevated in Addison's disease and results in higher levels of MSH, which causes the skin and buccal pigmentation found in this condition. Lack of body hair and amenorrhoea are features of hypogonadism in hypopituitarism. Postural hypotension is related to glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency and is more common in primary than secondary AI. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Edition, Page Number-2971.

text: What is the probable diagnosis for an overweight elderly man who arrived at the emergency department with intense chest pain lasting for two hours? He also experienced excessive sweating, pain in the left arm, nausea, and one instance of vomiting. During examination, his pulse rate was recorded as 58 beats per minute and his blood pressure was 90/60 mm of Hg. An electrocardiogram (ECG) was conducted and revealed the following results. Additionally, the patient's cardiac biomarkers indicated increased troponin levels.
expl: Explanation: The clinical presentation is classic for an acute Inferior Wall Myocardial Infarction (MI) . Key indicators include: Symptoms: Typical ischemic chest pain with autonomic features (sweating, nausea, vomiting). ECG: ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF) . Hemodynamics: Bradycardia and hypotension can occur due to vagal stimulation or right ventricular involvement, which is common in inferior MIs. Biomarkers: Elevated troponin confirms myocardial necrosis. Explanation of other options: Anterior wall MI (Option A): Presents with ST-elevation in precordial leads V1-V4. Posterior wall MI (Option C): Typically shows ST-depression in V1-V4 with a tall R wave; it is often associated with an inferior or lateral MI. Pericarditis (Option D): Causes diffuse ST-elevation (often concave up) in multiple leads not following a vascular territory, and PR segment depression is common. text: A patient presents to the OPD with a history of diarrhoea after consuming a salad. What is the most likely organism responsible for this illness?
expl: Explanation: Staphylococcus aureus causes food poisoning due to ingestion of preformed enterotoxin , often found in improperly stored salads, dairy products, and bakery foods . The illness is characterised by a rapid onset (1-6 hours) of vomiting, abdominal cramps, and sometimes diarrhoea . Because the toxin is preformed, antibiotics are not useful; management is supportive. Explanation of other options: Bacillus cereus (Option B): Classically linked to reheated rice ("fried rice syndrome"), not fresh salads. Vibrio cholerae (Option C): Causes profuse watery diarrhoea (rice-water stools) due to contaminated water/seafood, not typically linked to salads. Salmonella enteritidis (Option D): Causes invasive gastroenteritis with fever, abdominal cramps, and diarrhoea after contaminated poultry/eggs; onset is slower (12-72 hours).

text: With respect to gastric carcinoma, which of the following statements is true?

options.A: Aspirin use is a risk factor for gastric carcinoma
options.B: Early diagnosis of gastric carcinoma results in a five year survival rate of 20%
options.C: Endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning for local tumour staging
options.D: Helicobacter pylori infection is not associated with gastric carcinoma

ansText: Endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning for local tumour staging
expl: Incidence of distal stomach tumors is actually decreasing while the incidence of tumors in the proximal stomach is increasing. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use is associated with decreased risk of certain gastric tumors. pylori infection has been associated in a number of studies with increased risk of gastric carcinoma. Screening for gastric carcinoma in Japan detects up to 40% of gastric carcinomas at an early stage and in skilled hands five year survival can be upwards of 90%. Computed tomography (CT) with gastric dilatation is a useful complementary investigation in the staging of gastric carcinoma, but endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning as it is able to assess depth of infiltration and lymphatic dissemination of tumor. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 80, Pg: 629-632

text: Which of the following pharmacological agents is most likely to benefit a patient with angina due to cardiac syndrome X?
expl: Nitrates are often effective in patients with syndrome X, which is currently termed 'microvascular angina'. text: A patient is diagnosed with an ileal tumor, with elevated urinary 5-HIAA levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Carcinoid tumors arise from enterochromaffin (neuroendocrine) cells of the GI tract. They produce serotonin, metabolized to 5-HIAA in urine. Elevated urinary 5-HIAA is a diagnostic marker. Common sites: GI tract (small intestine, appendix, rectum), lungs. Clinical features: Local symptoms: obstruction, bleeding. Carcinoid syndrome (with metastasis): flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm, right-sided valvular heart disease. Diagnosis: Urinary 5-HIAA, chromogranin A, imaging with PET/Octreoscan, histopathology (synaptophysin+, chromogranin+). Management: Surgery; medical control with somatostatin analogs (octreotide). Liver metastasis → embolization, RFA. Explanation of other options: Neuroblastoma (Option B): Pediatric tumor, presents with abdominal mass and systemic features. Leiomyoma (Option C): Benign smooth muscle tumor, no 5-HIAA secretion. Chromaffinoma (Option D): Pheochromocytoma, secretes catecholamines, not serotonin. Key Takeaways: Carcinoid tumors → serotonin → urinary 5-HIAA. Classic carcinoid syndrome occurs after hepatic metastasis .

text: Which of the following is caused by a lesion of the parietal lobe?
expl: Lesions of the frontal lobe include: Difficulties with task sequencing and executive skills Expressive aphasia (receptive aphasia, a temporal lobe lesion) Primitive reflexes Perseveration (repeatedly asking the same question or performing the same task) Anosmia Changes in personality. Lesions of the parietal lobe include Apraxias Neglect Astereognosis (unable to recognise an object by feeling it) Visual field defects (typically homonymous inferior quadrantanopia). They may also cause acalculia (inability to perform mental arithmetic). Lesions of the temporal lobe cause Visual field defects (typically homonymous superior quadrantanopia) Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia Auditory agnosia Memory impairment. Occipital lobe lesions include Cortical blindness (blindness due to damage to the visual cortex and may present as Anton syndrome where there is blindness but the patient is unaware or denies blindness) Homonymous hemianopia Visual agnosia (seeing but not perceiving objects - it is different to neglect since in agnosia the objects are seen and followed but cannot be named). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3326-3328

text: What is the most probable diagnosis in an adult presenting with a pulsatile swelling in the neck, located below the angle of the jaw, showing an outward expansile impulse on examination, as confirmed by MRI angiography findings?
expl: Explanation: In this case, the presence of a pulsatile neck swelling along with the MRI angiography finding of Lyre's sign-which is the splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries-is diagnostic of a carotid body tumor. Carotid Body Tumor (CBT): Also known as paraganglioma or chemodectoma, CBT is a rare benign tumor arising from neural crest cells located in the adventitia at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery. CBTs typically grow slowly, have a low malignancy rate, and show no strong predilection for age or sex, although some studies suggest a slight female predominance. The exact cause is unclear but has been linked to chronic hypoxia and mutations in mitochondrial oxygen-sensing genes. Diagnosis: B-mode Ultrasonography: Reveals solid, hypoechoic masses adjacent to blood vessels. Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA): Demonstrates the tumor's blood supply and arterial displacement with nearly 100% diagnostic accuracy. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI): Shows a mass at the carotid artery bifurcation compressing and displacing the arteries. Tumors typically appear round or oval with heterogeneous or high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. The classic Lyre sign, representing the arterial splaying, is commonly seen on angiographic studies and can also be identified on CT angiography. Treatment: Surgical Removal: The primary and most effective treatment for carotid body tumors. Other Options: Radiotherapy, embolization, or a combination of therapies may be considered depending on the case. Explanation for other options: Grave's disease (Option A): is a hyperthyroid disorder characterized by protruding eyes, but the neck swelling in this condition is not pulsatile. Branchial cysts (Option B): are small, fluid-filled sacs that appear as lumps on the side of the neck and are more frequently seen in children than in adults. A thymic cyst (Option C): is a benign condition affecting the mediastinum and typically presents with symptoms such as shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8748146/ https://radiopaedia.org/articles/lyre-sign-carotid-artery

text: A patient has marked dizziness and unsteadiness during walking. On examination, he has a left sided Horner's syndrome and left sided ataxia. There is loss of sensation to pinprick on the right side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion

expl: The question describes the typical presentation of Lateral Medullary Syndrome Embolic occlusion or thrombosis of a V4 segment causes ischemia of the lateral medulla. The constellation of vertigo, numbness of the ipsilateral face and contralateral limbs, diplopia, hoarseness, dysarthria, dysphagia, and ipsilateral Horner's syndrome is called the lateral medullary (or Wallenberg's) syndrome. Ipsilateral upper motor neuron facial weakness can also occur. Most cases result from ipsilateral vertebral artery occlusion; in the remainder, PICA occlusion is responsible. Occlusion of the medullary penetrating branches of the vertebral artery or PICA results in partial syndromes. Hemiparesis is not a typical feature of vertebral artery occlusion; however, quadriparesis may result from occlusion of the anterior spinal artery. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3330

text: Infarctions secondary to low flow in the "watershed" between the distal PCA and MCA territories, as occurs after cardiac arrest is seen in which of the following?
expl: Bilateral visual association area lesions may result in Balint’s syndrome, a disorder of the orderly visual scanning of the environment, usually resulting from infarctions secondary to low flow in the “watershed” between the distal PCA and MCA territories, as occurs after cardiac arrest. Patients may experience persistence of a visual image for several minutes despite gazing at another scene (palinopsia) or an inability to synthesize the whole of an image (asimultagnosia). Anton’s syndrome occurs due to bilateral occlusion of distal posterior cerebral arteries. It produces cortical blindness (blindness with preserved pupillary light reaction). The patient is often unaware of the blindness or may even deny it. Wallenberg’s syndrome is lateral medullary syndrome which occurs due to occlusion of vertebral arteries. It results in acute onset ataxia, dizziness, Horner's syndrome and contralateral sensory loss. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Chapter:426 page number:3329

text: A patient presented with acute chest pain radiating to the left shoulder. An ECG was performed which showed ST elevations in leads II, III, and aVF. What is the probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF is diagnostic of an Inferior wall Myocardial Infarction . These leads correspond to the inferior wall of the left ventricle , which is usually supplied by the right coronary artery (RCA) (occasionally the left circumflex artery). Clinical features often include chest pain , radiation to left shoulder/jaw , bradyarrhythmias , or hypotension due to RCA involvement affecting the SA/AV nodes. Explanation of Incorrect Options Lateral wall MI (Option B): ST elevation occurs in leads I, aVL, V5, and V6 , not in II, III, aVF. Usually supplied by the left circumflex artery . Anterior wall MI (Option C): ST elevation is seen in precordial leads V1-V4 , indicating LAD artery involvement. Not the pattern described in this case. Posterior wall MI (Option D): Characterized by ST depression in V1-V3 with tall R waves, or reciprocal ST elevation in posterior leads V7-V9 . Not consistent with ST elevation in II, III, aVF.

text: An elderly woman came with a weight loss of 6 kg over 6 months and increased fatigue and prostration during febrile episodes. Investigation showed lowFree T3, low Free T4 and low TSH. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: The patient is likely to be suffering from multiple pituitary hormone deficieny. Low T3 and T4 in the presence of low TSH suggests central hypothyroidism. Isolated secondary hypothyroidism would not usually be associated with weight loss. Presence of significant weight loss and excessive fatigue during febrile episodes is suggestive of coexistent secondary adrenal insufficiency. Low cortisol and ACTH values would confirm the same. The investigation of choice to elucidate the cause is MRI of the pituitary fossa to exclude a pituitary tumor. Addison disease refers to primary AI and it may be associated with high TSH levels. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2898

text: A patient presents with lethargy, increased sleep, and weight gain. Lab values show low plasma TSH, low T3, and low T4. After TRH administration, TSH levels increase. Which condition is likely?

options.A: Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
options.B: Hypothyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
options.C: Hypothyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
options.D: Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus

ansText: Hypothyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
expl: Explanation: The lab profile (low T3, T4) confirms hypothyroidism (Option A and D ruled out) . The key to localization is the TSH response to TRH. Low TSH with Low T4: Indicates a problem at the pituitary or hypothalamus (secondary/tertiary hypothyroidism), not the thyroid itself (which would have high TSH). Positive TRH Stimulation Test (Increase in TSH): This demonstrates that the pituitary gland is intact and capable of producing TSH when stimulated. Therefore, the defect lies "upstream" in the hypothalamus , which is failing to produce adequate TRH to stimulate the pituitary under normal conditions. This pattern is diagnostic of Tertiary Hypothyroidism due to hypothalamic disease. Clinical Features of Hypothyroidism: Fatigue, weakness and increased sleep Cold intolerance, Weight gain Dry, coarse skin, Hair loss Constipation Depression and cognitive impairment Menstrual irregularities and infertility Bradycardia Myxedema Hoarse voice Carpal tunnel syndrome, Slow reflexes Goiter, Anemia, Hypercholesterolemia Primary hypothyroidism is due to thyroid gland dysfunction causing low thyroid hormones, commonly from Hashimoto's thyroiditis, surgery, radiation, iodine deficiency, medications, or infiltrative diseases. Secondary hypothyroidism results from pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction leading to insufficient TSH, caused by tumors, surgery, Sheehan's syndrome, trauma, or genetic/hypothalamic defects. Labs show high TSH in primary and low/normal TSH in secondary, with low free T3/T4 in both. (Option B ruled out) Clinically, both present with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, constipation, and myxedema, while secondary may have other pituitary hormone deficiencies. Treatment is levothyroxine, guided by TSH in primary and by free T4 in secondary hypothyroidism. Interpretation of thyroid function tests: Key Takeaways: Low T4 + Low/Normal TSH + Positive TRH test = Hypothalamic (Tertiary) Hypothyroidism. Low T4 + Low/Normal TSH + Blunted TRH test = Pituitary (Secondary) Hypothyroidism.

text: You are asked to review a 58-year-old woman who presents with a slowly enlarging hard mass in the anterior neck. Thyroid ultrasound reveals infiltration of the mass to adjacent structures,and biopsy reveal dense fibrous change and no atypical cells. Free T4 is low and her TSH is markedly raised, consistent with hypothyroidism. Thyroid autoantibodies are negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis given this clinical picture?
expl: By the nature of its presentation, Riedel's thyroiditis is often confused with thyroid carcinoma especially the anaplastic variant. It is characterised by marked fibrous infiltration of the thyroid gland, the aetiology of this being as yet unidentified. Treatment is with thyroxine replacement. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is autoimmune in aetiology and is characterised by lymphocytic infiltration and the presence of antimicrosomal antibodies(anti TPO). Grave's disease is associated with thyroid-stimulating autoantibodies and hyperthyroidism. Thyroid ultrasound reveals infiltration but no discrete mass is identified, and biopsy reveal dense fibrous infiltration of the gland. If the patient presents with severe compressive symptoms like dysphagia and dyspnea, then glucocorticoid therapy is useful. Other immunomodulators like mycophenolate and tamoxifen have also been tried. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2944

text: A 44-year-old woman presents to the Emergency department with palpitations and shortness of breath. Recent thyroid function tests on the hospital computer reveal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) of Which of the following findings would be most consistent with Grave's disease?
expl: Compared with normal subjects, hyperthyroid patients show significantly lower resting arterial CO2 tension, tidal volume and significantly higher mean inspiratory flow and pa(O2). This may of course lead to misdiagnosis of patients with hyperthyroidism as having hyperventilation syndrome. Patients with hyperthyroidism also show a greater ventilatory response to hypoxia than normal patients. These ventilatory changes are significantly correlated with T3 levels. text: A 26-year-old woman is referred by her family doctor. She is 10 week's pregnant and complaining of anxiety and an inability to sleep. Total thyroxine (T4) is noted to be 160 nmol/l (normal 70-140) Free T4 is noted to be 27 pmol/l (normal 9-25) thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 0.4 mU/l. Which of the following is the management of choice in this patient?

options.C: Observe and repeat thyroid function tests in 1 month
options.D: Start high dose carbimazole and thyroxine concomitantly

ansText: Observe and repeat thyroid function tests in 1 month
expl: Suppression of TSH is seen in the first trimester in around 10% women, small but transient rises in T3 and T4 are also seen, this is physiological and due to the thyroid-stimulating action of b-human chorionic gonadotrophin (b-HCG). Total T4 rises due to increases in thyroid-binding globulin and again is physiological. A 10-20% increase in thyroid mass also occurs. Physiological suppression of TSH is also seen in 4-5% of women in the second trimester. Maternal hyperthyroidism has an incidence of 0.2%, in women who are in remission from Grave's disease, exacerbation occurs most commonly in the first trimester. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2940

text: A 24-year-old pharmacist is admitted to the Emergency room with a panic attack. On further questioning it transpires that she has been suffering from palpitations and has lost weight over the past 6 months. Her periods stopped 3 months ago. On examination her BP is 145/90 mmHg, pulse is 92/min at rest. Her BMI is 20; the remainder of her clinical examination is unremarkable. Investigations; Hb 13.1 g/dl WCC 4.9 x 10^9/L PLT 145 x 10^9/L TSH Free T4 32 pmol/l Serum thyroglobulin low Decreased thyroid uptake on scintigraphy scan Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The combination of low thyroglobulin, decreased uptake on scintigraphy and raised T4 is suggestive of thyrotoxicosis factitia. Subacute thyroiditis will have neck tenderness with reduced uptake in thyroid scintiography, but elevated serum thyroglobulin. Thyroid scintiography will show diffuse uptake in Grave's disease while multiple areas of focal uptake is seen with toxic MNG. text: A 54-year-old woman complaining of a 4-kg weight gain, dry hair and skin, she feels slow and always has the heating up high. She has a small diffuse goitre. Her TSH level is 20 mU/l . Thyroid peroxidase antibody is positive at high titres. She has two sisters who have had thyroid disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune thyroid disorder found more often in women than men. It is associated with positive thyroid antibodies and there may be a goitre that tends to be diffuse rather than multinodular. The classical antibodies include anti thyroid peroxidase and anti thyroglobulin antibodies. The gland is infiltrated with lymphocytes and patients can become hypothyroid. DeQuervain's thyroiditis is not associated with positive antibodies and tends to present with painful goitre and thyrotoxicosis. Grave's disease is also an autoimmune thyroid disorder but patients have hyperthyroidism and not hypothyroidism. Follicular carcinoma can present with a thyroid swelling but not hypothyroidism. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Pg:2935

text: A 25-year-old male patient came with complaints of palpitations, sweating, and restlessness. He has a complaint of sweaty palms. Clinical findings are depicted in the image given below. What is the diagnostic finding seen in this patient?
expl: Explanation: Thyroid receptor antibodies (TRAb), especially thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI), are diagnostic of Graves' disease, which this patient exhibits. The patient's symptoms-palpitations, sweating, restlessness, and sweaty palms-are classic for hyperthyroidism. The most likely diagnosis is Graves' disease , an autoimmune disorder in which thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) bind to and activate TSH receptors on the thyroid gland. This leads to increased production of T3 and T4, causing hyperthyroid symptoms. In Graves' ophthalmopathy , characteristic signs include: Dalrymple's sign: Upper lid retraction due to Muller's muscle contraction (most common presenting sign) Von Graefe's sign: Lid lag on downward gaze and stare due to poor blinking, often earliest sign Enroth's sign: Lower eyelid fullness/edema Mobius sign: Weak convergence Griffith's sign: Lower lid lag on upward gaze Stellwag's sign: Infrequent/incomplete blinking Joffroy's sign: Absent forehead wrinkling on upward gaze Gellineck's sign: Hyperpigmentation of the eyelids Diagnosis is confirmed by: Elevated TSI or TRAb levels Thyroid function tests showing elevated T3/T4 and suppressed TSH Radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU): Increased in Graves' Management includes: Antithyroid drugs (Methimazole or PTU) Radioactive iodine ablation Surgery for large goiters or resistant cases Graves' ophthalmopathy: Corticosteroids, radiotherapy, or orbital decompression in severe cases Explanation of other options: Anti-thyroglobulin antibody (Option A): Commonly elevated in autoimmune hypothyroidism like Hashimoto's, not specific for Graves'. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody (Option B): Typically seen in Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Elevated ultrasensitive thyrotropin (TSH) levels (Option D): TSH is suppressed in hyperthyroid states like Graves'- disease due to negative feedback. text: A 36-year-old man with Grave's disease is being considered for subtotal thyroidectomy. What is the most common postoperative complication following this operation?
expl: Hypothyroidism occurs in about 10% of such patients within 1 year of surgery. This percentage increases with time and a high proportion of patients become hypothyroid in the long term. Laryngeal nerve palsy occurs in 1% of cases. Transient hypocalcaemia occurs in up to 10% of patients, but permanent hypoparathyroidism is seen in less than 1% of patients. Recurrent hyperthyroidism occurs in 1-3% of cases within 1 year and 1% per year thereafter. Early postoperative bleeding may cause tracheal compression. This is a rare complication. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2940-43

text: A 34-year-old man comes to the clinic complaining of tiredness, lethargy and an increasingly hoarse voice. He also tells you that he has been losing his hair over the past few months and has noticed fullness in his neck; he has gained 7kg in the past 3 months. On examination he has a puffy face and periorbital oedema and there is a firm, rubbery goitre. His pulse is 48/min and regular, his BP 142/73 mmHg. Investigations; TSH 70.1 U/l Total cholesterol 320 mg/dl Triglycerides 290 mg/dl LDL 150 mg/dl FNA thyroid Diffuse lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The features seen here are typical of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is autoimmune in aetiology and is characterised by lymphocytic infiltration and the presence of antimicrosomal (TPO) antibodies. De Quervain's thyroiditis is a self-limiting inflammatory disease of the thyroid gland that presents with pain and sore throat. It is not associated with positive antibodies and tends to present with painful swelling in the neck. Atrophic hypothyroidism is an organ-specific autoimmune disease with thyroid autoantibodies, functional hypothyroidism and absence of goiter. Usually seen in elderly women between 40-60 age groups. Grave's disease is associated with thyroid-stimulating autoantibodies and hyperthyroidism. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition page 2935

text: A 32-year-old woman with relapsed Grave's disease. TSH is less than 0.05 mU/l, with a Free T4 of 32.5 pmol/l(9-20). Which of the following statements best fits the management of her thyroid eye disease?

options.A: Systemic steroids are of no value in managing the eye disease
options.B: Orbital irradiation is commonly used to treat thyroid eye disease
options.C: Corrective eye muscle surgery should now be considered

ansText: Her thyroid eye disease may be worsened by radioiodine treatment
expl: Exacerbation of thyroid eye disease is more common after radioiodine treatment IV glucocorticoids are the mainstay in patients with severe inflammatory changes. text: A patient with Addison's disease presents with an acute onset of diarrhea and vomiting. He currently takes fludrocortisone and hydrocortisone. What is the most appropriate management?
expl: Patients receiving glucocorticoid replacement therapy should be advised to double the dose in the event of intercurrent febrile illness, accident, or mental stress such as an important examination. If the patient is vomiting and cannot take by mouth, parenteral hydrocortisone must be given urgently, as indicated above. There is no need to increase fludrocortisone dose during stress / inter current illness For minor surgery, 50-100 mg of hydrocortisone IV is given with the premedication. For major procedures this is then followed by the same regimen as for acute adrenal insufficiency. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2972

text: Addison's disease is characterized by all of the following symptoms except?
expl: Explanation: Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) is characterized by a deficiency of both cortisol and aldosterone. The symptoms listed are consequences of these hormonal deficits, making Hyperglycemia the exception . Pathophysiology of Symptoms Cortisol Deficiency: Leads to hypoglycemia (due to impaired gluconeogenesis), not hyperglycemia. It also contributes to weakness, weight loss, and hypotension. Aldosterone Deficiency: Causes renal sodium wasting ( hyponatremia ) and potassium retention ( hyperkalemia ). (Oprion B and D ruled out) Combined Effect: The loss of both hormones' permissive effects on vascular tone and volume contributes to hypotension . (Option D ruled out) ACTH excess causes Pigmentation Adrenal androgen insufficiency results in Decreased body hair and loss of libido, especially in females Key Takeaways: Addison's disease typically presents with hypoglycemia , hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension. Hyperglycemia is suggestive of diabetes or Cushing's syndrome (cortisol excess).

text: A 44-year-old with a history of travel presented with fever, mild bloody diarrhea which had lasted for two weeks. He had lost 2.5 kg in weight, had occasional lower abdominal cramping discomfort and a painful swelling of his left knee. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Campylobacter infection is one of the commonest causes of inflammatory diarrhea. Abdominal pain is often a prominent feature of the illness frequently localizing to the right iliac fossa. Diarrhea may be mild or very severe often with passage of blood. Symptoms may last a week or longer. Reactive arthritis and Reiter's syndrome can develop following infection with a number of enteric pathogens including Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter and Yersinia. Amoebiasis : presents with a gradual onset of lower abdominal pain and mild diarrhea is followed by malaise, weight loss, and diffuse lower abdominal or back pain. Cecal involvement may mimic acute appendicitis. Patients with full-blown dysentery may pass 10-12 stools per day. The stools contain little fecal material and consist mainly of blood and mucus. In contrast to those with bacterial diarrhea, fewer than 40% of patients with amebic dysentery are febrile. Virtually all patients have heme-positive stools. Crohn's disease is a cause of chronic diarrhea which is in contrast to the case given Gonococcal sepsis will cause prominent constitutional features with a maculopapular rash and may complicate to cause adrenal insufficiency. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 133, Pg: 1065

text: In treatment of Cushing's disease, which of the following drugs is useful?
expl: In Cushing's disease, steroidogenic inhibitors are used in combination with pituitary irradiation to block the adrenal effects of persistently high ACTH levels. Ketoconazole is an antimycotic drug that inhibits several P450 enzymes involved in adrenal steroidogenesis. Metyrapone inhibits 11 beta-hydroxylase activities & Mitotane suppresses cortisol hypersecretion by inhibiting 11 beta-hydroxylase and cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzymes & by destroying adrenocortical cells. Drugs acting at the level of pituitary to reduce ACTH include Pasireotide and Cabergoline Drugs that block cortisol action on receptor include Mifepristone. text: In a 60-year-old man, what is the most common underlying cause of Cushing's disease?
expl: Explanation: In a 60-year-old man, Cushing's disease is usually the result of a pituitary microadenoma . Cushing's disease is defined by a benign pituitary tumor that secretes ACTH, causing hypercortisolism due to excess ACTH release. This overproduction drives the adrenal glands to secrete elevated amounts of cortisol, producing the typical manifestations of Cushing's syndrome. Explanations of other options: Small-cell lung cancer (Option A): Small cell lung carcinoma may secrete ACTH or ACTH-like peptides, leading to paraneoplastic Cushing's syndrome. However, it is not the usual cause of Cushing's disease in older individuals. This cancer often presents with respiratory complaints and a faster development of hypercortisolism signs. Adrenal tumor (Option B): Adrenal tumors, whether adenomas or carcinomas, may lead to Cushing's syndrome by producing cortisol independently. Unlike pituitary microadenomas, which cause high ACTH levels, these adrenal tumors bypass the pituitary-adrenal axis and usually result in suppressed ACTH. Ectopic ACTH syndrome (Option C): Ectopic ACTH syndrome arises when tumors outside the pituitary, such as those in the lung, pancreas, or thymus, secrete ACTH. Although it can lead to Cushing's syndrome, it is less frequent than pituitary microadenomas as the main cause of Cushing's disease in elderly patients. This form usually presents with a faster onset and more pronounced metabolic disturbances.

text: A 45-year-old man presents with proximal muscle weakness, purple stretch marks, central obesity, and easy bruising. What is the underlying condition?

text: In comparison to a normal healthy person in the evening time. Which of these will not have an elevated cortisol?

options.A: Normal healthy person in the morning

ansText: Normal healthy person in the morning
expl: Normal circadian rhythm of ACTH starts to rise early in the morning prior to awakening, reaches a peak in the morning and levels will fall by evening. Reduction in ACTH pulse occurs between 6PM and midnight. Cortisol secretion increases in response to stress like hypotension, hypoglycemia, exercise, fever, surgery and burns. In cushing's disease, the ACTH pulse frequency and amplitude is increased and hence the cortisol response and hence the circadian rhythm is lost.

text: A 44-year-old man presents with a six month history of diarrhea and abdominal cramps. On further questioning it appears he has also noticed facial flushing. On examination there is wheeze on auscultation of his chest and abdominal examination reveals hepatomegaly. Which of the following investigations would confirm the likely diagnosis?
expl: This patient has carcinoid syndrome . The diagnosis is made by 24-hour urine collection for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) -excretion is greater than 0.3 mmol. Forty five per cent of carcinoid tumors arise in the appendix, 30% arise in the small bowel and 20% in the rectum. Most patients with carcinoid syndrome have liver metastases. 5-HT, kinins, prostaglandins and other vasoactive substances are secreted. Clinical features of carcinoid syndrome include diarrhea and abdominal cramps in the majority of patients.Flushing, which is often provoked by alcohol, bronchoconstriction and cardiac involvement with tricuspid or pulmonary incompetence are also features. Diagnosis also includes chest x ray, abdominal ultrasound scan, small bowel radiology and echocardiography to establish the extent of disease. Surgical resection of the primary tumor is possible in some cases; octreotide is the treatment of choice. In the majority of cases of Wilson's disease 24-hour urinary copper is greater than 3 micromol . In Cushing's syndrome 24-hour urinary free cortisol is elevated. Nephrotic syndrome is defined as proteinuria greater than 3.5 g/1.75 m2 of body surface per 24 hours, hypoalbuminemia and oedema. Screening for pheochromocytoma can be performed by 24-hour urine collection for 4-OH-3-methoxymandelate (HMMA, VMA). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 84, Pg:669

text: Which of the following statements is correct concerning the relationship between type 2 diabetes and colonic cancer?

options.A: Increased concentrations of C peptide are a marker of increased colorectal cancer risk
options.B: Insulin treatment increases recurrence free survival after treatment of colonic cancer
options.C: The increased risk of colorectal cancer in diabetes is related to BMI
options.D: The increased risk of colorectal cancer in diabetes is related to total cholesterol

ansText: Increased concentrations of C peptide are a marker of increased colorectal cancer risk
expl: Type 2 diabetes is associated with a 40-60% increase in the risk of cancer of the large bowel. This increase is linked to changes in HbA1c. Type 2 diabetes is associated with significantly higher rates of overall mortality and reduced disease free and recurrence free survival after chemotherapy/radiotherapy, and insulin has not been shown to have any effects on mortality. No association has been found between colonic malignancy and type 1 diabetes, nor gestational diabetes. A number of studies have independently linked high circulating concentrations of C Peptide, as a marker of insulin production, with increased colorectal cancer risk. The molecular basis has not been proven, but it may be reasonable to extrapolate that it is linked to the growth stimulation effects of insulin. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 81 Pg: 637

text: A 77-year-old male presented with a quadrantic hemianopia. Which of the following conditions is most likely to cause such a presentation?

options.B: A lesion of the optic chiasma

expl: Superior quadrantanopia is seen in temporal lobe lesion . inferior quadrantanopia is seen in parietal lobe lesion. Unilateral occipital lobe lesions (left or right) cause contralateral hemianopia or quadrantanopia, visual agnosia, visual illusions and elementary visual hallucinations. Left occipital lobe lesions cause these symptoms and alexia and colour agnosia. Right occipital lobe lesions cause impaired visual orientation and topographical memory in addition. Bioccipital lesions are rare, but cause cortical blindness, altitudinal hemianopia, impaired colour perception, Anton syndrome and prosopagnosia. A lesion of the optic chiasm would cause a Bitemporal hemianopia. Diabetic retinopathy can rarely cause an 'apparent quadrantic hemianopia' because the distribution of the retinal changes may just correspond to quadrantic hemianopia - but this is not the most likely. Tobacco amblyopia causes symmetric central or centrocecal scotomas. Chloroquine poisoning causes symmetric bilateral scotomas. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 219

text: A 54-year-old diabetic man presents with malaise and loss of libido. On examination there is evidence of hepatomegaly. Blood tests show Hb 14.1 g/dl (13-18), fasting glucose 144 mg/dl, serum iron 45 mmol/l (14-29) and serum ferritin 250,000 mmol/l (15-200). What would be the most appropriate treatment for his symptoms?
expl: This patient most probably has hereditary haemochromatosis which causes hypo gonadotrophic hypogonadism or rarely hyper gonadotropin hypogonadism due to iron deposition in pituitary and testis respectively. Although venesection is the treatment of choice for reducing the iron load, this will not correct testicular atrophy or hypopituitarism, either or both of which may contribute to a loss of libido. Testosterone replacement is used for improvement of symptoms in these patients. Desferrioxamine is indicated in rare cases who cannot tolerate venesection (because of severe cardiac disease or anemia). Insulin therapy would not be helpful in restoring libido. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:407 Page number:2890-82

text: A 35 year old male presents with history of weakness of both the lower limbs of insidious onset, for the past 2 years. He has mild difficulty in swallowing liquids too. There are no sensory symptoms. On examination, he has fasciculations and areflexia. You also notice gynecomastia. He is also undergoing investigation for infertility. What is the likely molecular abnormality be seen in this patient?
expl: The given patient has an LMN type of weakness without any sensory symptoms and with associated androgen insensitivity as evidenced by the gynecomastia and the sub fertility. This is classical of the Spinobulbar muscular atrophy or the Kennedy syndrome. It is an X linked disorder and is associated with CAG trinucleotide repeats on the androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome. CGG trinucleotide repeats is seen in Fragile X syndrome. It is associated with mental retardation. There may be ataxia and ovarian failure associated with it. GAA trinucleotide repeats are seen in Friedrich's Ataxia. CTG trinucleotides are seen in Myotonic dystrophy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 347, Pg: 3415

text: A 29-year-old female with Turner syndrome is referred by the GP concerned about her blood pressure which he has found to be persistently elevated at between 140-160/90 mmHg. On examination she is noted to have a blood pressure of 148/92 mmHg, with no radio-femoral delay and no murmur audible. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hypertension?
expl: Hypertension is quite common in Turner syndrome (10%) and is typically idiopathic i.e. essential hypertension. In a small proportion of cases, causes can include coarctation of the aorta and renal dysfunction due to horse-shoe kidney. In this case, the absence of specific features of coarctation would make essential hypertension the most appropriate option. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:271 pg:1896

text: A tall male presents with absent pubic and axillary hair, infantile genitalia, elevated LH/FSH, and an XXY karyotype. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Klinefelter syndrome results from the presence of an extra X chromosome (47,XXY) in males. It manifests as tall stature, hypogonadism, sparse body hair, gynecomastia, infertility, and small testes. Hormonal evaluation shows low testosterone with high gonadotropins (LH, FSH) . Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype analysis . Explanation of other options: Vanishing testis syndrome (Option A): Characterized by absent testes due to failure of descent, with otherwise normal phenotype and hormonal profile. Noonan syndrome (Option C): Presents with short stature, congenital heart disease, and distinctive facies, not XXY karyotype. Adrenal hyperplasia (Option D): Causes androgen excess, ambiguous genitalia, or early puberty, not hypogonadism with XXY pattern. Key Takeaways: 47,XXY is pathognomonic for Klinefelter's. Clinical triad: tall stature, hypogonadism, infertility .

text: All of the following tests are done for screening in patients with Turner's syndrome, except?
expl: Explanation: Turner syndrome is a genetic condition caused by the complete or partial absence of one X chromosome. Individuals with Turner syndrome require lifelong, multidisciplinary care to monitor and manage associated health complications. The ANA test is not typically performed as part of Turner mosaic screening. ANA testing is primarily used to help diagnose autoimmune conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or other connective tissue diseases. Explanation of other options: Audiometry (Option B): This test is a standard and recurring part of care. Individuals with Turner syndrome have a very high prevalence of hearing issues, including conductive hearing loss from frequent otitis media and sensorineural hearing loss . Therefore, serial audiology evaluations are mandated throughout their lifespan. Echocardiography (Option C): This is a critical and mandatory screening tool, not an exception. Cardiovascular anomalies are among the most serious complications of Turner syndrome. An echocardiogram is required to diagnose and monitor conditions like bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta, and aortic dilation/ dissection , which are significant causes of morbidity and require ongoing surveillance. Fasting Blood Glucose (Option D): Screening for metabolic disorders is a standard practice. Due to an increased risk of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes , regular assessment of fasting glucose (and often hemoglobin A1c) is a core part of the annual health evaluation for adolescents and adults with Turner syndrome. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK554621/

text: True with respect to the tumour lysis syndrome (TLS):

options.A: High-dose intravenous steroid therapy is a reasonable initial treatment option.
options.B: TLS is most commonly associated with squamous cell and neuroendocrine tumours.
options.C: Clinical TLS can be diagnosed in a patient with seizures and the presence of appropriate laboratory findings.
options.D: An increase in serum calcium and potassium levels by >25% is the hallmark feature of laboratory TLS.

ansText: Clinical TLS can be diagnosed in a patient with seizures and the presence of appropriate laboratory findings.
expl: Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is a potentially life-threatening complication of massive cellular lysis in cancer, often encountered in bulky, rapidly progressive or chemo-sensitive tumours. It is most commonly seen in haematological malignancy. Hypocalcaemia is a hallmark feature due to precipitation of ionised calcium with phosphate, which is released in large quantities in tumour lysis. Other laboratory features of TLS include: increase in serum uric acid by >25% from baseline; increase in serum potassium by >25% from baseline; increase in serum phosphate by >25% from baseline. Intravenous hydration and rasburicase are first-line treatments and prophylaxis agents in high-risk groups. Reference: Harrison 20 th 2103,3001

text: You got a reference from the Surgical dept to see a 36-year-old woman on the surgical ward who is 2 days' post-thyroidectomy. She is complaining of tingling around her mouth and in her hands and has developed a spasm of her hands. What immediate treatment can you give that is most likely to resolve her symptoms?

options.A: Ask her to breathe into a paper bag

expl: Postoperative complications of thyroidectomy include recurrent laryngeal damage, hemorrhage and inadvertent removal of the parathyroid glands, although actually less than 1% of patients suffer permanent hypocalcemia. The symptoms described are typical of hypocalcemia, although they can be seen in patients who are hyperventilating. The treatment of choice to relieve the acute symptoms is 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate. Hypocalcaemia can be transient after thyroid surgery. If it is permanent then the patient needs long-term therapy with calcium with calcitriol (activated vitamin D) to maintain her calcium levels. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3185

text: A 27-year-old woman is in end-stage renal disease. She has been started on regular haemodialysis. She complains of pain in her fingers. An X-ray shows digital subperiosteal erosions. What is the primary metabolic cause for her bony condition?
expl: Digital sub periosteal resorption is classical of Osteitis fibrosa cystica of hyperparathyroidism. In CKD secondary hyperparathyroidism may progress to tertiary hyperparathyroidism. The series of events that happen in CKD is: Declining GFR leads to reduced excretion of phosphate and thus, phosphate retention The retained phosphate stimulates increased synthesis of both FGF-23 by osteocytes and of PTH and also stimulates growth of parathyroid gland mass PTH production is stimulated by decreased levels of ionized calcium, which in turn, result from decreased levels of renal calcitriol production with reduced kidney mass and suppression of calcitriol production due to phosphate retention and elevated levels of FGF-23, which also increases degradation of calcitriol. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:311, Pg:2313

text: A 30-year-old woman presents with bone pain and abdominal cramps, and her family mentions a history of unusual behaviour. Based on these clinical features, the doctor suspects a diagnosis. Which investigation would be the most suitable to confirm it?
expl: Explanation: The clinical features of bone pain due to excessive bone resorption, abdominal discomfort from elevated calcium levels, and neuropsychiatric manifestations such as behavioural changes point toward primary hyperparathyroidism , for which the preferred imaging modality is a sestamibi scan . Explanation of other options: MRI (Option A): Although MRI can detect soft tissue lesions, it is not the preferred initial imaging technique for identifying parathyroid adenomas, as it is costlier, takes longer, and provides no clear benefit compared to sestamibi scanning in parathyroid evaluation. Ultrasonogram (Option B): Ultrasound can help visualise parathyroid enlargement, but its accuracy is limited by operator skill and difficulty in detecting ectopic glands. It is often used as an adjunctive test rather than the most reliable first-line diagnostic method. CT scan (Option D) : CT scan offers precise anatomical detail but does not provide the functional assessment available with sestamibi scans. Although helpful in preoperative planning, it is not considered the primary imaging method for diagnosing parathyroid adenomas.

text: Which of the following foods is not included in the DASH diet?
expl: Explanation: The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet specifically emphasizes limiting sodium intake . It is designed to be low in sodium while being rich in potassium, calcium, magnesium, and fiber to help lower blood pressure. Developed in 1990s (NIH); lowers systolic BP by 6-11 mmHg. Focuses on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean protein, low-fat dairy, and low sodium (~1500 mg/day). Key Nutrients: Carbs: Whole grains, legumes, greens Fats: Healthy oils, nuts, omega-3 fish; avoid trans fats Proteins: Plant-based preferred, lean meats, low-fat dairy Electrolytes: Potassium (bananas, spinach, beans) - lowers BP Sodium restriction (~1500 mg/day)- reduces HTN risk Calcium (dairy, greens) - bone/muscle health Magnesium (whole grains, nuts, seeds) - vessel relaxation, BP control Clinical Benefits: Lowers BP, glucose, LDL, triglycerides, and insulin resistance; beneficial in metabolic syndrome, diabetes, and HF. Reduces risk of colorectal cancer, liver disease, celiac disease, and improves HF outcomes. Explanation of other options: Rich in potassium ,Rich in calcium and Rich in magnesium (Option A,B and D): The DASH diet encourages the consumption of foods rich in these minerals, such as fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy, and nuts, which are integral to its blood pressure-lowering effects. Key Takeaways: The DASH diet is a low-sodium, high-potassium, high-calcium, and high-magnesium eating plan. Its primary goal is the prevention and management of hypertension.

text: A 74-year-old woman was brought in by her daughter for a complete physical examination. Her complaints include a poor appetite, weight loss, cramps and weakness. She was diagnosed with Crohn's disease 10 years ago but is not taking any medications. Routine evaluation showed a serum calcium of 7 mg/dl with normal phosphate. She has a creatinine of 0.8 mg/dl, albumin is 3.5 g/dl (normal range, 3.7-4.9 g/dl) and alkaline phosphatase is 350 U/l (normal range, 50-200 U/l). Which of the following diagnoses is most compatible with these lab data?
expl: This patient is suffering from Crohn’s disease which most commonly affects the terminal ileum; This interferes with the reabsorption of bile acids leading to steatorrhea, inadequate absorption of fat soluble vitamins and weight loss In vitamin D deficiency, decreased intestinal absorption of calcium leads to secondary hyperparathyroidism, which increases renal tubular loss of phosphate. Vitamin D deficiency can result from inadequate dietary intake, lack of sun exposure and malabsorption in this case due to the long-standing Crohn’s disease. Renal failure impairs 1α hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D, which results in the malabsorption of calcium. The body compensates by increased secretion of PTH, leading to increased mobilization of calcium from bone. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3188

text: A 52-year-old man has effort-related angina. His total cholesterol is 212 mg/dl. He has no other cardiac risk factors and no other relevant medical history. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
expl: The choice of first-line treatment for the prophylaxis of effort-related angina in someone without contraindications is a β-Blocker . β-Blockers also remain the choice in someone who has suffered a previous myocardial infarction. Calcium-channel blockers - especially diltiazem and verapamil can be used, although they should be avoided in the presence of significant left ventricular dysfunction. Nitrates are of good value, but they come after β-Blockers. Care should be taken before combining a β-Blocker and non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker, especially if there is evidence of conduction disturbance or LV dysfunction . The Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study showed that a statin given to patients with angina pectoris and a cholesterol level of 212-308 mg/dl significantly reduced the risk of MI. Aspirin would also of course be recommended for secondary prevention of ischaemic events and nitrates could be used for symptom relief. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2041

text: A 65-year-old man presents with bony pain that has been present for some months, particularly affecting his left femur, pelvis and lower back. Blood testing reveals a normal serum calcium and phosphorous level, but a raised alkaline phosphatase. X-rays of the femur and pelvis reveal mixed lytic and sclerotic change, with accentuated trabecular markings. Chest X-ray is normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Paget's disease is thought to be present in 2% of the population above 55 years of age, with 90% being asymptomatic. It is more common in Caucasian populations and rarer in populations of African descent. There are said to be three phases associated with the time course of radiological changes seen in Paget's disease. primarily lytic mixed lytic and sclerotic changes primarily sclerotic change with increasing bony thickening. The typical named X-ray signs associated with Paget's disease include 'flame sign/blade of grass sign' in long bones, 'ivory vertebra', 'cotton wool skull' and 'Mickey Mouse pelvis' Goals of treatment are to normalize bone turnover, maintain the alkaline phosphatase level within the normal range, minimize symptoms and prevent long-term complications. Bisphosphonates (IV zoledronic acid) is the treatment of choice. Long-term complications include deafness (in up to 50% of patients with skull-base Paget's disease), high output cardiac failure, fractures and very rarely osteogenic sarcoma. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3210

text: A 75-year-old woman was brought to the hospital following a fall. Her neighbour thinks that she was on the floor for about 4 days. Her blood results show: sodium 132 mEq/l, potassium 6.5 mEq/l, urea 110 mg/dl, creatinine 7.3 mg/dl, calcium 7.6 mg/dl, phosphate 7.5 mg/dl.(Ref values: s. creatinine: 0.6-1.4 mg/dl; S. urea: 17 - 43 mg/dL; s. sodium: 135-145 mEq/L; S. potassium: 3.5-5 mEq/L; S. calcium: 8.8 - 10 mg/dl; S. phosphate: 3.0-4.5 mg/dL)Which of the following investigations is most likely to reveal the diagnosis?
expl: The question deals with renal impairment, probably acute, in an elderly woman, who was found unresponsive and who is suspected to have fallen at least 4 days back. Muscle compression due to prolonged immobilization, as in this case will result in release of myoglobin. It is toxic to the renal tubules and will result in AKI. The most likely diagnosis is rhabdomyolysis and acute renal failure. The history is suggestive along with hyperkalemia, hypocalcaemia, and hyperphosphatemia. Serum creatine kinase and myoglobin will be elevated. Other causes of rhabdomyolysis are: Traumatic crush injuries Muscle ischemia during vascular or orthopedic surgery Compression during coma or immobilization Prolonged seizure activity Excessive exercise Heat stroke Malignant hyperthermia Infections Metabolic disorders (e.g., hypophosphatemia, severe hypothyroidism) Myopathies (drug-induced, metabolic, or inflammatory). Urine dipstick will be positive for blood (myoglobinuria) but microscopy will not show red cells. A renal biopsy may also reveal the diagnosis. Treatment is with hydration (normal saline) and alkalinisation of urine with sodium bicarbonate infusion. Option A: Ultrasound is useful only to distinguish obstructive Etiologies and cystic kidney diseases Option B: MRA is useful to assess for renal vascular diseases Option C: A DMSA scan is a radionuclide scan that uses dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) in assessing renal morphology, structure and function Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 310 Pg: 2301
