text: A 30-year-old man has returned from a trip to India recently. He presents with bloody diarrhoea which started three weeks ago. He now has malaise and swelling of his legs. He has poor urine output. Blood tests show: Hb 8 g/dL WBC: 14,000/ µL Neutrophils: 9000/ µL Platelets: 20,000/ µLPT 13s, APTT 33sFibrinogen 4 g/dL, sodium 136 mmol/ L, potassium 6.1 mmol/L, urea 420 mg/dl creatinine 7.8 mg/dl albumin 3 g/dL. Urine dipstick: blood ++, protein +. (Ref values: Hb: 1B-14 g/dl; WBC: 4000-10000/ µL; Platelets: 1.5 to 4.5 lakh/µL; s. creatinine: 0.6-1.4 mg/dl; S. urea: 17 - 43 mg/dL; s. sodium: 135-145 mEq/L; S. potassium: 3.5-5 mEq /L; S. calcium: 8.8 - 10 mg/dl; S. phosphate: 3.0-4.5 mg/dL; S. albumin: 3.5 -5 g/dl) What is the next best investigation to confirm the likely diagnosis?
expl: The patient gives history of a diarrhoeal illness, following which he develops renal impairement. In addition to renal failure, he has anemia, thrombocytopenia. All these favor the diagnosis of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombotic microangiopathy following an infection. The diagnosis is haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) . The typical presentation is with a triad of acute renal failure, Microangiopathic haemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. Most commonly the cause is E coli O157:H7 (verotoxin producing E coli), hence stool cultures would be the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis in this case. Other diagnostic measure will be the demonstration of Shiga toxin in the stool specimen. Other causes are shigella, cyclosporine and connective tissue diseases. The thrombocytopenia is thought to be a consequence of platelet consumption at sites of endothelial injury. Despite this blood clotting times (prothrombin time, kaolin clotting time) are normal. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:317, Pg:2364.

text: A 68-year-old man has a new-patient screen carried out by his GP. He is noted to have microscopic haematuria. His GP also notes a raised ESR and a calcium concentration of 12.4 mg/dl. On examination he appears to have a varicocele. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
expl: Elderly male with microscopic hematuria and varicocoele with hypercalcemia best fits into the diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma. Renal-cell adenocarcinoma makes up 3% of all adult malignancies, with peak incidence being 50-70 years. There is a male to female preponderance of 2:1. Haematuria is the presenting feature in 50-60% of cases, raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate(ESR) in 50-60% and abdominal mass a presenting feature in 25-45%. Varicocele, resulting from obstruction of venous drainage, is found in 2-3% of cases. Hypercalcaemia occurs due to raised parathyroid-related protein in around 3% of cases. Erythrocytosis, non-metastatic hepatic dysfunction(Stauffer's Syndrome) and dysfibrinogenemia are other paraneoplastic syndromes associated. Anemia occurs in advanced cases. Genetic causes of RCC include Tuberous Sclerosis and Von Hippel Lindau syndrome Imaging studies to detect renal-cell adenocarcinoma include ultrasound scan, intravenous pyelography(IVP), abdominal CT with contrast and MRI. Commonest sites of metastases are lung(50-60%) and bone(30-40%). Treatment of choice is nephrectomy in localized disease. Metastatic RCC is resistant to cytotoxic chemotherapy. They are treated with TKI and mTOR inhibitors. Immune check point inhibitor Nivolumab is the second line agent. Prognosis is related to tumour staging: the 5-year survival rate is around 80-100% in those with TNM stage-1 lesions, but this falls to 5-10% in those with stage-4 lesions. text: A 47-year-old woman comes to your office for a sick visit. This morning she reports passing blood instead of urine. On review of symptoms, she denies any other symptoms except for occasional recurrent attacks of severe abdominal pain for which she has had other urgent care visits but no etiology was found. She has no other past medical history. You repeat a complete blood count. The results are below: White blood cell count 2900/mm 3 Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL (mean corpuscular volume 82 fL) Platelet count 119000/mm 3 Her complete blood count 1 year ago was normal. Her chemistries are only notable for an elevated unconjugated bilirubin and a markedly elevated lactate hydrogenase. Which of the following diagnostic test results would you consider in this patient?
expl: This patient presents with the classic signs, symptoms, and laboratory abnormalities of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PHN). PNH is an acquired chronic hemolytic anemia (HA) characterized by persistent intravascular hemolysis with occasional or frequent recurrent exacerbations. In addition to (1) hemolysis , there may be (2) pancytopenia and (3) a distinct tendency to venous thrombosis . This triad makes PNH a truly unique clinical condition; however, when not all of these three features are manifest on presentation, the diagnosis is often delayed, although it can always be made by appropriate laboratory investigations. When seeking medical attention, the patient may report that one morning, she or he 'passed blood instead of urine'. This distressing or frightening event may be regarded as the classic presentation; The definitive diagnosis of PNH must be based on the demonstration that a substantial proportion of the patient's red cells have an increased susceptibility to complement (C), due to the deficiency on their surface of proteins (particularly CD59 and CD55) that normally protect the red cells from activated C. Other Options: The presence of the Donath-Landsteiner antibody will prove paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (occurring mostly in children, usually triggered by a viral infection, usuallyself-limited). Mutations in the 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) gene lead to G6PDdeficiency, which can lead to hemolysis with treatment of certain drugs. Blood cultures would identify septicemia which can contribute to intravascular hemolysis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 100 pg. 788, 789

text: An 18-year-old woman from Pakistan has been observed for a lifelong severe microcytic and hypochromic anemia. Her hemoglobin levels have generally been in the range of 7 to 10 g/dL, but she recalls needing blood transfusions only twice in her life, on both occasions after traumatic bone fractures. Throughout childhood, her parents had kept her from playing sports or participating in activities requiring significant physical exertion because they had been told by pediatricians that she had a 'heart'. She had markedly delayed puberty but now had regular menses. Physical examination shows marked hepatosplenomegaly; laboratory test abnormalities include indirect hyperbilirubinemia and hyperglycemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The clinical picture is most consistent with thalassemia intermedia. In the case of α-thalassemia, this would be most like hemoglobin H disease (most frequently resulting from the interaction of α + - and α o -thalassemia), with the β4 tetramers of hemoglobin H forming red cell inclusion bodies leading to chronic hemolysis. Patients with α- or β-thalassemia intermedia become severely iron overloaded from lifelong hyperabsorption of dietary iron, even without needing blood transfusions. A similar gut hyperabsorption of iron occurs in familial hemochromatosis states, but those individuals are not typically anemic. This patient's hyperglycemia, growth retardation, possibly her bone fragility, and even the history of a 'weak heart' (perhaps due to cardiomyopathy) are all manifestations of systemic iron overload. Thalassemias are especially prevalent not only in people of Mediterranean and Middle Eastern origin but also in those from the Indian subcontinent. In contrast to thalassemia intermedia, a patient with β-thalassemia major would be expected to be transfusion dependent throughout life. Hydrops fetalis , in which all four α-globin genes are deleted, is incompatible with life. Hemoglobin E, even in its homozygous state, causes little if any anemia and microcytosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed chap: 98 pg. 764

text: A patient with hemolytic anemia presents with dactylitis and chest pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Symptoms of dactylitis and chest pain in a patient with hemolytic anemia are characteristic of a sickling crisis , seen in sickle cell disease due to vaso-occlusion by sickled RBCs. Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a point mutation on chromosome 11 , where glutamic acid is replaced by valine at position 6 of the β-globin chain . This mutation produces abnormal hemoglobin (HbS) , which polymerizes under low oxygen tension , causing red blood cells to become sickle-shaped, rigid, and fragile . These deformed cells lead to vaso-occlusion , tissue ischemia , and hemolysis , resulting in the characteristic acute painful crises . The term "sickle cell crisis" includes several acute manifestations such as vaso-occlusive crisis , aplastic crisis , splenic sequestration crisis , hyperhaemolysis crisis , hepatic crisis , dactylitis , and acute chest syndrome . Types of Sickle Cell Crises Explanation of other options: Microangiopathic anaemia (Option A): Occurs due to mechanical destruction of RBCs as they pass through damaged small vessels, as in DIC, HSP. Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs) are seen on peripheral smear. It does not cause dactylitis or chest pain. Intravascular haemolysis (Option C): Refers to the destruction of RBCs within blood vessels, releasing free haemoglobin, causing haemoglobinemia, haemoglobinuria, and jaundice. It is a mechanism of anaemia, not a specific disease causing vaso-occlusion or dactylitis. Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (Option D): Caused by autoantibodies against RBCs, leading to extravascular destruction in the spleen. Patients present with jaundice, pallor, and splenomegaly, but not with dactylitis or chest pain.

text: The most common type of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is:
expl: Autoimmune processes account for 90% of adult cases of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, usually caused by GM-CSF autoantibodies . It also can be congenital or secondary to dust exposure or hematologic malignancy and is the most common form overall. Most patients (72%) are smokers. Patients present with the insidious onset of dyspnoea and cough , which may be dry or occasionally productive of grayish material. Bilateral alveolar opacities with “crazy paving ” and diffuse areas of ground-glass attenuation on CT scan are characteristic of PAP. Mild cases can be managed with smoking cessation; severe cases require whole lung lavage. Reference: Goldman Cecil Medicine 26th edition chapter 85 page number. 554

text: Which of the following is recommended for a newborn born to a mother suffering from acute viral hepatitis B infection?
expl: HBIG is indicated for newborn infants of HBsAg-positive mothers, with initiation of the vaccine series at the same time, both within 12 hours of birth (administered at different injection sites). text: A 45 year old man has had long standing jaundice, malaise and poor appetite. Over the past 6 months he has lost 2 stones in weight. On examination he has palmar erythema, jaundiced sclera, spider naevi, hepatomegaly and ascites. His bloods reveal: Bilirubin 2.5 mg/dl ALT: 150 U/l ALP: 240 U/l Hep C core antibody Positive HBsAg: Negative Hep A antibody Negative What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: This patient has features of chronic liver disease, as evidenced by the presence of ascites and spider angiomas. The patient also gives history of jaundice with deranged SGPT , which indicates an active hepatitis. Acute infection with Hepatitis E or C will cause SGPT elevation of the order of 1000. So from among the options the most probable option is HCC. The risk of HCC is increased as well in patients with chronic hepatitis C almost exclusively in patients with cirrhosis, and almost after at least several decades, usually after three decades of disease. Among such cirrhotic patients with chronic hepatitis C, the annual risk of HCC is ~1-4%. 30% of patients with hepatitis C develop hepatocellular carcinoma over 30 years. 20% develop cirrhosis over 20 years. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 82, Pg: 643

text: Which of the following regions of the abdomen is preferred for abdominal paracentesis?
expl: The lower quadrants are the most frequent sites for paracentesis. The left lower quadrant is preferred because of the greater depth of ascites and the thinner abdominal wall. Paracentesis is a safe procedure even in patients with coagulopathy; complications, including abdominal wall hematomas, hypotension, hepatorenal syndrome, and infection, are infrequent. Cirrhosis accounts for 84% of cases of ascites. Cardiac ascites, peritoneal carcinomatosis, and 'mixed' ascites resulting from cirrhosis and a second disease account for 10-15% of cases Reference : Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 50 pg. 323

text: Which of the following is not included in the Child-Pugh score assessment?
expl: Explanation: The Child-Pugh score is utilized to evaluate the extent of liver disease, estimate prognosis in cirrhosis, and guide decisions regarding suitability for liver transplantation. Liver function enzymes such as ALT (alanine aminotransferase) and AST (aspartate aminotransferase) are not included in the Child-Pugh scoring system. The Child-Pugh classification uses a scoring method based on the following factors: Bilirubin INR Albumin Presence of ascites Degree of hepatic encephalopathy The Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP) classification is calculated by adding up the points assigned to each parameter. However, the Child-Pugh score has limitations, as ascites and encephalopathy may not always be graded with precision. This drawback is addressed more effectively by the MELD scoring system

text: A 47-year-old male with a long history of alcohol abuse presents with a two day history of deteriorating confusion.On examination he is drowsy, has a temperature of 39&deg:C, a pulse of 110 beats per minute, a small amount of ascites and has features of a left side hemiparesis.What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: This man with chronic alcohol abuse now presents with a fever and left hemiparesis. The most likely diagnosis would therefore be cerebral abscess. The fever would not itself be explained by a subdural haematoma nor would a simple CVA explain this. Similarly, delirium tremens or encephalopathy would not be associated with the hemiparesis since they cause global cerebral dysfunction. In patient with CLD, there is a high risk of infections. And also, there will be pulmonary shunting in patients with CLD, called the Hepatopulmonary syndrome, which predisposes the patient to brain abscess. text: A 77-year-old male is admitted with acute confusion and is agitated and aggressive to staff. His relatives who accompany him assert that he had been entirely self-caring, does not drink alcohol and was taking no previous medication. He was diagnosed with a urinary tract infection and commenced antibiotics but remained agitated and distressed. Which one of the following treatments is the most appropriate for his agitation?
expl: The patient in this question is suffering from Delirium. From among the options Quetiapine is the drug used in delirium, though with limited proven benefits. Chlorpromazine is another antipsychotic, but its use is associated with significant adverse effects and should be avoided in elderly. Management of delirium: Treating the underlying cause. Sensory aids to promote wakefulness at day time. Like keeping the windows open, using glasses and hearing aids, engaging in walking. Attempting to mimic home environment. Maintaining dark environment at night. Minimizing restrains. Drugs to calm the patient should be avoided, and should be given only if there is a risk of self harm or harm to the care givers. Typical or atypical antipsychotics should be given, in a very low dose, on an as needed basis. But they don't have a proven benefit in treating delirium. Benzodiazepines should not be used as it worsens confusion. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 27, Pg: 182

text: CFTR gene mutation involves which ion and which mutation?

options.A: Chloride ion and deletion of phenylalanine at 508 positions
options.B: Chloride ion and deletion of tryptophan at 508 positions
options.C: Chloride ion and deletion of phenylalanine at 708 positions
options.D: Chloride ion and deletion of tryptophan at 708 positions

ansText: Chloride ion and deletion of phenylalanine at 508 positions
expl: The gene product responsible for CF is CFTR, which serves as an anion channel in the luminal surfaces of epithelial cells, where it regulates the volume and consistency of exocrine secretions. CFTR mutations lead to abnormally thick secretions. In the lung it leads to recurrent infections. In the pancreas, it leads to the obstruction of the pancreatic duct leading to malabsorption and steatorrhoea . Obstruction of intrahepatic bile duct leads to cirrhosis, in males it leads to involution of vas deferens and infertility. CFTR mutations: Class I mutation: Absence of synthesis of CFTR. CFTR nonsense mutations like G542X, R553X, or W1282X are examples. Class II mutation: Defective protein maturation and premature degradation. F508 deletion. Most common mutation. Lumacaftor and Tezacaftor repair CFTR misfolding and promote cell surface localization of F508 CFTR. Elexacaftor, is a third generation molecule effective for F508 as well as a variety of other CFTR mutations. Class III: Disordered gating, ATP binding or hydrolysis. G551D, leads to inability to transport Cl or HCO3. Ivacaftor overcomes the defect. Approved for 96 other variants apart from G551D. Class IV: Defective conductance through the pore. Class V: A reduced number of CFTR transcripts. Class VI: Accelerated turnover from the cell surface. Ivacaftor tezacaftor and Elixacaftor are approved as triple combination therapy for CF. it benefits >90% cases with the disease . Improvements in FEV1, fewer infections, improvement in QOL and diminished sweat chloride levels. Designated as Highly Effective Modulator Treatment.

text: A 30-year-old woman presents with symptoms of an unsteady gait, memory loss, and mood swings. During the neurological examination, the findings shown in the image below are observed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The image displays fine pigmented, granular deposits characteristic of Kayser-Fleischer rings, which result from copper buildup in the Descemet's membrane of the cornea. This finding is highly suggestive of Wilson's disease. Wilson's Disease Also called hepatolenticular degeneration, Wilson's disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by abnormal copper accumulation in the liver, brain, eyes, and other organs. This leads to elevated free copper levels, increased copper in the liver and urine, and decreased serum ceruloplasmin. Genetic Cause: The disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13. This gene encodes a copper-transporting ATPase responsible for removing copper from the liver into bile. Pathogenesis: Mutation in the ATP7B gene Impaired biliary copper excretion Copper accumulates in liver cells (hepatocytes) Excess copper causes oxidative damage, promoting inflammation and fibrosis in the liver When liver storage capacity is exceeded, copper is released into the bloodstream Copper then accumulates in other tissues: Brain: Particularly basal ganglia, causing neurological symptoms Cornea: Forms Kayser-Fleischer rings Kidneys: Can lead to renal dysfunction Joints: Causes arthritic changes Copper accumulation causes tissue damage through oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and enzyme inhibition Explanation of Other Options: Neurofibromatosis 2 (Option A): typically presents with juvenile cataracts in children, retinal hamartomas, and similar features. Neurofibromatosis 1 (Option C): is characterized by Lisch nodules, which are small, raised brown spots on the iris. Cataracts (Option D): usually appear as wedge-shaped opacities (cortical cataracts) or darkened lenses (nuclear cataracts) with distinct clinical signs. text: The KF ring is associated with which of the following conditions?
expl: Explanation: The Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring is due to copper deposition in Descemet's membrane of the cornea . It is a hallmark feature of Wilson's disease , an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism characterised by hepatic, neurological, and psychiatric manifestations . Explanation of other options: Hemochromatosis (Option A): Characterised by iron overload affecting the liver, pancreas, heart, and skin ("bronze diabetes"), but no KF ring is seen. Alzheimer's disease (Option C): A neurodegenerative disorder with memory loss and amyloid plaques, not associated with copper deposition. Huntington's disease (Option D): A genetic movement disorder due to CAG repeats, with chorea and psychiatric features, but no ocular signs like KF rings.

text: All of the following increase risk of Alzheimer's disease except?
expl: A history of head trauma with concussion increases the risk for AD. AD is more common in groups with low educational attainment, but education influences test-taking ability, and it is clear that AD can affect persons of all intellectual levels. Diabetes increases the risk of AD threefold. Elevated homocysteine and cholesterol levels; hypertension; diminished serum levels of folic acid; low dietary intake of fruits, vegetables, and red wine; and low levels of exercise are all being explored as potential risk factors for AD. Several retrospective studies suggest that nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents and 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase inhibitors (statins) may have a protective effect on dementia if used prior to the onset of disease but do not influence clinically symptomatic AD. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 431, Pg: 3372

text: Which of the following is true regarding laboratory findings of Zieve's Syndrome?
expl: A unique form of hemolytic anemia (with spur cells and acanthocytes) called Zieve's syndrome can occur in patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis. Platelet counts are often reduced early in the disease, reflective of portal hypertension with hypersplenism. Serum total bilirubin can be normal or elevated with advanced disease. Prothrombin times are often prolonged and usually do not respond to administration of parenteral vitamin K. Serum sodium levels are usually normal unless patients have ascites and then can be depressed, largely due to ingestion of excess free water. Transient hyperlipidemia may also be seen. Reference : Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 344 pg. 2625

text: Which of the following diseases presents with Thrombotic microangiopathy without Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia?
expl: Thrombotic microangiopathy(TMA) is a pathological lesion characterized by the presence of endothelial injury in the terminal arteriole and capillaries of organs, causing hyaline platelet thrombi, resulting in partial or complete occlusion of vessels. text: Which one of the following features is characteristic of Bartter's syndrome?

options.B: Reduced urinary excretion of potassium and chloride

expl: Bartter's syndrome is a childhood disease inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Pathophysiology impaired loop sodium NaK2Cl reabsorption leads to increased renin and aldosterone secretion with juxtaglomerular hyperplasia. Enhanced sodium-chloride delivery to the collecting duct stimulates potassium secretion leading to hypokalemia . It also causes hydrogen ion secretion resulting in metabolic alkalosis . Accelerated kinin and prostaglandins secretion may account for the vascular unresponsiveness to the pressor effect. This explains the absence of increase in blood pressure and oedema despite the elevated levels of renin and aldosterone. Indomethacin inhibits prostaglandin and restores normal physiological vascular response. Hypokalemia with hypertension is seen with disorders that are related to the ENaC Conn's Syndrome, Liddle syndrome. Bartter's syndrome is associated with increased urinary excretion of potassium and chloride. IN Bartter's syndrome, the addition of Spironolactone, Amiloride or ACE inhibitors improves hypokalemia, but worsens the hypovolemia. NSAIDS may be useful in Bartter's syndrome, as they inhibit the tubuloglomerular feedback. Potassium supplementation and liberal salt intake should be given. Gitelman syndrome also should be treated similarly, but NSAIDS have no role. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 53, Pg:353.

text: Which of the following is not true regarding the cardiac biomarkers in myocardial infarction?

expl: The order of rise of cardiac biomarkers is Myoglobin (2-3 hours) → CK-MB (3-6 hours) → Troponins (3-12 hours) → LDH (24 hours) CK-MB levels rise by 3-6 hours, reaches its peak by 12-24 hours and return to baseline by 48-72 hours. text: A 56-year-old man presents with a history of abdominal discomfort that is relieved by passing stool. In the past month his stools have been looser in nature and he has had a feeling of urgency and incomplete evacuation. His symptoms seem to be worse with eating. He has also noticed that he has passed mucus per rectum. He is overweight with a BMI of 28 kg/m2. His weight has fallen. He says that he has adjusted his diet in the last six months. expl: Weight loss, tenesmus and a recent change in bowel habit all point towards an underlying diagnosis of colorectal cancer. Onset of symptoms in later life and a relatively short duration (that is, weeks rather than years) also point towards a 'biological' cause rather than irritable bowel syndrome. The passage of mucus per rectum is a normal physiological function and not indicative of underlying pathology. The symptoms are not suggestive of malabsorption. Diverticulitis and inflammatory bowel disease are both potential diagnoses but given the duration of symptoms less likely than a colonic neoplasm. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, CH: 81, Pg: 639

text: What is the differentiating feature between IBS and organic GI disease?
expl: Irritable bowel syndrome is a functional bowel disorder which is non inflammatory. The unifying feature of inflammatory diarrhea due to any cause is the presence of leukocytes or leukocyte derived protein Calprotectin in stools. Another inflammatory marker in stool is Fecal Lactoferrin, which is also present in activated neutrophils. Both of them can be used in diagnosis of relapses of inflammatory bowel disease from IBS or bacterial overgrowth. Fecal calprotectin is also having the advantage of being a sensitive marker of Colonic or ileocolonic inflammation rather than isolated ileal inflammation. Abdominal pain, diarrhea and presence of mucous in stools can be seen in IBS as well as inflammatory diarrhea. Blood in stools, nocturnal symptoms and weight loss is uncommon in IBS.

text: A 24 year old man presents with a 10 month history of weight loss, oral ulceration and diarrhoea. A flexible sigmoidoscopy is performed and a colonic biopsy was taken. Which of the following histological features would favour a diagnosis of Crohn's disease over ulcerative colitis?
expl: Crohn's disease is characterized by transmural inflammation (inflammation of all layers of the gut), fissures, preservation of crypt architecture and non caseating granulomata. Ulcerative colitis is typified by mucosal inflammation, general inflammatory cell infiltration, goblet cell mucus depletion and crypt abscesses. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg:2474-2475

text: A 19-year-old woman returns from her gap year travels with chronic low grade fever, intermittent abdominal pain and diarrhoea. She has been feeling unwell for the past few months and has returned to the UK because she has begun to lose weight. Her only medication is the combined oral contraceptive pill. On examination she looks pale, her BP is 110/60 mmHg, pulse is 75, and her BMI is 18 kg/m2. Her abdomen is soft, but she does complain of some right-sided abdominal pain. Investigations show Hb 11.0 g/dl(11.5-16.5) WCC 9.8 x 10^9/L (4-11) PLT 187 x 10^9/L (150-400) CRP 67 mg/l ( Na 139 mmol/l (135-146) K 4.8 mmol/l (3.5-5) Cr 1.3 mg/dl Colonoscopy reveals areas of discrete ulceration identified, punctuated by normal mucosa. The biopsy reveals transmural noncaseating granulomata. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The presence of skip lesions and full thickness inflammation with granuloma formation is typical of Crohn's disease . Corticosteroids and 5-ASA compounds are the mainstay of therapy for Crohn's. Whilst an infectious agent is a possibility, it is less likely than inflammatory bowel disease here. We are not given a history of significant oral or genital ulceration, which makes Behcet's less likely. Ulcerative colitis does not have granulomas. Only mucosal inflammation is seen in UC. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg:2474-2475

text: A 36 year old woman presents with abdominal pain, weight loss, diarrhoea and mouth ulcers. Full blood count reveals normocytic normochromic anaemia, inflammatory markers are raised, and biochemical investigation reveals a raised alkaline phosphatase. Barium follow through shows terminal ileal inflammatory disease. Long term remission may be maintained by the use of which of the following drugs?
expl: This is a case of Crohn’s disease . Remission of Crohn's disease may be achieved by the use of steroids, elemental diet, surgery or infliximab. Mesalazine may maintain remission if induction has been achieved by surgery and if an 8-week course of metronidazole is administered. It has many side effects. In other scenarios, the most useful drug to maintain long term remission is azathioprine . Steroids (prednisolone) are only used for induction of remission. They are not appropriate for long term maintenance therapy. Cyclosporine is used in severe cases of ulcerative colitis refractory to steroid therapy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg: 2488

He has been a smoker for 40 years and had a myocardial infarction 5 years ago. He has a family history of colon carcinoma. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: The history of pain, diarrhea and bleeding per rectum in a patient with vascular risk factors suggest large bowel infarction. Ischaemic bowel disease may be acute or chronic. text: A patient with known ulcerative colitis (UC) who has failed to respond to anti-TNF-α therapy requires an alternative drug for moderate to severe disease. Which of the following Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors is most appropriate in this setting?
expl: Explanation: Tofacitinib is an orally active JAK inhibitor approved for the management of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis , particularly in patients who are refractory or intolerant to anti-TNF-α therapy . It acts by inhibiting Janus kinases (JAK1 and JAK3) , thereby blocking the JAK-STAT intracellular signaling pathway , which mediates the action of multiple proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21 , and interferons . This suppression of cytokine-driven immune activation helps reduce intestinal inflammation, promote mucosal healing, and maintain remission in ulcerative colitis. Mechanism of Action Normal Pathway: Cytokine → JAK receptor activation → STAT phosphorylation → Gene transcription → Inflammation Tofacitinib action: Inhibits JAK1 and JAK3 → prevents STAT activation → reduces transcription of proinflammatory cytokines → controls mucosal inflammation Side effects include an increased risk of infections, venous thromboembolism, and lipid elevation, requiring careful patient selection and monitoring. Explanation of Other Options: Vedolizumab (Option A): Class: Gut-selective anti-integrin monoclonal antibody. Mechanism of Action: Targets α4β7 integrin , a cell adhesion molecule present on the surface of gut-homing T lymphocytes. Prevents these activated T cells from binding to MAdCAM-1 (mucosal addressin cell adhesion molecule-1) on intestinal endothelial cells. This selectively blocks lymphocyte trafficking into the gastrointestinal mucosa , thereby reducing inflammation in the colon. Acts primarily in the gut , with minimal systemic immunosuppression. Clinical Use: Approved for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease , especially when conventional therapies (steroids, azathioprine, 5-ASA) or anti-TNF agents fail. Effective for induction and maintenance of remission . Often preferred in patients who are at higher risk of systemic infections , given its gut-selective mechanism. Adverse Effects: Infusion reactions (headache, arthralgia, nausea). Risk of upper respiratory tract infections. Rarely, hypersensitivity reactions. No association with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), unlike natalizumab. Ozanimod (Option C): Class: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulator . Mechanism of Action: Selectively binds to S1P1 and S1P5 receptors on lymphocytes. Causes functional sequestration of lymphocytes in lymph nodes → prevents them from entering systemic circulation and reaching inflamed intestinal tissue. Reduces local intestinal inflammation by decreasing immune cell infiltration. Clinical Use: Approved by the FDA (2021) for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis . Also indicated for multiple sclerosis (MS) . Used when patients are refractory to anti-TNF agents or cannot tolerate JAK inhibitors. Dosing and Route: Oral, once daily - convenient compared to injectable biologics. Dose titration is required initially to minimize cardiac side effects. Adverse Effects: Cardiac: Bradycardia and atrioventricular (AV) block, especially with the first dose (due to S1P1 receptor modulation on cardiac tissue). Hepatic: Elevated liver enzymes. Respiratory: Mild reduction in FEV��� in some patients. Infectious: Risk of reactivation of viral infections such as VZV. Ophthalmologic: Rare macular edema (requires baseline eye exam). Leflunomide (Option D): Class: Disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) ; pyrimidine synthesis inhibitor. Mechanism of Action: Inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase , an enzyme essential for de novo pyrimidine synthesis in rapidly dividing lymphocytes. Decreases proliferation and activation of T and B cells → immunomodulatory effect. Clinical Use: Primarily used in rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis . Sometimes used as an alternative to methotrexate in patients with intolerance or contraindications. Not used in ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease. Adverse Effects: Hepatotoxicity (requires regular liver function monitoring). Teratogenicity - contraindicated in pregnancy. Gastrointestinal upset, diarrhea. Hypertension, weight loss, rash, and alopecia. Key Takeaway Points: Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6535722/

text: A patient with a known history of inflammatory bowel disease presents with the skin lesion shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The clinical presentation and image suggest Pyoderma gangrenosum, a condition more frequently seen in ulcerative colitis, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Pyoderma gangrenosum is a rare inflammatory skin disorder characterized by painful, ulcerative lesions, often affecting the lower limbs. These ulcers typically have undermined edges and may appear necrotic or purulent. Extraintestinal manifestations of IBD include: Erythema nodosum (Option A ruled out): Painful red nodules usually on the shins Ankylosing spondylitis (spinal arthritis) Pancreatitis Uveitis (inflammation of the uveal tract of the eye) Osteoporosis and osteonecrosis are among the most common extraintestinal complications of IBD. Pyoderma gangrenosum and primary sclerosing cholangitis are especially common in ulcerative colitis, while renal calculi are more typical in Crohn's disease. Explanation for other options: Diabetic ulcer (Option C): is not linked to inflammatory bowel disease; it typically occurs as a complication of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus. Venous ulcer (Option D): generally, results from chronic conditions such as long-standing varicose veins and is commonly found around the ankles.

text: Which of the following interleukins chiefly drive PsA?
expl: The chief interleukins that drive PsA are IL17 and IL 23. The biologics that are used in treatment of PsA act by antagonizing these cytokines. They include: Anti IL 17: secukinumab and ixekizumab Anti IL-23/IL-12p40 : ustekinumab, a monoclonal antibody to the shared subunit. text: A 57 year old man is suspected of having a duodenal ulcer recurrence despite being on omeprazole. Which of the following is the most sensitive test in detecting ongoing infection with Helicobacter pylori?

options.B: The urease test on a gastric biopsy

expl: The urea breath test is expensive but has up to 98% sensitivity . It requires stringent test conditions like fasting and may not be convenient as serology. It can be used for detecting response to treatment. Serology is simple and convenient and is not affected by the use of PPI or antibiotic use. So in this patient who is already on PPI this may be the most convenient investigation. The gastric biopsy culture has high specificity but sensitivity of 90%. Histology of gastric biopsy (not listed above) has both high sensitivity and specificity . Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, ch: 163, Pg: 1281

text: A 62 year old man with history of colorectal polyps presents with low grade fever, weight loss and night sweats. ECHO showed vegetations on the aortic valve. Which is the most likely organism to be grown in blood culture?
expl: Streptococcus bovis bacteremia and endocarditis have been strongly associated with colorectal neoplasia. Patient identified to have S. bovis endocarditis should be evaluated for the presence of colorectal polyps or cancer. Penicillin G is the treatment of choice for S. bovis endocarditis typically given for 4 weeks. Staphylococcus aureus is the most commonly isolated organism from endocarditis occurring in IV drug abusers, which preferentially affects the tricuspid valve. text: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with complaints of fever for 1 week. He also has cracked lips, which are painful. On examination, his eyes are red and he has a lymph node in the cervical region. Kawasaki syndrome is suspected. Which of the following is the best treatment choice?
expl: This is a case of Kawasaki's syndrome, which is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome and occurs mainly in children under 10 years of age. It is a form of vasculitis, which affects coronary arteries and is associated with the development of coronary aneurysms. Aspirin and IV immunoglobulin at high doses is the treatment of choice. Corticosteroids used to be contraindicated, but recently trials have shown that it reduced the risk of heart damage caused by coronary vessel vasculitis. Infliximab is also being used in trials. Warfarin is used if coronary aneurysms develop as a complication. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch: 363 Pg: 2816

text: A 45 year old man presents with acute, profuse, watery diarrhea some days after returning from a holiday. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
expl: The most likely cause of travellers diarrhoea is E. coli. Ciprofloxacin would cover for this as well as shigella, salmonella and campylobacter. However, if giardiasis was cultured in the stool then metronidazole is recommended. Most secretory forms of traveler's diarrhea (usually due to enterotoxigenic or enteroaggregative E. coli or to Campylobacter) can be treated effectively with rehydration, bismuth subsalicylate, or antiperistaltic agents. Antimicrobial agents can shorten the duration of illness from 3-4 days to 24-36 h but may be associated with the acquisition of multidrug-resistant organisms; their use should therefore be reserved for severe cases Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 133, Pg: 1065

text: Which of the following statements regarding von Willebrand disease is incorrect?

expl: Explanation of answer: Type 1 von Willebrand disease causes only mild to moderate bleeding symptoms and typically does not present with severe bleeding early in life. Von Willebrand Disease (vWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, resulting from a quantitative or qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor (vWF), a glycoprotein critical for platelet adhesion and stabilization of factor VIII. Classification of vWD: Clinical Manifestations: Mild bleeding (Type 1): Easy bruising, epistaxis, prolonged bleeding after dental procedures, menorrhagia. Moderate bleeding (Type 2): Subtypes show qualitative dysfunction in vWF. Severe bleeding (Type 3): Presents like severe Hemophilia A due to virtual absence of both vWF and Factor VIII. Common symptoms: Mucocutaneous bleeding Post-surgical or dental procedure hemorrhage Prolonged bleeding time despite normal platelet count Treatment:

text: A 50-year-old man is evaluated for hyperaldosteronism because of difficult to-control hypertension. He is otherwise healthy. Evaluation was done during treatment with agents that do not affect aldosterone or renin levels and include an aldosterone-to-renin ratio of more than 40 and lack of aldosterone suppression to oral salt loading. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the adrenal glands shows a 1-cm mass on the right with a density of 10 HU. What is the next best step?

options.D: Review of CT scan to exclude hyperplasia of the left adrenal gland

expl: Adrenal venous sampling should be performed to identify the source of excess aldosterone. It is possible that the visualized mass is a non functioning tumor. Adrenal venous sampling is the gold standard investigation for lateralisation of aldosterone excess. This man is a good surgical candidate, and laparoscopic adrenalectomy would be recommended if venous sampling is consistent with unilateral disease. The CT scan is not helpful in identifying bilateral disease. Treatment with eplerenone or spironolactone would be done if he were not a surgical candidate; eplerenone would be an appropriate treatment for bilateral disease. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2966

expl: The question deals with treatment endpoints in SLE. Complete permanent remission(no disease activity without any treatment) is seen in Aim of treatment in SLE is disease remission on treatment or low level disease activity. text: A 58-year-old male presents with dysphagia, retrosternal discomfort and weight loss. Studies reveal achalasia. Which of the following is most definitive way to provide symptomatic relief?
expl: The only durable therapies for achalasia are pneumatic dilation and LES myotomy (Heller myotomy). The patient shows excellent symptom improvement. Reflux is the most common side effect and a concomitant anti-relfux procedure (Nissen's fundoplication) may be performed. Both calcium channel blockers (nifedipine) and nitrates relax the lower oesophageal sphincter. However the effect on symptoms is variable, short-lived and usually suboptimal. Use is frequently limited by adverse effects. Consequently medical therapy is typically limited to those patients too frail or unwilling to undergo definitive treatment or other therapies. Latest treatment is POEM. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 23,Pg: 2427-2428

text: Drug of choice for treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is
expl: Nitrofurantoin, ampicillin, and cephalosporins are considered relatively safe in early pregnancy. One retrospective case-control study suggesting an association between nitrofurantoin and birth defects has not been confirmed. Sulfonamides should clearly be avoided both in the first trimester (because of possible teratogenic effects) and near term (because of a possible role in the development of kernicterus). Fluoroquinolones are avoided because of possible adverse effects on fetal cartilage Ampicillin and the cephalosporins have been used extensively in pregnancy and are the drugs of choice for the treatment of asymptomatic or symptomatic UTI in this group of patients. Generally, pregnant women with ASB are treated for 4-7 days in the absence of evidence to support single-dose therapy. For pregnant women with overt pyelonephritis, parenteral ß-lactam therapy with or without aminoglycosides is the standard of care. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 135, Pg: 1077

text: A 63-year-old diabetic woman presents with fever, flank pain, dysuria, and elevated WBC count. Imaging reveals mild hydronephrosis. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. She is diagnosed with a complicated urinary tract infection (UTI). Which of the following is the best initial treatment?
expl: Explanation: She is diagnosed with a complicated urinary tract infection (UTI) and hence the patient should be treated with Meropenem. Meropenem is the best initial treatment in this case because: The patient has a complicated UTI (due to diabetes, systemic signs, and possible urinary tract obstruction). There is a high risk of infection with resistant organisms , particularly ESBL-producing Gram-negative bacilli like E . coli . Meropenem , a carbapenem , offers broad-spectrum coverage including Gram-negative organisms , anaerobes , and ESBL producers . It is effective when oral agents or narrower-spectrum antibiotics are likely to fail or when systemic illness is present. Explanations for other Options: Ceftriaxone (Option A): Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin that is commonly used for UTIs, but it may not be effective against ESBL-producing organisms , which are often found in complicated infections, especially in diabetic or hospitalized patients. While it can be used in some uncomplicated cases, it is not the preferred choice for severe or high-risk infections like the one described. Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Option C): Amoxicillin-clavulanate is an oral antibiotic with some activity against common urinary pathogens, but it has limited effectiveness against resistant Gram-negative bacteria , including ESBL-producing strains. It is not suitable for treating complicated UTIs , especially when there are systemic signs such as fever or flank pain, or imaging findings like hydronephrosis. Nitrofurantoin (Option D): Nitrofurantoin is only effective for lower urinary tract infections (cystitis) because it does not reach adequate concentrations in the renal tissue . Therefore, it is ineffective for pyelonephritis or complicated infections involving the kidneys or upper urinary tract, such as in this case with flank pain and hydronephrosis .

text: What is the drug of choice for Legionnaire's disease?
expl: Explanation: Azithromycin is the preferred agent for treating Legionnaire's disease due to its superior efficacy, better tolerability, and lower potential for drug interactions compared to erythromycin. Legionella Features: Thin, Gram-negative, non-capsulated bacilli. Poor Gram staining; best visualized by Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA) staining. Requires Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract (BCYE) agar for growth. Mode of Infection: Microaspiration and aerosol inhalation; no human-to-human transmission. Epidemiology: Associated with air conditioners, showers, coolers; commonly seen in smokers, immunocompromised, and elderly patients. Treatment: First-line: Macrolides [Azithromycin preferred over Erythromycin], ciprofloxacin, tetracyclines. Severe cases: Rifampicin may be added. Ineffective: Beta-lactams and aminoglycosides. Explanation of other options: Vancomycin (Option A): Active against Gram-positive bacteria like Staphylococcus and Enterococcus; ineffective for Legionella. Streptomycin (Option C): Aminoglycoside used in TB and plague; lacks efficacy against Legionella. Erythromycin (Option D): Previously first-line, now replaced by Azithromycin due to better tolerability. References: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK7619/

text: A 15-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhoea. She represents her school in athletics and is now training for the national championships. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for her?
expl: Menarche may be delayed in girls who are involved in strenuous physical activity. This is termed as"Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea" in which strenuous physical activity, caloric restriction and extreme stress can lead to reduced GnRH and gonadotropins production from hypothalamus and pituitary. Treatment with GnRH or gonadotropins are not required as the reversal of these risk factors would lead to resumption of normal menstrual cycles. Provision of an adequate diet and the relief of stress would be the most appropriate treatment in this case. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3035

text: What is the treatment of a patient diagnosed with H.pylori?

options.A: A combination of a proton pump inhibitor and an antibiotic

ansText: A combination of a proton pump inhibitor and an antibiotic
expl: Explanation: The treatment regimen for a patient with H.pylori is a combination of a proton pump inhibitor and antibiotics. Although pylori is sensitive to many antibiotics in vitro, monotherapy is generally ineffective due to insufficient antibiotic delivery to its colonization site. The failure of single-drug therapy led to the development of multidrug regimens. At present, standard treatment consists of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) combined with two or three antimicrobial agents for 10-14 days. Common Treatment Regimens for H.pylori

text: A 25-year-old male presents with fever, chills, and malaise, and is diagnosed with malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax. He has a history of hemolytic anemia among males in his family. Before initiating treatment, which of the following should be checked to ensure the safety of antimalarial therapy
expl: Explanation: Primaquine is used for the radical treatment of Plasmodium vivax malaria to eradicate persistent liver stages and prevent relapse. However, primaquine can cause hemolysis in individuals with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. This genetic condition is more prevalent in certain populations and can lead to severe hemolytic anemia if drugs like primaquine are administered. Since the patient has a history of hemolytic anemia among males in his family, which is suggestive of a possible G6PD deficiency, it is crucial to check G6PD levels before initiating treatment with primaquine. Primaquine Use in Malaria Treatment : Used to eradicate persistent liver stages and prevent relapse in Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale infections. Recommended dose is 0.5 mg/kg in East Asia and Oceania and 0.25 mg/kg elsewhere, daily for 14 days. G6PD Testing : Essential to test for G6PD deficiency before administering primaquine due to the risk of hemolysis in deficient individuals. In mild variants of G6PD deficiency, primaquine is administered weekly for 8 weeks at 0.75 mg/kg. Alternative Treatment Strategies : Pregnant women should not receive primaquine but rather suppressive prophylaxis with chloroquine until they can undergo radical treatment post-delivery. Tafenoquine : A slowly eliminated 8-aminoquinoline that can be administered as a single dose for radical cure. Requires a quantitative G6PD test before administration; only patients with >70% of normal G6PD activity should receive it. Its radical curative efficacy is noted to be lower than primaquine in Southeast Asia. Implications for Patients : The need for quantitative testing of G6PD activity is underscored due to the severe potential complications associated with hemolysis, particularly in those with unrecognized or borderline G6PD deficiency. Explanation of other option: Liver function tests (LFTs) (Option B): Although antimalarials like quinine or chloroquine can affect liver function, primaquine-related hemolysis is the primary concern. LFTs are not necessary before treatment unless there is a known hepatic disease. Complete blood count (CBC) (Option C): A CBC can help monitor anemia or thrombocytopenia in malaria, but it does not predict hemolytic risk. Checking G6PD status is the priority before primaquine use. Reticulocyte count (Option D): A high reticulocyte count may indicate ongoing hemolysis, but it does not determine whether the patient has G6PD deficiency. Testing G6PD directly is necessary. Key Takeaways: Before prescribing primaquine or tafenoquine for Plasmodium vivax malaria, G6PD levels must be checked to prevent life-threatening hemolysis.

text: A 36-year-old man who is known to drink three bottles of wine per day presents to the Emergency department with dull abdominal pain. He tells you that he has suffered from increasing abdominal swelling over the past month.On examination his BP is 105/72 mmHg, his pulse is 92 and regular. He is pyrexic with T: 37.9°C. His abdomen is generally tender but there are bowel sounds on auscultation. He is penicillin allergic. Investigations show: Hemoglobin 10.5 g/dl(13.5-17.7) White cell count 11.5 x 10^9/L (4-11) Platelets 125 x 10^9/L (150-400) Sodium 134 mmol/l (135-146) Potassium 3.6 mmol/l (3.5-5) Creatinine 0.9 mg/dl 280 neutrophils / ml in ascitic fluid( Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
expl: The diagnosis here is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis - note the history of alcohol excess, gradually increasing abdominal girth and elevated neutrophil count in the ascitic fluid. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis should be managed aggressively, and whilst piperacillin and tazobactam or a third generation cephalosporin are an appropriate choice in those who are not penicillin allergic, in this case ciprofloxacin and vancomycin are the default choice due to the presence of penicillin allergy. Oral continuation therapy is with ciprofloxacin alone or co-trimoxazole. Co-amoxiclav is not appropriate due to the presence of penicillin allergy, nor is the piperacillin and tazobactam combination. The two erythromycin combinations do not provide an adequate breadth of coverage. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 344, Pg: 2632

text: When present with dynamic ileus, the C.difficile infection is identified by
expl: Diarrhea is the most common manifestation caused by C. difficile. Stools are almost never grossly bloody and range from soft and unformed to watery or mucoid in consistency, with a characteristic odor. Clinical and laboratory findings include fever in 28% of cases, abdominal pain in 22%, and leukocytosis in 50%. When dynamic ileus (which is seen on x-ray in ~20% of cases) results in cessation of stool passage, the diagnosis of CDI is frequently overlooked. A clue to the presence of unsuspected CDI in these patients is unexplained leukocytosis , with ≥15,000 white blood cells (WBCs)/uL. Such patients are at high risk for complications of C. difficile infection, particularly toxic megacolon and sepsis . Reference : Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:134 Pg: 1068

text: A 35-year-old woman with Crohn's disease has a history of a right hemicolectomy for ileo-colonic disease. Since the operation she has had frequent diarrhoea but no blood in the stools. Investigations show: ESR 10mm (0-20mm/1st hour) Platelets 240 x 10^9/L (150-400 x10^9) Serum CRP 7 mg/L ( Which is the best treatment?
expl: The history includes a previous right hemicolectomy for ileo-colonic disease. The diseases affecting the terminal ileum or if If large area of ileum is affected,>100cm, there will be spillage of the bile acids into the colon and also there will be malabsorption due to loss of large areas of the small bowel. This is called Fatty acid Diarrhoea. This will not respond to Cholestyramine and will be associated with steatorrhoea. Loss of the terminal ileum frequently leads to bile salt malabsorption which causes a secretory diarrhoea . Treatment with the bile salt chelator cholestyramine quickly relieves the problem. Also the diarrhoea is not bloody which goes against active Crohn's colitis. Hence mesalazine or prednisolone would not be effective here. Metronidazole is typically given for peri-anal disease. text: A 65-year-old man was advised to start oral digoxin at a dose of 250 μg daily. His doctor explained that the full effect of this treatment would not be apparent for at least a week. Which one of the following pharmacokinetic variables did the doctor use to give this explanation?
expl: Digoxin follows first order kinetics and has a half-life of 36 to 48 hours in a patient with normal renal function. Sixty-five per cent of the drug absorbed remains in the system after one day. text: A 26 year old man has had behavioural disturbance recently. His parents mentioned that his brother has been investigated for liver problems recently. On examination, he has a MMSE score of 28/30. He has a mask like face and was noticed to have hypersalivation. When investigations are complete, which drug is most likely to be used for treatment?
expl: The likely diagnosis is Wilson's disease. Most patients who present with neuropsychiatric manifestations have cirrhosis. The most common presenting neurologic feature is asymmetric tremor, occurring in approximately half of individuals with Wilson disease. Frequent early symptoms include difficulty speaking, excessive salivation, ataxia, masklike facies, clumsiness with the hands, and personality changes. The disease is autosomal recessive. Zinc is used for treatment of Wilson disease. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 415Pg: 3236

text: What is the treatment of choice for restless leg syndrome?
expl: Most RLS sufferers have mild symptoms that do not require specific treatment. General measures to improve sleep hygiene and quality should be attempted first. If symptoms remain intrusive, low doses of dopamine agonists, e.g., pramipexole (0.25-0.5 mg), ropinirole (1-2 mg), or patch rotigotine (2-3 mg), taken 1-2 h before bedtime are generally effective. Levodopa may also be effective but is more likely to be associated with augmentation (spread and worsening of restlessness and its appearance earlier in the day) or rebound (reappearance sometimes with worsening of symptoms at a time related to the drug's short half-life). Augmentation can also be seen with dopamine agonists, particularly if higher doses are employed. Other drugs that can be effective include anticonvulsants, analgesics, and opiates. Management of secondary RLS should be directed to correcting the underlying disorder; for example, iron replacement for anemia. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 436, Pg: 3402

ansText: Inj Cytarabine (100-200mg/m2) + Inj Daunorubicin (60-90 mg/m2) [7+3 regimen]
expl: The treatment for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is divided into two phases - induction and postremission management (consolidation). The initial goal is to induce complete remission. The regimen most commonly used in younger patients is - Cytarabine (S-phase–specific antimetabolite) used at standard dose (100-200 mg/m 2 ) is administered as a continuous intravenous infusion for 7 days . With cytarabine, anthracycline therapy (DNA intercalator) generally consists of daunorubicin (60-90 mg/m 2 ) or idarubicin (12 mg/m 2 ) intravenously on days 1, 2, and 3 ( the 7 and 3 regimen ). With the 7 and 3 regimen, it is now clearly established that 45 mg/m 2 dosing of daunorubicin results in inferior outcomes. Older patients , especially those >65 years or with adverse risk disease, or those who are unfit for intensive anthracycline + cytarabine regimens, may be considered for investigational therapy alone or in combination with lower intensity chemotherapy (azacitidine, decitabine, cytarabine), or lower intensity chemotherapy in combination with venetoclax. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 104, Pg: 813

text: A 28 year old intravenous drug user complains about severe epigastric pains, nausea and vomiting. He has upper GI endoscopy which shows small areas of ulceration and white plaques. Which of the following is the best treatment option?
expl: This is a patient with possible HIV who has oesophageal candidiasis (white plaques on endoscopy). Candida is normally found in the throat but can become pathogenic and produce esophagitis in a compromised host. Candida albicans is most common cause. Oral fluconazole for 14-21 days is the preferred treatment. Patients refractory to fluconazole may respond to voriconazole or posaconazole. text: A girl presents with prolonged menstrual bleeding. Her platelet count, PT, and aPTT are all normal, but bleeding time is prolonged. Further testing reveals a deficiency of GpIIb-IIIa. What is the diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The clinical history and lab findings point to Glanzmann Thrombasthenia, a congenital platelet disorder caused by defective platelet aggregation due to a deficiency of the Gp IIb/IIIa receptor, which is crucial for platelet-to-platelet adhesion. Recombinant Factor VIIa (rFVIIa) can be useful for patients undergoing surgery or those who do not respond to platelet transfusions. It works by enhancing thrombin generation at the site of vascular injury, promoting hemostasis despite platelet dysfunction. Glanzmann Thrombasthenia Type: Congenital bleeding disorder Inheritance: Autosomal recessive, often associated with consanguinity Genetics: Mutations on chromosome 17 Pathophysiology: Absence of platelet Gp IIb/IIIa receptors, essential for platelet aggregation and blood clot formation Clinical Features: Lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding episodes Frequent epistaxis, especially in children Gingival bleeding Gastrointestinal bleeding Menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding) Investigations: Treatment: Explanation for other options: Bernard-Soulier syndrome (BSS) (Option A): also known as Hemorrhagiparous Thrombolytic Dystrophy, is a rare inherited bleeding disorder characterized by abnormally large platelets, thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), and prolonged bleeding time. It usually presents at birth and persists throughout life. Hemophilia A (Option C): typically presents severely within the first few months of life, while milder forms are often detected later in childhood or adolescence, frequently after trauma or incidentally. About two-thirds of cases are diagnosed shortly after the birth of an affected son to a carrier mother. Laboratory findings show a prolonged aPTT with a normal PT. Von Willebrand disease (Option D): often goes undiagnosed as many affected individuals do not have significant bleeding symptoms. In coagulation studies, aPTT may be prolonged while PT remains normal. Von Willebrand factor deficiency or dysfunction underlies this disorder. Reference: Glanzmann Thrombasthenia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf GLANZMANN's THROMBASTHENIA-SPECTRUM OF CLINICAL PRESENTATION ON SAUDI PATIENTS IN THE EASTERN PROVINCE - PMC

text: What is the recommended immediate medical treatment for a patient with a severe history of a road traffic accident who exhibits signs of elevated intracranial pressure upon examination?

options.B: Initiate anticoagulant therapy to prevent blood clot formation

expl: Explanation: In a trauma patient with signs of elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), the immediate goal is to reduce brain edema and prevent herniation. Mannitol is a first-line hyperosmolar agent used for this purpose. Mechanism of Action Osmotic Effect: Mannitol creates an osmotic gradient that draws water out of the brain parenchyma (across an intact blood-brain barrier) into the vasculature, reducing cerebral edema and intracranial volume. Rheologic Effect: It temporarily expands plasma volume, reduces blood viscosity, and improves cerebral blood flow and oxygen delivery. Explanation of other options: Administer antibiotics (Option A): Antibiotics are crucial for preventing infection in open skull fractures or base of skull fractures with CSF leak, but they do not directly address acute raised ICP. Initiate anticoagulant therapy (Option B): Anticoagulants are contraindicated in the acute phase of traumatic brain injury due to the high risk of promoting or worsening intracranial hemorrhage. Perform immediate surgical intervention (Option C): Surgery (e.g., evacuation of a hematoma, decompressive craniectomy) may be the definitive treatment, but it requires prior imaging (CT scan) to identify the surgical lesion. Medical management with agents like mannitol is often initiated before or while preparing for surgery to stabilize the patient. Key Takeaways: Mannitol (or hypertonic saline) is a key medical therapy for rapidly lowering raised ICP in traumatic brain injury. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10329884/

text: Which of the following statements is false?

options.A: Hematological abnormalities may not be seen in approximately 40% of patients with Sub acute combined degeneration due to cobalamine deficinecy.
options.B: In patients with food cobalamine malabsorption, oral cobalamine is sufficient to correct the deficiency.
options.C: Treatment of cobalamine deficiency will completely reverse the neurological manifestations.
options.D: Methylmalanoic acid and Homocysteine levels may be elevated in Cobalamine deficiency.

ansText: Treatment of cobalamine deficiency will completely reverse the neurological manifestations.
expl: This question deals with the clinical features of Cobalamine deficncy. Haematological abnormalities like macrocytic anemia will not be seen in 40% of patients with Subacute combined degeneration. In cobalamine deficiency, there will be blocade of steps that require cobalamine as cofactor and hence homocysteine and methyl manioc acid will be accumulated. In patients with pernicious anemia, the management is parenteral cyanocobalamine. But in food cobalamine malabsorption, the patients can absorb free cobalamine and hence oral supplementation is enough, at the dose of 1000mcg/day. The haematological abnormalities completely respond to cobalamine replacement. But the neurologoical manifestations tend to be permanent in about 50% patients. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, ch:446, Pg: 3496

text: A 22-year-old woman with type-1 diabetes presents with an unusual lesion on her shin. It began as a patch of spreading erythema, but now looks yellow and has begun to ulcerate. What diagnosis best fits this lesion?
expl: Necrobiosis lipoidica occurs in patients with type-1 diabetes, beginning as a patch of erythema that spreads across the shin, begins to yellow and then may ulcerate. Acanthosis nigricans is associated with insulin resistance and may occur in those with type-2 diabetes and is usually found in the axillas. Granuloma annulare is normally diffuse in diabetes and occurs as a ring of papules. Dermatitis herpetiformis is, of course, associated with coeliac disease (gluten enteropathy). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Ch:398 Pg:2882

text: A 26 year old bartender has had abdominal pains and loose stools for 3 years. He also has symptoms of myalgia and profound fatigue. He mentions that the abdominal pains are often worse after he has bread. An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay test was conducted and it showed positive reactions to gluten, albumin, lactose, barley, and rye. Which of the following is not found in the disease?
expl: This is a case of celiac disease . The following antibodies are found- Antibodies against tissue transglutaminase IgA Antiendomysial antibodies Deamidated anti-gliadin antibodies. Serum IgA levels are measured to detect false-negative results from IgA deficiency. Deamidated anti-gliadin IgG antibodies or tissue transglutaminase IgG antibodies are detectable and diagnostic in IgA-deficient patients. Small intestinal biopsy is the confirmatory test . Biopsies typically show characteristic villus blunting, crypt hyperplasia, and inflammation, including increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 318, Pg: 2251 - 2253

text: A 40-year-old patient presents with chronic diarrhea, fatigue, and exhibits the nail findings shown below (Koilonychia). Hemoglobin is 8 gm%. What is the most appropriate treatment?
expl: Explanation: The presentation of microcytic anemia (implied by low Hb) with Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) is pathognomonic for chronic, severe Iron Deficiency Anemia . The chronic diarrhoea suggests a possible gastrointestinal source of blood loss or malabsorption. Rationale for Treatment Iron Supplementation: This is the definitive treatment to correct the deficiency and replenish stores. It addresses the root cause of the anemia and the associated nail changes. Investigate the Cause: The chronic diarrhea necessitates investigation for underlying GI pathology like celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or a occult bleeding source. Explanation of other options: Folic acid & Vitamin B12 (Option A and D): These are used to treat macrocytic anaemia's, not microcytic anaemia. Koilonychia is not a feature of these deficiencies. Metronidazole(Option B): This is an antibiotic/antiparasitic agent. It would only be indicated if a specific infection (e.g., giardiasis) causing the diarrhoea and malabsorption were diagnosed, but it does not treat the iron deficiency itself. Key Takeaways: Koilonychia is a classic sign of severe, long-standing Iron Deficiency Anemia. The presence of anemia with GI symptoms like diarrhea should prompt a search for a GI cause of iron loss or malabsorption

text: A 22-year-old woman presented with painful oral ulcers. Her mother had history of thyroidectomy. Which of the following would suggest polyglandular syndrome type 1?
expl: Polyglandular syndrome type 1 is an autosomal recessive condition due to mutation in AIRE gene. It is associated with: hypoparathyroidism in around 90% mucocutaneous candidiasis in 100% adrenal insufficiency in around 60% primary gonadal failure primary hypothyroidism Ectodermal dystrophy There may be associated malabsorption, pernicious anaemia, chronic active hepatitis or vitiligo. Polyglandular syndrome type 2 may be autosomal-recessive, autosomal-dominant or polygenic. It leads to: Adrenal insufficiency (all patients) hypothyroidism (hashimoto thyroiditis) type-1 diabetes gonadal failure diabetes insipidus. Associated conditions include vitiligo, myasthenia gravis, alopecia, immune thrombocytopaenic purpura or pernicious anaemia. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3186

text: A 43 year old woman has previously had a right hemicolectomy and resection of 30 cms of terminal ileum for ileocaecal Crohn's disease. She has persistent diarrhoea, which is not explosive. She does not have abdominal pain, bloating, or loss of weight. Investigations have failed to demonstrate evidence of recurrent Crohn's disease. Which is the best therapy for the symptoms?
expl: The patient has had resection of the terminal ileum and the cause of the diarrhoea is likely to be due to Bile Acid Malabsorption (BAM). This causes a secretory diarrhoea that worsens with eating . Bile acids are required for absorption of fat. Cholic acid and Chenodeoxycholic acid are the primary bile acids, that are conjugated by liver with Taurine and Glycine, to maintain their levels in the small bowel and facilitate the absorption of lipids. Once the lipids are absorbed, the bile acids are reabsorbed by enterohepatic circulation from the terminal ileum. So the disease processes that affect any of these steps will result in luminal deficiency of bile salt and malabsorption. Examples are Of these, the diseases affecting the terminal ileum or if If large area of ileum is affected, >100cm, there will be spillage of the bile acids into the colon and also there will be malabsorption due to loss of large areas of the small bowel. This is called Fatty acid Diarrhoea. This will not respond to Cholestyramine and will be associated with steatorrhoea. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 325, Pg: 2461

text: A 62 lady has symptoms of intermittent abdominal pain and loose stool which have occurred over 1 year. Investigations reveal: Hb 8.5 g/dl MCV 85 fl WCC 6 x 10^9/l Iron 11 (14-29) μmol/l Ferritin 20 (15-200) μmol/l Folate 2 (3-20) microg/l What investigation should be done?
expl: The combined iron and folate deficiency anaemia as well as symptoms suggestive of malabsorption makes celiac disease a likely diagnosis. Celiac disease involves the proximal small bowel - duodenum and jejunum. Biopsy typically shows characteristic villus blunting, crypt hyperplasia, and inflammation, including increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Patients with suspected Celiac disease is first screened for by measuring the tissue trans glutaminase IgA, anti endomysial and deamidated anti gliadin antibody. A total IgA levels should be measured to detect false negative values due to IgA deficiency. Small intestinal biopsy will be done in those with a positive antibody screening. HLA DQ2 and DQ8 are the host genetic factor associated with Celiac Disease. But most of the carriers of these will not develop the disease and is of negative predictive value. This is of value in patients who self discontinued gluten in the diet prior to serology or endoscopy, in whom, the antibodies may be negative and the endoscopy may be normal. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 325, Pg: 2463

text: A 65-year-old male presents with a four month history of diarrhoea with pale stools and weight loss. Relevant results show: Calcium 6.9 mg/dL Alkaline phosphatase 350 U/L (45-105) What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The patient has a marked hypocalcaemia associated with malabsorption. The raised alkaline phosphatase may represent osteomalacia, pancreatic carcinoma, metastasis or even biliary obstruction/disease. In this age pancreatic carcinoma is the most probable diagnosis. Celiac disease very seldom causes such an increased alkaline phosphatase and is more likely to present with iron deficiency anaemia. Giardia commonly involves the proximal small bowel and does not cause elevated alkaline phosphatase. Whipple's is extremely rare, found in middle aged men and caused by a bacillus, Tropheryma whippeli. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 83, Pg: 659

text: A 30 year old male who was staying in Cuba for the past one year, now comes with history of chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and multiple nutritional deficiencies. He had tried stopping wheat and barley in his diet, but with no improvement in symptoms. A small bowel biopsy showed villous blunting with dense mononuclear infiltrate. The tissue transglutaminase antibody is negative. What will be the next best step?

options.A: Broad spectrum antibiotics with folate supplementation

ansText: Broad spectrum antibiotics with folate supplementation
expl: The history of malabsorption with a recent stay in Cuba points to the diagnosis of Tropical sprue. However, it could be a refractory celiac disease also, where the patient stops responding to gluten restriction, will have negative antibody screen and have active histopathological findings. In such cases an HLA DQ testing should be the next best step. But here since the history states that he is coming from a country in the tropics, a course of antibiotics and folate supplementation will be the next best cost effective step. Tropical sprue is considered to be post infectious complication. It is seen in countries like Southern India, Phillipines, Puerto- Rico, Pakistan and Cuba. It is characterized by severe malabsorption and two or more unrelated nutritional deficiencies including Vitamin B12 and Folic acid. The histopathology is very much similar to Celiac disease, but there will be more dense mononuclear infiltrate and they will have a negative antibody screen and will not respond to gluten restriction. The management is prolonged course of tetracyclines with folate supplementation, since folate malabsorption is prominent Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 325, Pg: 2464-2465

text: A 70-year-old male presents with progressive dysphagia for solids, significant weight loss, and cachexia over the past few months. Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation for this patient?
expl: Explanation: The presentation of progressive dysphagia for solids with significant weight loss and cachexia in an elderly patient strongly suggests oesophageal carcinoma. Upper GI endoscopy (UGIE) is the gold standard diagnostic tool. It allows direct visualization of the tumor and enables tissue biopsy for definitive diagnosis. UGIE also permits thorough examination of the larynx, trachea, and bronchi, which is crucial as this population has a higher risk of head and neck malignancies. Additionally, CT scanning of the chest and abdomen is typically performed to assess tumour spread to mediastinal and para-aortic lymph nodes. Explanation of other options: Manometry (Option B): While manometry is useful in diagnosing esophageal motility disorders such as achalasia. Manometry cannot provide visual confirmation of tumors or allow for tissue sampling. Barium swallow (Option C) : Barium swallow is indicated only in motility disorders like achalasia, gastroparesis and in detecting perforations or fistula. Barium meal follow through (Option D) : Primarily used to evaluate the small intestine and helps in evaluating suspected malabsorption, Crohn's disease etc.

text: Which of the following is most commonly associated with the development of pseudomembranous colitis?
expl: Clostridium difficile a Gram positive anaerobic bacterium is the cause of pseudomembranous colitis. Studies show that when C. difficile colonise the gut they release two potent toxins, toxin A and toxin B, which bind to certain receptors in the lining of the colon and ultimately cause diarrhoea and inflammation of the large intestine or colon (colitis). Commonly the disease is caused by broad spectrum antibiotics most commonly cephalosporins , broad spectrum penicillins and clindamycin . Less commonly, macrolides and quinolones have been reported to cause the disorder. Oral Vancomycin and Fidaxomycin are the agents used for mild infections. Metronidazole is reserved for fulminant cases. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 138, Pg: 1069
