text: A 20 year old male was brought for psychiatric evaluation for intellectual disability. On examination, his IQ was 45. He has a long face, large ears, large testis and a cardiac murmur and history of poor intellectual function is present in the paternal family. What is his diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The clinical presentation is classic for Fragile X syndrome , an X-linked dominant disorder caused by CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion (>200 repeats) in the FMR1 gene , with premutation carriers having 55-200 repeats and the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability . Key features include: Intellectual disability (IQ ~45) Characteristic facial features : Long face, large prominent ears. Macroorchidism (large testicles) Mitral valve prolapse (causing murmur) Positive family history on the paternal side (X-linked inheritance) It is more common in males, while females are usually carriers.Female carriers may present with premature ovarian failure, and about 10% can show low IQ or intellectual impairment. Explanation of other options: Cushing's syndrome (Option A): Characterized by centripetal obesity, moon facies, hypertension, and hyperglycemia, not intellectual disability or the described dysmorphic features. Rett syndrome (Option B): An X-linked dominant disorder almost exclusively affecting females, characterized by developmental regression, loss of purposeful hand skills, and stereotypic hand movements. Williams syndrome (Option D): Characterized by "elfin" facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis, and a highly sociable personality, not macroorchidism or a strong X-linked family history. Key Takeaways: Fragile X syndrome should be suspected in males with intellectual disability, characteristic facies, and macroorchidism. It is caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome.

text: A 29 year old man presents with a 4 week history of a painful swollen left knee. He has a past medical history of a treated sexually transmitted disease 6 months ago. On examination there was a large effusion in the left knee. Synovial fluid analysis shows a white cell count of 15 x 10^9/L but culture was negative. Which one of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
expl: History of sexually transmitted disease, followed by a monoarthritis favors the diagnosis of Gonococcal Arthritis. Gonococcal arthritis is caused by an infection with the gram-negative diplococcus N gonorrhoeae. Neisseria gonorrhoea occurs in young adults, often preceded by a migratory arthritis. The bacteremic phase is a classic triad of migratory polyarthritis, tenosynovitis, and dermatitis. This patient was treated previously for a sexually acquired infection hence may be the reason for the culture to be negative. Also, gonococci are rarely recovered from joint effusions. The initial treatment of choice for gonococcal arthritis is a third-generation beta-lactamase resistant cephalosporin (eg, ceftriaxone, ceftizoxime, cefotaxime) or a penicillin, if the organism is sensitive. Multiple intracellular gram negative diplococci Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 156 Pg: 1239

text: A 27-year-old man is noted to have cyanosis of the lower limbs and clubbing of the toes but not the fingers. The blood pressure in the arm and lower limb is the same. Which of the following statements is true?

options.B: He has coarctation of the aorta.
options.C: He is likely to have a loud continuous 'machinery' murmur below the left clavicle.
options.D: He is likely to need urgent surgery.

expl: Differential cyanosis (cyanosis only in lower extremities) is seen in a patient with patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) when there is reversal of shunt. There is a right-left shunt from the pulmonary artery to the aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery. This is Eisenmenger's syndrome. Coarctation causes radiofemoral delay and a lower blood pressure in the leg as compared to the arm. It may be associated with PDA but there is no suggestion in this patient. Continuous machinery murmur is the classic murmur of PDA but when the shunt reverses (as in patients with a large PDA and/or pulmonary disease) the murmur becomes softer and shorter. When Eisenmenger's syndrome has developed surgery is associated with a very high mortality. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:264 pg:1838,1839

text: A 42 year old man who usually drinks only 2 units of alcohol a day went on an alcohol binge with his friends. On that day, he vomited 10 times and was brought to hospital feeling very unwell. He has not previously had any symptoms of dyspepsia or abdominal pains. During physical assessment, he vomits a large bowlful of blood. What is the likely cause of his haemetemesis?
expl: This is a case of Mallory Weiss tear . Longitudinal tear in the mucosa at the gastroesophageal junction . Caused by forceful or prolonged vomiting or coughing. They may also be caused by epileptic convulsions. Usually seen in alcoholics, bulimia nervosa patients. The tear may be followed by vomiting bright red blood or by passing blood in the stool. Active bleed can be treated by endoscopy (band ligation or coaptive coagulation). A transmural rupture at gastroesophageal junction is called Boerhaave's syndrome. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2433

text: Medial calcification is seen in -
expl: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Monckebergs sclerosis First see types of arteries Based on their size and structural features, arteries are divided into three types. Large or Elastic arteries Aorta Its large branches, eg. - Innominate, Subclavian, common carotid, iliac. Pulmonary arteries. Medium sized or muscular arteries Small branches of aorta → Coronary, Renal Small arteries and arterioles Within substance of the tissue Now see their affection ? Arteriosclerosis Dont get confuse with atherosclerosis. Arteriosclerosis means hardening of arteries by thickening and loss of elasticity of arterial wall. o There are three patterns of arteriosclerosis. Atherosclerosis Characterized by intimal lesions, i.e. atheromas, which project into vascular lumen and may obstruct it. o This is the most common pattern of arteriosclerosis. It is a degenerative and apparently non-inflammatory disease. Media of these arteries becomes calcified. It occurs in patients older than 50 years.

text: Dystrophin absent and presence of small muscle fibrils cause?
expl: Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy are the Dystrophinopaties. DMD is characterized by absent dystrophin and Becker's muscular dystrophy is characterized by either decreased level or size of dystrophin. Total absence of dystrophin points to the diagnosis of DMD. Biopsy is not diagnostic in myopathies. So the microscopy will be almost the same for DMD and BMD. Muscle biopsy in young ages will show degeneration and regeneration of muscle fibres with preserved architecture. There is no active inflammation except for myophagocytosis. As the disease progresses, the muscle fibers are replaced by fatty infiltration. The remaining muscle fibers show varying size from atrophic to hypertrophic. Immunohistochemical staining shows absence of sarcolemmal staining in DMD and reduced staining in BMD. They are both XL recessive inheritance. Dystrophin provides stability to the muscle fibre by acting as a bridge between the cytoskeleton inside the muscle fibre and the basement membrane outside the cell. DMD results from deletions or frameshift mutations in the dystrophin gene, leading to total absence of the protein, whereas BMD results in the formation of truncated variant of dystrophin that leads to partially functional protein.

text: A 25-year-old female presents with red crusted lesions around the mouth and finger pulps, three months after having had small bowel resection for Crohn's disease. What is the most likely cause of her skin condition?
expl: The features of this patient who had bowel resection suggest zinc deficiency . Zinc deficiency can lead to a condition called acrodermatitis enteropathica which presents with diarrhea, alopecia, muscle wasting, depression, irritability, and a rash involving the extremities, face (perioral), and perineum . The rash is characterized by vesicular and pustular crusting with scaling and erythema. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:333 Pg: 2532

text: Which of the following statements regarding SSc is false?

options.A: ESR is usually normal in SSc, and an elevated ESR indicates coexisting myositis or malignancy
options.B: Sicca Syndrome can occur with SSC and is due to lymphocytic infiltration
options.C: Trigeminal neuropathy may occur with SSc
options.D: SSc may represent a paraneoplastic manifestation in those with malignancies of breast, lung or ovarian carcinoma and is associated with RNA polymerase III

ansText: Sicca Syndrome can occur with SSC and is due to lymphocytic infiltration
expl: Sicca symptoms are common in SSc, but unlike in Sjogren's Syndrome, it is due to fibrosis of the glands rather than lymphocytic infiltration. ESR is usually normal in SSc, since there is no active inflammation of vessel walls. A high ESR indicates myositis or malignancy. The CNS is usually spared in SSc, the only CNS manifestation could be unilateral or bilateral trigeminal neuropathy. Breast, lung, ovarian malignancy and lymphoma may occur in temporal association with SSc, where SSc may represent a paraneoplastic manifestation and is associated with antibodies to RNA polymerase III Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 360, Pg: 2783

text: A 21-year-old woman with no underlying health conditions presents with numbness and tingling in the fingers of both hands. The image below shows a characteristic finding. She reports that these episodes typically occur during periods of high stress or exposure to cold weather. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: This patient is most likely experiencing Primary Raynaud's phenomenon because: She is a young female (age 20-40 years; female-to-male ratio 5:1) There is no underlying disease Symptoms are symmetrical Episodes are triggered by cold Raynaud's Phenomenon Overview: Primary Raynaud's: Typically affects young women No associated underlying illness Normal nail fold capillaries with regular hairpin loops Accounts for over 50% of cases Has a better prognosis-improves in 15%, worsens in 30% Characterized by classic triphasic color changes (white, blue, red) Secondary Raynaud's (Option B ruled out): Commonly caused by connective tissue diseases, especially scleroderma (Option D ruled out) Other causes include arterial occlusive diseases, blood disorders, certain drugs (ergot, beta-blockers, bleomycin), and occupational exposures (vibrating tools) Clinical Features: Sequential color changes: White (ischemia) → Blue (deoxygenation) → Red (reperfusion) Triggered by cold or emotional stress Can involve fingers, toes, nose, ears May be accompanied by pain, numbness, or tingling Treatment: Conservative: Warm clothing, avoiding cold, smoking cessation Medications for severe cases: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, alpha-1 blockers (prazosin), phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, topical nitroglycerin Digital sympathectomy for refractory cases Explanation of other options: Cold sores (Option C): are caused by the herpes virus and present as small fluid-filled blisters on the lips, mouth, nose, or cheeks, which does not fit this patient's symptoms or presentation.

text: A 26 year old patient who is a known case of SLE is coming to you with a positive UPT. She is on 5mg prednisolone and 200 mg HCQ daily and her disease is well controlled. What advice will you give her?

options.A: It is safe to continue both prednisolone and HCQs
options.B: Prednisolone has to be changed to Dexamethasone, HCQS is safe and may be continued
options.C: Prednisolone is safe and can be continued, but HCQS has to be stopped
options.D: No need to continue treatment as the disease is well controlled

ansText: It is safe to continue both prednisolone and HCQs
expl: SLE and Pregnancy: Rate of fetal loss is high in people with SLE than in general population and hence treatment has to be continued. So option D is incorrect. Risk of fetal loss in SLE is associated with high disease activity, APLA, Lupus nephritis and Hypertension. Prednisolone is the drug that can be given in pregnancy since 11β degydrogenase in placenta inactivates it and prevents fetal exposure. 11β dehydrogenase cant inactivate fluorinated glucocorticoids like dexamethasone and hence it is contraindicated in pregnecy, except for neonatal lupus. HCQS is also recommended by FDA for controlling disease activity in pregnancy. Drugs used in treatment of SLE in pregnancy First line agents: prednisone, prednisolone, HCQ Second line agents: Azathioprine. (May cause fetal harm) Breast feeding is contraindicated with immunosuppressants Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21th edition Ch:346 Pg:2747

text: What is the entry criteria in the new ACR/EULAR classification scheme for SLE?
expl: It is important to know that ANA is a highly sensitive test and thus a good screening test. In the new ACR/EULAR classification scheme, ANA positivity of more than 1:80 by ELISA is the entry criterion for classification to SLE. SLICC does not have such entry criteria. The old SLICC criteria did not have any such entry criterion. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:356 Pg:2741

text: Which of the following statements is false?

options.B: It spares fingers and Raynaud's phenomenon is rare
options.D: Linear scleroderma can cross joints leading to contractures and can cause growth retardation of long bones

expl: Localized scleroderma is more common in children. Raynaud's phenomenon is rare. There is no finger involvement. Internal organ involvement is rare. Linear scleroderma can cross joints causing contractures and growth retardation of long bones. Eosinophilic fasciitis is a disorder of adults which presents as skin thickening, having the same features as above. There will not be auto antibodies in SSc. Fingers will be spared and there will be no internal organ involvement. It is often seen in association with myelodysplastic syndrome or multiple myeloma. text: A 25-year-old female presented with a sudden onset of left sided head and neck pain. 24 hours later she presents with sudden onset of right hemiparesis, facial weakness and homonymous hemianopia and left Horner's syndrome. A CT brain showed a left middle cerebral artery territory infarction. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The presence of neck pain on the left side, followed by a right sided weakness points to the diagnosis of carotid dissection. The two commonest causes of young onset stroke (less than 40 years) are cardio-embolism and carotid artery dissection. Carotid artery dissection is either spontaneous or traumatic. Facial/head/neck pain and Horner's syndrome are characteristic features. Migrainous stroke usually affects the posterior circulation (posterior cerebral artery territory is the commonest). text: A 38-year-old woman is referred to the gastroenterology clinic. The patient has persistent lethargy and blood results have demonstrated iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following statements regarding iron deficiency anemia is correct?

options.A: Endomysial antibody serology to investigate for coeliac disease should always be requested in addition to duodenal biopsies
options.B: Low serum iron with a low total iron-binding capacity confirms iron deficiency
options.C: Microcytosis may be absent where there is combined iron and folate deficiency
options.D: The presence of Howell-Jolly bodies on blood film would go against coeliac disease

ansText: Microcytosis may be absent where there is combined iron and folate deficiency
expl: Distal duodenal (D2) biopsies should be taken in any patient with iron deficiency anemia undergoing a gastroscopy as 2-3% of patients will have celiac disease. Endomysial antibody serology can be useful to confirm that subtotal villous atrophy found at histology is not due to another cause.Antibody titres help to determine whether or not the patient is adhering to a gluten free diet. In the investigation of iron deficiency anemia serology for coeliac disease would be performed prior to an OGD. Low serum iron ( high total iron-binding capacity (> 70 pmol/L) confirms iron deficiency. Howell-Jolly bodies on blood film indicate hyposplenism and are consistent with a diagnosis of coeliac disease. Thrombocytosis may occur in acute hemorrhage but is also found in a number of other situations such as inflammatory conditions. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 325, Pg: 2463

text: A 42 year old man is referred to the renal physician due to symptoms of haemoptysis and haematuria. These symptoms have been going on for 6 months. expl: The patient has pulmonary renal syndrome, and among the given options, the diagnosis would fit Wegener's granulomatosis, which is commonly cANCA positive. text: A 54 year old man presents with a 6 week history of lethargy and diffuse purpuric rash. He is noted to have a right foot drop and a left ulnar nerve palsy. He complains of arthralgia but has no clinical evidence of inflammatory joint disease. Echocardiogram is unremarkable, blood cultures are negative, ESR 80 mm/hr, ANCA negative, ANA negative, rheumatoid factor strongly positive, C3 1.1 g/l (0.75 - 1.6), C4 0.03 g/l (0.14 - 0.5). Dipstick urinalysis shows blood ++. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: A low C4 together with a strongly positive rheumatoid factor suggests cryoglobulinemia as a cause of mononeuritis multiplex and rash. Palpable purpura, arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly, diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis, Raynaud's phenomenon and thrombosis may occur. Type I cryoglobulinemia may be associated with lymphoproliferative disorders, multiple myeloma, and monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance, and macroglobulinemia. Plasmapheresis may reduce the levels of cryoglobulin. Type II cryoglobulinemia (mixed monoclonal) is usually composed of a monoclonal component (usually IgG, IgM or IgA) and a polyclonal component (mainly IgG). Causes are connective tissue diseases, Hepatitis B and C infection, infectious mononucleosis and lymphoma. Reference: Harrison's Principles Of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:363 Pg:2814

text: A 24-year-old lady presents to the clinic with a painfully swollen hot right knee. She gives a 2-week history of migratory polyarthritis and urethritis. Clinical examination reveals a pustular skin rash, right Achilles tendinitis and left plantar fasciitis. She is HLA-B27 negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The presence of arthritis, urethritis and enthesitis makes the possibility of Reactive arthritis as well as Gonococcal arthritis. 10-15% of reactive arthritis may be HLA B27 negative. But the point in favour of Gonococcal arthritis is the migratory arthritis. The arthritis in Reactive arthritis is additive. The rash in Gonococcal infection is pustular. Disseminated Gonococcal infection is a rare entity having a bacteremic phase, characterized by fever, migratory arthritis, enthesitis and rash, followed by a septic arthritic phase characterised by a monoarthritis. text: A patient presents with severe pain and swelling in his knee joint for 10 days. He also complains of pain and discomfort during urination. He says that he had diarrhea one month ago and he has been unwell since then. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation : This is a classic presentation of Reactive Arthritis (Reiter's Syndrome) , which is characterized by an asymmetric oligoarthritis (often affecting the knees) that develops 1-4 weeks after a genitourinary (e.g., Chlamydia) or gastrointestinal infection (e.g., Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter). Urethritis is a common extra-articular feature. Explanation of other options: Enteropathic arthritis (Option B): Associated with active Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) , not a preceding episode of infectious diarrhea. Rheumatoid arthritis (Option C): A symmetric polyarthritis of small joints, not typically triggered by infection or associated with urethritis. Psoriatic arthritis (Option D): Associated with psoriasis and can cause arthritis, dactylitis, and enthesitis, but not typically linked to a preceding GI or GU infection. Key Takeaways: Reactive arthritis is an autoimmune condition triggered by an infection at a distant site, often presenting with the classic triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis (can be incomplete).

text: Which of the following clinical feature cannot help in differentiating psoriatic arthritis from other forms of inflammatory arthritis?
expl: Explanation: Diarrhea is not a specific clinical marker for psoriatic arthritis (PsA). While some patients with PsA may have coexistent inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) , diarrhea is non-specific and can also occur in other arthritides such as reactive arthritis or enteropathic arthritis associated with IBD. In contrast, dactylitis (sausage digits) , enthesitis , and nail pitting are characteristic hallmarks that help distinguish PsA from other types like rheumatoid arthritis (RA) or osteoarthritis (OA) .

expl: This is a case of acute gout which has not settled on medical therapy (NSAIDs or colchicine). The raised inflammatory markers can be due to acute gout. text: A 32 year old woman has a 3 month history of arthralgia joint pain and early morning stiffness. There is swelling of the distal interphalangeal joints of the ring fingers of the hand. The wrist on the right and ankles are swollen as well. Onycholysis was noted on the nails. Her serum inflammatory markers are raised.Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
expl: The presence of joint pains and early morning stiffness points towards an inflammatory arthritis. The patient in the given question is suffering from an asymmetric oligoarthritis, with involvement of DIP, which rules out RA. The sparing of large proximal joints and the age of the patient speaks against a Polymyalgia rheumatica. There are no other indicators to suggest a chronic gout, like tophi. An asymmetric oligoarthritis with onycholysis points to the diagnosis of Psoriatic Arthritis. Wright and Moll described five patterns of Psoriatic Arthritis: arthritis of the DIP joints asymmetric oligoarthritis symmetric polyarthritis similar to RA axial involvement (spine and sacroiliac joints) arthritis mutilans, a highly destructive form of the disease. A simpler scheme in recent use contains three patterns: oligoarthritis, polyarthritis, and axial arthritis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 362, Pg: 2799

text: A 55-year-old male presents with symmetric polyarthritis involving the small joints of hands excluding the DIP, along with both wrist joints of 3 months duration. Which of the following statements favours the diagnosis of Psoriatic arthritis in this patient?

options.A: Psoriatic skin lesions are universally present in all patients with Psoriatic arthritis
options.B: Presence of axial spondylitis involving the Thoracolumbar spine favors the diagnosis of Psoriatic Arthritis
options.C: Presence of acute anterior uveitis favours the diagnosis of Psoriatic arthritis
options.D: The presence of nail changes favours the diagnosis of Psoriatic arthritis

ansText: The presence of nail changes favours the diagnosis of Psoriatic arthritis
expl: The usual presentation of Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) is arthritis involving the DIP. When it is symmetrical and sparing the DIP it may be mistaken for RA. However, it can be distinguished from RA by the presence of typical Psoriatic skin lesions. But skin disease occurs only in 70% of patients. In 15% cases, skin disease and arthritis occur within one year of onset of each other. In 15% cases, the skin lesions occur after the onset of arthritis. So it is possible that PsA can present even without skin lesions. In such cases, the clinician should search for psoriatic lesions in areas like scalp, behind the ears, umbilicus and in the gluteal region. Or, the clinician should look for nail changes. The nail changes will be seen in most of the patients with PsA. The nail changes include pitting, horizontal ridges, yellowish discolouration of nails, dystrophic hyperkeratosis and onycholysis. PsA is a spondyloarthritis, making other like AS DDs. But what makes it different from AS is that PsA involves the cervical spine more where as AS involves the thoracic spine and will not have the nail changes of psoriasis. Also the uveitis in AS is acute anterior uveitis, where as in PsA is insidious onset bilateral chronic posterior uveitis. So among the options, the answer is nail changes. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 362. Pg: 2799

text: Which of the following is not a characteristic finding of Gaisbock syndrome?
expl: Explanation: Hypotension is not a characteristic finding of Gaisbock syndrome . Gaisbock syndrome , commonly linked with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), involves secondary polycythemia caused by long-standing hypoxemia. In response to low oxygen levels, the body increases erythropoietin production, resulting in erythrocytosis. Patients usually present with high blood pressure rather than low blood pressure, due to the underlying lung condition and greater blood viscosity.

text: A 60-year-old man presents with a small amount of haemoptysis and breathlessness. He does not have pleuritic chest pain and has normal oxygen saturation. In considering the potential diagnosis, haemoptysis can occur with which of the following diagnoses?

text: For which of the following groups is pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine not routinely recommended?

options.A: Otherwise healthy adults aged 50 to 65 years
options.B: Adults aged 19 to 65 years who have immunocompromising conditions

ansText: Otherwise healthy adults aged 50 to 65 years
expl: Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is not recommended for otherwise healthy adults aged 50 to 65 years. This vaccine is, however recommended for persons who have immunocompromising conditions or lung disease (such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or asthma) and for persons who are cigarette smokers and heavy consumers of alcohol. Post splenectomy or hyposplenism is another indication There are 2 types of pneumococcal vaccine pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) and a protein conjugate pneumococcal vaccine (PCV13) Routine use of PCV13 is recommended among adults aged 65 and older . Individuals 65 years of age or older who have never received a pneumococcal vaccine should first receive PCV13 followed by a dose of PPSV23 6-12 months later . Individuals who have received more than one dose of PPSV23 should receive a dose of PCV13 more than 1 year after the last dose of PPSV23 was administered. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 146, Pg: 1177

text: A 13 year old male has recent onset breathlessness. He has a history of wheezing particularly during the summer when the pollen count is high.Which of these tests would help to confirm the diagnosis?
expl: The history of wheezing during pollen exposure suggests asthma. The best diagnostic test for asthma would be demonstration of variable airways obstruction with Bronchodilator reversibility and serial peak flow measurements. Reversibility is defined as a ≥12% increase in the FEV1 and an absolute increase of ≥200 mL at least 15 min after administration of a β2 -agonist or after several weeks of corticosteroid therapy. Diurnal peak flow variability of >20% has also been proposed as an indicator of reversible airways disease, but it is less reliable due to difficulties with quality control and variability of home assessments Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:287 Pg:2154

text: Patient presents with fever, nocturnal cough, breathlessness and wheezing for 4 weeks. Absolute eosinophil count >5000. X-ray shows a military pattern. Diagnosis?
expl: The given history and lab findings suggestive of tropical pulmonary Eosinophilia. TROPICAL PULMONARY EOSINOPHILIA Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE) is a distinct syndrome that develops in some individuals infected with the lymphatic- dwelling filarial species. The majority of cases have been reported from India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Brazil, Guyana, and Southeast Asia; the decreasing incidence of TPE in last decade probably reflects global MDA efforts. CLINICAL FEATURES The main features include a history of residence in filaria-endemic regions, paroxysmal cough and wheezing (usually nocturnal probably related to the nocturnal periodicity of microfilariae), weight loss, low-grade fever, lymphadenopathy, and pronounced blood eosin- ophilia (>3000 eosinophils/µL). Chest x-rays or CT scans may be normal, but generally show increased bronchovascular markings. Diffuse miliary lesions or mottled opacities may be present in the middle and lower lung fields. Tests of pulmonary function show restrictive abnor- malities in most cases and obstructive defects in half. Characteristically, total serum IgE levels (4-40 KIU/mL) and anti filarial antibody levels are markedly elevated.

text: A 71-year-old man presents with difficulty speaking. He has a history of diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He is currently on aspirin, simvastatin, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. On examination the patient is awake, his blood pressure is 150/70 mmHg. His pulse is irregularly irregular. He has 4/5 strength in the right arm and leg and 5/5 strength on the left. When asked to point to the window he does this correctly. When told to raise his arms and place his hands out he is seen to have a pronator drift on the right. He is shown a pen and asked what it is. He responds fluently but makes some paraphasic errors. He is asked to use it appropriately and begins to write on a piece of paper. When asked to repeat 'Today is a sunny day', he is unable to do so. Which of the following terms best describes these signs?
expl: In Broca's or nonfluent or expressive aphasia the patient is unable to name objects with poor comprehension and repetition. It localises to the Broca's area in the left posterior inferior frontal gyrus. In transcortical motor aphasia, which localises to the anterior superior frontal lobe, the patient is has good comprehension and repetition but has halting, effortful speech. Patients also have impaired writing skills. Transcortical sensory aphasia is characterised by impaired auditory comprehension with intact repetition and fluent speech, and is caused by damage to the temporal lobes. It differs from Wernicke's aphasia in that patients still have intact repetition, and exhibit echolalia (the compulsive repetition of words). Improvement may be seen with speech therapy. Anomic aphasia (also known as nominal aphasia) results in word finding difficulties. On closer examination there may also be repetition problems and comprehension problems but these are typically mild compared to other aphasia syndromes. This scenario describes conduction aphasia. It is characterised by frequent speech errors, impaired repetition, reduced phonological short-term memory and naming difficulties. In contrast to other forms of dysphasia, speech output is otherwise fluent and grammatically correct. Comprehension is intact. It is thought to be caused by left temporo-parietal region damage. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 30, Pg: 196

text: A 65-year-old man presents with a five day history of lower abdominal pain and diarrhea.He has a history of chronic obstructive airways disease (COAD) and has had numerous acute infective exacerbations over the last three months.On examination he was dehydrated, with a temperature of 38.6°C, a blood pressure of 102/72 mmHg and has a distended, tender abdomen.Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation for this patient?
expl: This is pseudomembranous colitis due to Clostridium difficile secondary to antibiotic usage for his COPD. Plain AXR is useful for diagnosing toxic dilatation and would be the investigation of choice here due to his abdominal distension, so toxic dilatation should be excluded prior to sigmoidoscopy. However it does not establish the diagnosis.Stool microscopy has no value but stool toxin assay is useful. A patient with diarrhea normally has involvement of the distal colon and rectum, and sigmoidoscopy with biopsy is helpful for rapid diagnosis but should not be performed if toxic dilatation is suspected.Patients with involvement of right colon usually have little or no diarrhoea. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 138, Pg: 1069

text: A 74-year-old man presents with difficulty speaking. He has a history of diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He is currently on aspirin, simvastatin, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. On examination the patient is awake, his blood pressure is 150/70 mmHg. His pulse is irregularly irregular. He has 4/5 strength on the right arm and leg and 5/5 strength on the left.When asked to point to the window he appears unable to do so. When told to raise his arms and place his hands out he does not. When visually shown the same action he is able to perform it. When asked to repeat 'Today is a sunny day', he is able to do so.With what is this type of dysphasia consistent?
expl: In Broca's or non-fluent or expressive aphasia the patient is unable to name objects with poor comprehension and repetition. It localises to the Broca's area in the left posterior inferior frontal gyrus. In Wernicke's or fluent or receptive aphasia the patient is able to form correct grammatical sentences but language content is incorrect. It localises to the dominant superior temporal gyrus. There is poor comprehension and repetition but verbal output is fluent. In transcortical motor aphasia, which localises to the anterior superior frontal lobe, the patient has good comprehension and repetition but has halting, effortful speech. Patients also have impaired writing skills. Global aphasia results in an almost mute patient: there is poor verbal output, comprehension, repetition and understanding. Transcortical sensory aphasia is what is described in this case. It is characterised by impaired auditory comprehension with intact repetition and fluent speech, and is caused by damage to the temporal lobes. It differs from Wernicke's aphasia in that patients still have intact repetition, and exhibit cholalia (the compulsive repetition of words). Improvement may be seen with speech therapy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 30, Pg: 196

text: A patient with Parkinson's disease had aspiration pneumonitis. How will you manage this patient?
expl: Explanation: PEG gastrostomy tube insertion is the best appropriate step for long-term prevention of recurrent aspiration pneumonia. Chronic neurological illnesses such as Parkinson's disease or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis often cause oropharyngeal dysphagia , creating a high risk of recurrent aspiration. Nasogastric feeding can provide temporary nutrition but does not prevent aspiration of saliva or refluxed gastric contents. For long-term support, a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) is frequently chosen to deliver food directly into the stomach and reduce episodes of aspiration pneumonia. A PEG tube offers several advantages: it avoids nasal irritation, is less prone to accidental displacement, and allows more reliable feeding. After placement, a fibrous tract typically matures in about 10 days . If the tube is removed or dislodged before this tract is established, gastric contents can leak into the peritoneal cavity, posing a significant risk of peritonitis . Explanation for other Options: High frequency chest oscillation (Option A): This airway-clearance technique is used in conditions with thick secretions (e.g., cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis). It does not address the root cause of aspiration in Parkinson's disease and will not prevent further aspiration episodes. Macrolides (Option B): Antibiotics such as azithromycin are indicated for bacterial pneumonia , not for chemical aspiration pneumonitis , which is an inflammatory injury from gastric/oral contents.They do not prevent future aspiration. N-acetylcysteine (Option C): Functions as a mucolytic or an antidote for acetaminophen toxicity . It has no established role in treating or preventing aspiration pneumonitis.

text: A 28-year-old woman is referred with intermittent diarrhoea present for a couple of years. She states that her weight has been steady but describes watery motions up to six stools per day and has also noted abdominal discomfort with bloating. She has not been aware of any blood in the motions or melaena. She describes no other medical history and denies taking any medication. Investigations show: Complete blood count : Normal Urea and electrolytes : Normal Albumin 3.9 g/dL(3.7-4.9) Corrected Calcium 8.6 mg/dl Alkaline phosphatase 94 U/L(45-105) C-reactive protein 6 mg/L ( Prothrombin time 12 s(11.5-15.5) What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The normal albumin and C-reactive protein levels count against a diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's or ulcerative colitis) or an infectious pathology such as intestinal tuberculosis. Whilst small bowel bacterial overgrowth does not typically produce a raised C-reactive protein level it is very unusual in patients without risk factors for the condition (previous bowel surgery, Crohn's disease, motility disorders such as scleroderma). This leaves laxative abuse as the most likely diagnosis. Laxative abuse, where not a function of chronic constipation, is usually closely linked to eating disorders (Bulimia and Anorexia) and as such is typically over-represented in young, female patients. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 46 Pg: 303

text: A 20 year old Armenian man presents with pain and swelling of the left knee. He also gives a history of recurrent episodes of fever, pleuritic pains in the chest,and generalised rash. These episodes typically last for 2-3 days. Examination reveals splenomegaly, swollen knees and ankles.Urine dipstick reveals 2+ proteinuria. What is the likely diagnosis ?
expl: A young male presenting with history of recurrent fevers, arthritis and serositis especially in a person belonging to the Armenian descent points to the possibility of an autoinflammatory syndrome. Among the given options, Familial Mediterranean fever is the autoinflammatory syndrome seen in Armenians. Autoinflammatory syndromes are characterized by recurrent fevers, serosal, synovial and cutaneous inflammation and the eventual development of AA amyloidosis. They are called so because of the relative infrequency of autoantibodies or antigen specific T cells. The diseases included in this disease are: Familial Mediterranean Fever. TNF receptor associated periodic syndrome Hyperimmunoglobulinemia D with periodic fever syndrome NLRP 3 associated autoinflammatory disease. FMF occurs predominantly in Armenians, Arabs and Non Ashkenazi Jews. Hyperimmunoglobulin D with periodic fever is seen predominantly in Dutch and northern European. The rest of the autoinflammatory syndromes don't show any ethnic propensity. Familial Mediterranean fever: AR mainly, can be AD too. Fever lasting for 24-72 hours. Associated with abdominal pain in 90% cases. Unilateral pleurisy. Monoarticular arthritis, non erosive, without warmth or erythema. Skin rash resembling erysipelas. Exercise induced myalgia. Mutations in PYRIN gene, which is involved in host defense, where the threshold of activation of pyrin is reduced. Treatment is Cochicine or anti IL1β( Canakinumab) Rash seen in familial mediterranean fever Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:369 Pg:2841-2842

text: Which of the following statements is NOT true of primary pulmonary tuberculosis:

options.B: Miliary spread is commoner in a younger age group
options.C: pleural effusion occurs before tuberculin skin testing is positive
options.D: A positive tuberculin skin test develops within two weeks of infection

ansText: A positive tuberculin skin test develops within two weeks of infection
expl: Primary TB is usually asymptomatic, with miliary TB most likely to occur in young children. The Ghon focus is the area of consolidation from cellular infiltration and response to uptake of organisms by macrophages, which transform into epithelioid cells and group into granulomata. Bacilli are transported via lymphatics early in the disease process to regional lymph nodes to cause marked lymphadenopathy. Positive tuberculin test occurs between 3 weeks to 3 months after primary infection. Pleural and pericardial infections occur at or shortly after primary infection. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1362

text: A 35-year-old woman presents with fever, shortness of breath, and productive cough with expectoration. A CT chest scan was performed (shown below). What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The combination of fever, dyspnea, and expectoration , along with CT findings of consolidation accompanied by an air bronchogram , is highly suggestive of lobar pneumonia leading to pneumonic consolidation . Clinical manifestations of Lobar Pneumonia Common Symptoms: Fever Cough Mucopurulent sputum production Pleuritic chest pain (localized, sharp pain - especially in lobar disease) Constitutional Symptoms: Fatigue, headache, myalgia, arthralgia Severe Cases: Dyspnea Confusion, sepsis, multi-organ dysfunction Clinical Signs Respiratory signs: Tachypnea (↑ respiratory rate) Increased vocal fremitus Egophony (E-to-A changes) Dullness on percussion Crackles/rales and bronchial breath sounds (tubular type) Investigations & Findings Initial Evaluation: Based on history and clinical exam Chest Radiography: Most important initial test for pneumonia Detects pulmonary infiltrates (lobar, interstitial, unilateral, or bilateral) Cannot reliably separate bacterial vs. non-bacterial causes CT Scan: More sensitive than chest X-ray Dense opacification of an entire lobe with sparing of major airways May show ground-glass opacities and lobar/segmental pattern of involvement Image finding: Left upper lobe consolidation of heterogeneous density with multiple air bronchograms and a small pleural effusion Laboratory Tests: CBC: Leukocytosis (left shift) → infection marker; leukopenia → poor prognosis Inflammatory markers: ESR, acute phase reactants Sputum Analysis: Gram stain and culture critical in suspected lobar pneumonia Culture = most specific diagnostic test Influenza Testing: Recommended in winter due to co-infection risk Risk Stratification: CURB-65 / Pneumonia Severity Index → hospitalization decisions Other Diagnostic Measures: Blood cultures, urine antigen tests (before antibiotics) Thoracocentesis, bronchoscopy, pleural biopsy/culture (rare) Open lung biopsy = gold standard diagnostic test Explanation of Other Options Mediastinal Mass (Option B): Causes chest pain, cough, dyspnea, but not classical pneumonia features (fever, productive cough). Appears as a well-defined localized lesion with mass effect in mediastinum. Pleural Effusion (Option C): Appears on CT as fluid collection in pleural cavity. Leads to breathlessness, but not consolidation with air bronchograms. Typical finding = homogeneous pleural opacity. Diaphragmatic Hernia (Option D): On CT shows abdominal organs (stomach/bowel) in thoracic cavity . Not associated with fever, expectoration, or pulmonary consolidation. Key Takeaways Air bronchogram within consolidation is a hallmark of lobar pneumonia. Diagnosis requires clinical-radiological correlation. CT is more sensitive, but X-ray remains the first-line test . Always confirm etiology with sputum culture when possible. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK534295/ https://radiopaedia.org/articles/lobar-pneumonia

text: A 30-year-old female presents with a history of weightloss, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and pleural effusion. HRCT shows a “tree-in-bud" appearance with lung consolidation and effusion. Pleural fluid analysis reveals low ADA levels and lymphocytic predominance. What is the most likely finding on a biopsy from the lymph node?

options.C: C) Fungal Hyphae surrounded by lymphocytes

ansText: C) Fungal Hyphae surrounded by lymphocytes
expl: Explanation: The combination of: Weight loss and mediastinal lymphadenopathy Tree-in-bud pattern (suggestive of endobronchial spread of infection) Lymphocytic pleural effusion all point toward tuberculosis (especially pulmonary or lymph node TB). Even though ADA is low , this can occur in: Healed/fibrotic TB lesions , or Immunocompromised individuals (where cellular response is suppressed). Explanation of Other Options: Reactive Hyperplasia (Option A): Represents non-specific immune response of lymph nodes to infections or inflammation. Histology: Prominent germinal centers with active mitotic figures . Polyclonal B-cell proliferation. No necrosis or granuloma formation. Seen in: Viral infections (e.g., EBV, CMV) Autoimmune conditions Chronic inflammatory states Fungal Hyphae Surrounded by Lymphocytes (Option C): The "tree-in-bud" appearance and low ADA are not characteristic of fungal infections. Indicates fungal lymphadenitis (e.g., Histoplasmosis , Aspergillosis , Coccidioidomycosis ). Histology: Fungal hyphae or yeast forms within granulomas or necrotic tissue. PAS or GMS stains highlight fungal elements. Clinical features: Usually occurs in immunocompromised or HIV-positive May present with high ADA levels and neutrophilic effusion , not lymphocytic. Anthracosis Pigment (Option D): Benign finding , not associated with lymphocytic effusion, weight loss, or tree-in-bud appearance. Refers to carbon deposition in the lungs and lymph nodes from inhaled pollutants or smoke. Histology: Black carbon pigment seen within macrophages . No necrosis or granulomatous reaction. Seen in: Urban dwellers Smokers Coal workers (anthracotic lymph nodes)

text: A 63 year old man complains of a 6 month history of lethargy, fever, weight loss, arthralgia and diarrhoea. Jejunal biopsy reveals flattened mucosa with evidence of periodic acid Schiff (PAS) positive macrophages. What is the diagnosis?
expl: The presence of PAS positive inclusions in the macrophages in a patient with chronic malnutrition, with arthralgia and fever may be either Tuberculosis or Whipple's Disease. Both of them cause PAS positive macrophages. But Mycobacterium tuberculosis is acid-fast, where as Trophyrema whipplei is non acid fast. Since the question does not mention anything about the acid fastness, we assume it to be negative. Moreover, Tuberculosis mainly affects the ileum, here jejunum is involved. This is a case of Whipple's disease . It is a chronic, multiorgan disease caused by Tropheryma whipplei - gram-positive, non-acid-fast bacillus. Most commonly occurs in middle-aged men. Classically presents with arthralgias, weight loss, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Central nervous system and cardiac involvement is common and occur later in the disease. The intestinal lesion is also characterized by PAS-positive macrophages , that fills the lamina propria. Figure showing H and E staining of the jejunum, where the lamina propria is replaced by foamy macrophages. The PAS staining will be positive in the macrophages as shown below: Treatment is with a prolonged course of antibiotics, optimal regimen is uncertain. Penicillin + streptomycin for 2 weeks, followed by 1 year of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 325, Pg: 2464

text: Which of the following statements regarding the lung manifestation of SSc is false?

ansText: New onset ILD can occur in patients with long standing ILD
expl: ILD and other organ involvement occurs within the first few years of diagnosing SSc, especially during the edematous phase of skin disease. Skin involvement reaches a plateau after around 4 years of onset of symptoms, even after which, visceral involvement can progress. New onset ILD, occurring late in the course is very rare. Pulmonary complications are major cause of mortality in patients with SSc. Esophageal dialation with sever reflux is an important risk factor for developing ILD. text: A physician is evaluating a patient for an occupational disease and finds that a coproporphyrin test has been performed. Which of the following conditions is most likely suspected?
expl: Explanation of answer: Lead poisoning disrupts heme biosynthesis, resulting in elevated urinary coproporphyrin , making it a key diagnostic clue. Lead poisoning, particularly from occupational exposure, interferes with heme synthesis by inhibiting several key enzymes such as δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD) and ferrochelatase, leading to accumulation of heme precursors including coproporphyrin and δ-ALA (aminolevulinic acid) in the urine. Investigations in Lead Poisoning: Blood Findings: Microcytic hypochromic anemia Basophilic stippling of RBCs Cabot rings ↑ Zinc protoporphyrin (ZnPP) ↑ Free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP) ↑ Blood lead levels (>5 µg/dL is significant; >40 µg/dL may show symptoms) Urine Findings: ↑ Urinary ALA (>5 µg/L) ↑ Urinary coproporphyrin (>150 µg/L) ↑ Urinary lead (>0.25 mg/L) Radiological Findings (especially in children): "Lead lines" (dense metaphyseal bands) seen at long bone metaphyses due to inhibited osteoclastic activity. Special Tests: Calcium disodium EDTA mobilization test (especially in children) to assess response to chelation therapy. Pathophysiology of Coproporphyrin Elevation: Lead inhibits the enzymes involved in the conversion of porphyrin precursors to heme, including: δ-ALA dehydratase Ferrochelatase This leads to an accumulation of porphyrin intermediates like coproporphyrin and ALA, which are excreted in urine and used diagnostically. Explanation of other options: Berylliosis (Option B): Occupational granulomatous lung disease due to beryllium exposure. Diagnosed via imaging and lung biopsy, not associated with porphyrin abnormalities. Silicosis (Option C): Caused by inhalation of silica dust leading to nodular pulmonary fibrosis. Diagnosis is based on chest imaging and history of exposure, not urinary porphyrin tests. Asbestosis (Option D): Chronic interstitial lung disease from asbestos exposure. Diagnosed via imaging (e.g., pleural plaques on X-ray/CT), not via heme biosynthesis markers.

text: A 26 year old woman with cystic fibrosis presents with abdominal pain. The abdominal pain is colicky and localized in the lower abdomen. On examination, she has pyrexia and tachycardia. Her abdomen was distended. There was guarding and bowel sounds were present. Which of the following is likely to be the cause?
expl: Meconium Ileus is the earliest clinical manifestation of cystic fibrosis (CF) and occurs in approximately 16% of patients with CF. Contents of the intestinal lumen are often difficult to excrete, leading to meconium ileus (a presentation in 10–20% of newborns with CF) or distal intestinal obstructive syndrome in older individual. Signs of peritonitis include tenderness, abdominal wall edema, distension, and clinical evidence of sepsis. A palpable mass may indicate pseudocyst formation. Surgical exploration is indicated for patients with progressive distension, signs of peritonitis, or clinical deterioration. Complicated Meconium Ileus requires resection more often than simple cases and always requires temporary stomas. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:291 Pg: 2176

text: Regarding diagnostic lumbar puncture (LP), true statement is:

options.B: Aspirin should be stopped for at least 24 hours prior to LP.
options.C: LP can be attempted in patients with a suspected spinal epidural abscess.
options.D: It is recommended that LP is not performed in patients with platelet counts of <100000/ul.

ansText: Suspected bacteremia is not a contraindication to LP.
expl: It is contraindicated in patients with a suspected spinal epidural abscess. Suspected bacteremia is NOT a contraindication to LP. Antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents has not been demonstrated to be clearly associated with increased bleeding after LP. It is recommended to suspend therapy, when possible,prior to elective LP. The antiplatelet effect of aspirin will take around a week to wear off. Performing an LP is not recommended in patients with coagulation defects who are actively bleeding, have severe thrombocytopenia (e.g. platelet counts 1.4, without correcting the underlyin abnormalities) Reference:www.accessmedicine.com/harrisons.

text: Hemoglobinopathies are
expl: Hemoglobinopathies are autosomal codominant traits-thus, compound heterozygotes who inherit a different abnormal mutant allele from each parent exhibit composite features of each. For example, patients inheriting sickle β thalassemia exhibit features of β thalassemia and sickle cell anemia. The α chain is present in HbA, HbA2 and HbF; α-chain mutations thus cause abnormalities in all three. The α-globin hemoglobinopathies are symptomatic in utero and after birth because normal function of the α-globin gene is required throughout gestation and adult life. In contrast, infants with β-globin hemoglobinopathies tend to be asymptomatic until 3-9 months of age, when HbA has largely replaced HbF. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 98, Pg: 755

text: In restrictive lung disease due to respiratory muscle weakness, which of the following statements is true?

options.D: Low VC, low TLC, high RV/TLC

ansText: Low VC, low TLC, high RV/TLC
expl: The lung itself can function normally yet muscle weakness will result in grossly low lung volumes including FEV1, FVC and TLC. text: A 24-year-old man was found to have iron deficiency anemia when he went to donate blood. Generally, the patient was very well. He had a good appetite, his weight was steady and he ate a normal diet. He had a normal bowel habit and had never passed any blood, mucus or diarrhea in his stools. There is no history of any overt blood loss. His general practitioner got an open access endoscopy which was normal; duodenal biopsies were unremarkable. His father had died of what he thought was secondary liver and lung cancer but he was unsure. On general physical examination he was fit and athletic. The skin and mucosal membranes were unremarkable. Vitals were normal. Heart sounds were normal and the chest was clear. His abdomen was soft and nontender with no palpable masses or organs. Rectal examination was normal. On viewing the rectal mucosa through a rigid sigmoidoscope the colonic mucosa was covered in innumerable polyps. What specific genetic abnormality is responsible for this appearance?

options.A: Germline mutation of the STK11 gene on chromosome 19
options.B: Heterozygous mutation of the MYH gene
options.C: Loss of the APC gene on chromosome 5
options.D: Mutations in mismatch repair genes (for example, MSH2)

ansText: Loss of the APC gene on chromosome 5
expl: The patient will need a full colonoscopy and biopsy but the information presented is highly suggestive of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) , caused by the loss of the APC gene on the short arm of chromosome 5. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant inherited disorder caused by a germline mutation of the STK11 (serine threonine kinase 11) gene, usually located on the long arm of chromosome 19. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is associated with intestinal hamartomatous polyps, but is usually (90%) associated with perioral pigmentation . Hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC) and MYC polyposis do not cause multiple polyps as suggested in this case. InHNPCC, affected individuals inherit a mutation in one of several genes involved in DNA mismatch repair, including MSH2, MLH1, and PMS2. Homozygous mutations in the MYH gene have been associated with a phenotype of multiple colorectal adenomas with or without cancer. This accounts for a proportion of FAP patients without a pathogenic APC mutation. Mutations in the p53 tumor suppressor gene are found in many different cancers. While mutations in p53 are seen in cases of colon cancer, the question asks for the specific mutation associated with polyposis coli. The main differential in this question is between FAP and PJS but the lack of perioral pigmentation favors FAP as the diagnosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 81, Pg: 638

text: A 55 year old shipbuilding worker presents with dyspnea. He has been working in this industry for the past 25 years. Which is the most specific malignancy that we can expect in this patient?
expl: Explanation: A long-term history of occupational asbestos exposure (common in shipbuilding) is the primary risk factor for malignant mesothelioma , a cancer arising from the mesothelial cells of the pleura. While asbestos also increases the risk for bronchogenic carcinoma, mesothelioma is the most specific malignancy linked to this exposure. Pathology: Advanced pleural thickening/fibrosis makes the hemithorax rigid; mediastinal fixation may occur, but mediastinal shift is uncommon . Most common cytogenetic abnormality: 9p homozygous deletion (CDKN2A loss) . Clinical Features: Progressive dyspnea, chest pain, weight loss, chronic cough, hemoptysis; decreased breath sounds and dull percussion due to effusion or thickening. Diagnosis: CT scan: Pleural thickening, effusion, 'frozen hemithorax'(no mediastinal shift). Biopsy: Epithelioid: Tubules/nests/papillary structures, uniform nuclei, eosinophilic cytoplasm Sarcomatoid: Spindle cells, fibrosarcoma-like Biphasic: Mixed pattern Markers: Calretinin, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), cytokeratin, mesothelin. Gross Findings: Lobulated pleural mass encasing lung, rib erosion, massive effusion, calcified pleural plaques (bilateral, prior asbestos exposure). Explanation of other options: Bronchogenic carcinoma ,Small cell carcinoma and Squamous cell carcinoma (Option A,C and D): These are types of lung cancer. Asbestos exposure is a risk factor, especially when combined with smoking, but they are not as specifically linked to asbestos as mesothelioma. Key Takeaways: Malignant mesothelioma is strongly and specifically associated with asbestos exposure. Shipbuilding, construction, and insulation work are high-risk occupations.

text: A 61-year-old, heavy smoker, with a BMI of 37 kg/m2, presents with impotence, nocturia and depression. He is hypoxic at rest on air and has ankle oedema. Which is the most appropriate investigation to determine the aetiology?
expl: The clinical scenario describes cor pulmonale secondary to diurnal respiratory failure This occurs in patients with severe obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA). Most patients who develop this complication have lower airway obstruction (from smoking), gross obesity or respiratory muscle weakness. Hypercapnia out of proportion to the degree of lung disease should suggest OSA as a possible cause. The most appropriate or diagnostic investigation would be a sleep study. text: Which of the following diseases present mainly as Glomerulonephritis?
expl: Glomerular diseases can present in 2 ways- Nephritic Syndrome or Nephrotic Syndrome. Clinical distinction of both is required to identify the disease process and to plan investigations. NEPHRITIC SYNDROME: Hematuria. RBC cast. Hypertension. Proteinuria of the range 1-2g/day. Varying degrees of decline in GFR. Diseases that present predominantly as Nephritis are: Post streptococcal Glomerulonephritis, Sub acute bacterial endocarditis, Lupus Nephritis, IgA Nephropathy, Basement Membrane Disease, ANCA associated vasculitis, Membraneoproliferative glomerulonephritis. NEPHROTIC SYNDROME: Heavy proteinuria, >3gm/day Edema/anasarca Hypertension Hypercholesterolemia Hypoalbuminemia Hematuria, variable. Diseases that predominantly present as Nephrotic syndrome: Minimal change disease, Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, Membranous glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, Amyloidosis, Light chain deposition disease, Fabry’s Disease. There can be overlap between these two, eg: heavy proteinuria in Glomerulonephritis, known as Nephritic-nephrotic Syndrome. Reference: Harrison's principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2334.

text: Which one of the following is the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults?
expl: The incidence of FSGS is increasing, and it now represents up to one third of cases of nephrotic syndrome in adults and one-half of cases of nephrotic syndrome in African Americans. MCD causes 70–90% of nephrotic syndrome in childhood but only 10–15% of nephrotic syndrome in adults MGN, or membranous nephropathy as it is sometimes called, accounts for ~25% of cases of nephrotic syndrome in adults, with a peak incidence between the ages of 30 and 50 years and a male-to-female ratio of 2:1. IMN is rare in childhood and the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in the elderly. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 21 st edition, Ch: 314 Pg: 2341

text: Which of the following features are characteristic of glomerular hematuria? Statements: 1. Brown-colored urine 2. Dysuria absent 3. Crystals present 4. Edema rare
expl: Explanation: Glomerular hematuria occurs when damage to the glomerular filtration barrier allows red blood cells (RBCs) and plasma proteins to leak into the urinary space. It typically presents with cola-colored (brown) urine , absence of dysuria , and may be associated with edema when part of a nephritic syndrome . The presence of urinary crystals is not a feature of glomerular bleeding, it suggests a metabolic or post-renal cause such as stones or hyperuricosuria. Explanation of Other Statements: Brown-colored urine (Statement 1) - True The urine appears cola- or tea-colored due to oxidation of hemoglobin released from RBCs that have traversed damaged glomeruli. Indicates bleeding originating above the renal pelvis. Dysuria absent (Statement 2)- True Dysuria (painful micturition) suggests inflammation or infection of the lower urinary tract (urethra, bladder). Glomerular hematuria is non-irritative and painless. Crystals present (Statement 3) - False Crystalluria is associated with renal calculi or metabolic disorders (e.g., hyperuricemia, cystinuria), not glomerular diseases. Edema rare (Statement 4) - True in isolated glomerular hematuria Mild or no edema may be seen in isolated microscopic hematuria. However, when hematuria occurs as part of nephritic syndrome , edema can be marked.

text: A 45-year-old woman presents with dipstick positive haematuria. Her blood tests reveal a urea of 150 mg/dl and creatinine of 2.9 mg/dl. Which of the following most strongly suggests post streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
expl: Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis is caused by Group A beta haemolytic streptococci. A second episode is unusual in those who have previously had the disease because there is good immunity to the cell wall proteins of Group A strep. Acute Rheumatic Fever, which is also a disease caused by β hemolytic Sterptococci, is known for recurrences without secondary prophylaxis. Although features of hypertension with papilledema, complete anuria and nephrotic syndrome can occur, the strongest predictor is the clinical history of sore throat suggesting infection with streptococci leading to nephritic syndrome. PSGN due to skin infection develops after 2-6 weeks while that after a throat infection develops after 1-3 weeks. text: A 17-year-old male presents with proteinuria >4g/day, edema, and hypoalbuminemia, consistent with nephrotic syndrome. What is the recommended management for this patient?
expl: Explanation: Management of Nephrotic Syndrome in a 17-Year-Old Male First-line Treatment : Steroids (Prednisone) Based on high remission rates in minimal change disease (MCD), the most common cause in children and adolescents. Leads to complete remission in 90 -95% of children , 80 -85% of adults . Given daily or on alternate days . Other immunosuppressants (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, mycophenolate mofetil) are used for frequent relapsers , steroid-dependent , or steroid-resistant Presentation & Epidemiology Features : Proteinuria >4 g/day , edema , hypoalbuminemia , hypercholesterolemia Minimal hematuria , possible hypertension Without treatment : Risk of progression to renal failure Therapeutic Overview Edema : Managed with diuretics Hypercholesterolemia : Treated with lipid-lowering agents Hypercoagulability : May need anticoagulants Proteinuria : May use RAAS inhibitors Minimal Change Disease (MCD) Prevalence : 70 -90% of pediatric cases 10 -15% of adult cases Histology : Normal on light microscopy , foot process effacement on electron microscopy Etiology : Linked to T-cell dysfunction ; triggered by infections , allergies , or medications Clinical Features of MCD Sudden onset of edema Classic nephrotic syndrome signs Hypertension and microscopic hematuria are uncommon Renal function usually returns to normal after remission Outcomes & Prognosis Relapses common, especially in children Long-term prognosis is poorer in cases of acute renal failure or steroid resistance Children : Remission typically within 8 weeks Adults : Remission may take 20 -24 weeks Explanation of other options: Steroids and Cyclophosphamide (Option B): Cyclophosphamide is NOT first-line for nephrotic syndrome. It is reserved for steroid-resistant or frequently relapsing cases . IV Albumin (Option C): Albumin infusion can be used temporarily for severe edema but does NOT treat the underlying disease. Main treatment is still steroids . Cyclophosphamide (Option D): Cyclophosphamide is used for steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome or frequent relapses, NOT as initial therapy. text: A 65-year-old man is brought in with a sudden inability to speak coherently, producing nonsensical grammar despite speaking fluently and rapidly. He had normal communication ability before this event. Which type of defect does this patient have?
expl: Explanation: The given clinical scenario of quick speech, which does not make sense, is suggestive of fluent aphasia , also known as Wernicke's aphasia . Fuent aphasia, or Wernicke's aphasia, arises from injury to Wernicke's area in the brain. It is characterised by effortless and well-structured speech, but the content is nonsensical or filled with invented words. Patients usually retain normal rhythm and fluency yet produce meaningless language, and they are generally unaware of their communication difficulties. Explanation of other options: Motor aphasia (Option A): Motor aphasia, or Broca's aphasia, is marked by impaired speech production , including reduced vocabulary, slow and effortful speech, and poor grammar. Affected individuals find it hard to construct complete sentences and often become frustrated with their inability to communicate. Since the patient can speak smoothly and rapidly, this condition is unlikely. Anomic aphasia (Option B): Anomic aphasia involves difficulty retrieving words , causing pauses and the use of substitute terms, though grammar and speech fluency are usually preserved. Since the patient shows meaningless speech content rather than problems with word retrieval, this diagnosis is improbable. Conduction aphasia (Option D): Conduction aphasia arises from injury to the arcuate fasciculus , which links Broca's and Wernicke's areas. It is marked by impaired ability to repeat words or phrases , despite having relatively preserved comprehension and spontaneous speech. Because this patient's main problem lies in the meaning of their speech rather than repetition, this diagnosis is less likely.

text: Two weeks after an episode of infective diarrhoea, a 15-year-old child presents with fever, hypertension and haematuria. A possible diagnosis could be:
expl: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura(TTP) and hemolytic-uremic syndrome(HUS) represent a spectrum of thrombotic microangiopathies. TTP and HUS share the general features of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemolytic anemia, fever, renal failure and neurologic disturbances. When patients, particularly children, have more evidence of renal injury, their condition tends to be called HUS. In adults with neurologic disease, it is considered to be TTP. Childhood HUS is caused by a toxin released by Escherichia coli 0157:H7 and occasionally by Shigella dysenteriae . This shiga toxin(verotoxin) directly injures endothelial, enterocytes and renal cells, causing apoptosis, platelet clumping and intravascular hemolysis by binding to the glycolipid receptors(Gb3). Investigations reveal anemia with schistocytes; a normal bleeding profile and impaired renal function. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2348.

expl: The given patient has hypoalbuminemia, hyper cholesterolemia, edema and pleural effusion. So the edema is attribute to hypoalbuminemia. Hypoalbuminemia can be due to either decreased albumin production as in CLD or excessive albumin loss through urine or gut. However here the cholesterol levels are high which is an indirect indicator of nephrotic syndrome. So the next investigation will be to confirm the urinary loss, which is 24 hour urine estimation. Followed by a renal biopsy, once proteinuria is confirmed. text: A 10-year-old child presents with flank pain, fatigue, and red-colored urine. Investigations reveal more than 20 RBCs per high-power field, with microscopy showing dysmorphic RBCs. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The presentation of flank pain, fatigue, hematuria with >20 dysmorphic RBCs/hpf on microscopy is consistent with Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Dysmorphic RBCs on urine microscopy signify glomerular bleeding , a hallmark of PSGN. PSGN is an acute glomerulonephritis that develops after a streptococcal infection , caused by immune complex deposition in the glomeruli and the resulting inflammatory response. Explanations of other options: Minimal change disease (Option A): This type of nephrotic syndrome shows heavy proteinuria with only minimal alterations on light microscopy. It usually presents with proteinuria and oedema, with blood pressure being normal or mildly increased. Gross hematuria, flank pain, and dysmorphic RBCs are not typical features. UTI (Option C): Although a urinary tract infection may lead to hematuria, it usually does not show dysmorphic RBCs on urine microscopy. Moreover, UTIs are generally associated with symptoms like dysuria and increased frequency, which are not reported here. Bladder calculi (Option D): Bladder stones can produce hematuria, but they do not account for dysmorphic RBCs, which are a marker of glomerular disease. Furthermore, the pain from bladder stones is usually felt in the lower abdomen or suprapubic area rather than in the flanks.

text: A 42-year-old man has generalised oedema. Urine dipstick shows protein +++, blood -ve. Which one of the following findings is suggestive of amyloidosis?

options.D: Large numbers of granular casts, fat bodies and red cells in the urine

expl: The presence of anasarca, proteinuria and absence of RBC in urine suggests diagnosis of Nephrotic syndrome. Amyloidosis is a known cause of nephrotic syndrome. Amyloidosis occurs due to the deposition of light chain of immunoglobulins. It occurs with myeloma, lymphoproliferative disorders, Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia. Amyloidosis can also occur in MGUS and smouldering myeloma. The clonal plasma cells produce immunoglobulin, which will be fragmented by macrophages so that they can self aggregate and get deposited as AL amyloid. It is usually formed of the lambda light chain. 10% of patients with AL amyloid have overt myeloma. The paraprotein(Light chain or whole immunoglobulin) in Myeloma associated amyloidosis can be detected by SPEP or urine BJP. But if the quantity of immunoglobulin is not sufficient, SPEP will be negative and immunofixation electrophoresis or quantification of free light chains. AL Amyloidosis often has other manifestations like cardiomyopathy, neuropathy etc in addition to renal involvement. AA amyloidosis can also present as nephrotic syndrome. It is seen with chronic inflammatory diseases like Ankylosing Spondylitis, Rheumatoid Arthritis, Familial Mediterranean fever etc. Diagnosis of AL Amyloidosis can be done by biopsy of liver or kidney in 90% and abdominal fat pad in 70%. Serum light chain can be used for following up the disease. In AL amyloidosis renal impairment improves with treatment of myeloma. But in AA amyloidosis, it progresses to daialysis dependence in majority of cases. Abnormal liver function can cause anasarca, but here urine albumin will be negative. Cryoglobulinemia causes nephritis rather than nephrotic syndrome. Granular cast RBC in urine is a feature of nephritic syndrome. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:112, Pg:880.

text: Which of the following is most likely to cause CKD?
expl: All the other conditions cause acute renal failure. Berger's disease(IgA nephropathy) is associated with chronic renal failure in up to 30% of adult cases. It is the commonest glomerular disease worldwide. It usually follows a viral upper respiratory tract infection. Heavy proteinuria, renal failure and hypertension indicate a poor prognosis. Option A: Leptospirosis, also called Weil's disease, is spread by contact with infected rat urine. Features include meningitis, myocarditis, acute renal failure and haemolytic anemia. Option B: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is associated with acute damage and occlusion of small blood vessels(arterioles and capillaries) in the kidney. Thrombotic microangiopathy associated with Escherichia coli infection(especially O157 serotypes) is now the most common cause of acute renal failure in children in developed countries. Option C: Vancomycin is a bactericidal antibiotic. Indications are limited to serious infections such as endocarditis and septicaemia. It is nephrotoxic and can precipitate acute renal failure. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:314, Pg:2339.

text: Which of the following statements is false regarding CKD?

options.A: CKD poses risk for bleeding as well as thrombosis.
options.B: Uremic peripheral neuropathy occurs in stage 4 CKD
options.C: Glucose metabolism is impaired in CKD.
options.D: Uremic pruritis improves dramatically with dialysis.

ansText: Uremic pruritis improves dramatically with dialysis.
expl: Dermatological manifestations in CKD include hyperpigmentation due to accumulation of Urochromes. Most of the cutaneous abnormalities improve with dialysis, but pruritis does not fully improve. Hyperphosphatemia can contribute to itch. Kappa opioid receptrs have shown to be promising in CKD pruritis. CKD increases the risk of bleeding by impairment of platelet aggregation, adhesion and impaired action of Platelet factor III and also prothrombin consumption. Thrombosis is common in conditions where there is nephrotic range proteinuria. Desmopressin may be used to gtemporarily improve bleeding. Optimal dialysis will improve bleeding time. Uremic neuromuscular diseases become prominent after stage 3 CKD. Insomnia, memory disturbance, hiccups, cramps, twitching are the early manifestations. Uremic peripheral neuropathy begins at stage 4 CKD, with sensory more than motor, distal more than proximal, lower limb more than upper limb. CKD causes mild glucose intolerance and does not require treatment. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 311, Pg: 2317, 2318.

text: Which of the following is the best equation to determine eGFR?
expl: This question deals with the measurement of GFR: The different methods used are: 1. S Cr: It is good in the outpatient setting and roughly estimates GFR. 2. Creatinine Clearence: Urine volume×Urine Creatinine/Plasma Cr×time. 3. Cockcroft and Gault equation for estimating the Cr Cl 4. MDRD for measuring eGFR 5.CKD EPI measurement of EGFR: MDRD and CKD EPI measure the e GFR, Cockcroft and Gault measures the CR Clearance. The Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes workgroup recommends estimated GFR(eGFR) formulae as the primary method for evaluating GFR. They recommend using the 2009 CKD-Epidemiology(EPI) Collaboration creatinine equation (https://www.kidney.org/content/ckd-epi-creatinineequation-2009). The creatinine clearance(CrCl) is approximately 100 mL/min/1.73 m 2 in healthy young women and 120 mL/min/1.73 m 2 in healthy young men. The creatinine clearance declines by an average of 0.8 mL/min/yr. after age 40 years as part of the aging process, but this is variable Option B: Creatinine clearance can also be estimated using the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease(MDRD) Study equation, but multiple studies across many populations show that the CKD-EPI equation is more accurate. Option C: Cockcroft Gault formula, is still commonly used to determine drug dosing, but it was developed before the standardization of creatinine assays currently in use today and thus, its use is not recommended. Option D: A Kidney Failure Risk(KFR) equation has been devised to predict the risk of progression to stage 5 dialysis-dependent kidney disease. It is therefore a prognostic score. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 311, Pg: 2311

text: A 45-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because she saw something moving in her mother's eye. The patient is visiting from Africa where she lives in the rainforest. The patient reports some occasional eye swelling and redness. On examination, you find a worm in the subconjunctiva see Figure .Which of the following medications is indicated for therapy?
expl: This patient has loiasis caused by the African eye worm Loa loa. It is endemic to the rain forests of Central and West Africa. Microfilaria circulate periodically in blood with macrofilaria living in subcutaneous tissues including the subconjunctiva. Loiasis is often asymptomatic in indigenous regions with recognition, as in this case, only with visualized macrofilarial migration. Angioedema and swelling may occur in affected areas. Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is effective treatment for the macro- filarial and microfilarial stages of disease. Multiple courses may be necessary. Albendazole and ivermectin are effective in reducing microfilarial loads but are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. There are reports of deaths in patients with heavy loads of microfilaria receiving ivermectin. Terbinafine is the treatment for ringworm. Voriconazole is an antifungal with no activity against worms. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 233Pg 1783-1784
