text: A 49-year-old man presents with flu-like symptoms and a palmoplantar rash. On examination, epitrochlear lymphadenopathy is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The classic rash and accompanying symptoms strongly suggest a diagnosis of secondary syphilis. Key Features of Secondary Syphilis: Mucocutaneous and cutaneous lesions along with generalized, non-tender lymphadenopathy. The primary chancre may still be present in about 15% of cases, particularly more common in HIV-positive individuals. Skin Rash: Presents as macular, papular, papulosquamous, or sometimes pustular lesions (syphilides). Lesions can be subtle, and up to 25% of patients with visible rash may not notice it. Typically begin as pale red or pink, non-itchy macules on the trunk and limbs. Progress to papular lesions, often involving the palms and soles. In HIV patients, severe necrotic lesions known as lues maligna can occur. Hair and Mucosal Involvement: Patchy hair loss on the scalp, eyebrows, or beard occurs in about 5% of cases. Condylomata lata- moist, highly infectious lesions can develop in skin folds such as the perianal area, vulva, or scrotum (seen in 10% of cases). Mucous patches, painless silver-gray erosions, commonly appear on oral or genital mucosa in 10-15% of patients. Constitutional Symptoms: Sore throat (15-30%), fever (5-8%), weight loss (2-20%), malaise (25%), anorexia (2-10%), headache (10%), and meningismus (5%). Acute meningitis may occur in 1-2% of patients, with cerebrospinal fluid abnormalities seen in up to 40% of early syphilis cases. Ocular and Ear Involvement: Ocular symptoms include pupillary changes, optic neuritis, iritis, or uveitis, which can cause permanent vision loss if untreated. Ear symptoms may include sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, or tinnitus. Less Common Complications: Hepatitis, kidney disease, gastrointestinal conditions (such as hypertrophic gastritis and proctitis), arthritis, and periostitis. Liver involvement is often asymptomatic, while renal issues arise from immune complex deposition, leading to proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome. Resolution: Most signs and symptoms of secondary syphilis resolve spontaneously within 1 to 6 months. Options A, C and D are incorrect.

text: A 50 year old male presents with unsteadiness of gait of one year duration. On examination, he has sensory loss in the stocking and glove pattern, with absent ankle jerk and pyramidal signs and sensory ataxia. Which of the following statements is false?

options.A: Cobalamine deficiency may be a cause of the above findings.
options.B: Dietary deficiency of copper may also lead to similar clinical features.
options.C: Haematological abnormalities if present points to the diagnosis of Vitamin B12 deficiency.
options.D: Excess Zinc is an known factor that reduced copper absorption.

ansText: Haematological abnormalities if present points to the diagnosis of Vitamin B12 deficiency.
expl: Symmetric sensory loss with distal areflexia and UMN signs is seen in Vitamin B12 deficiency, Copper deficiency and Vitamin E deficiency. It is also seen in adrenomyelkoneuronopathy. So all these can cause symptoms similar to subacute combined degeneration. Haematological abnormalities are known to occur not only in B12 deficiency, but also Copper deficiency and Vitamin E deficiency. In Vitamin B12 deficiency, there will be macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils and pancytopenia. In copper deficiency, there will be microcytic anemia, neutropenia and occasionally pancytopenia. In Vitamin E deficiency, there will be acanthocytosis. Excess zinc upregulates intestinal metalothionine and decreases copper absorption. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Intrenal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3496, 3497

text: A 40-year-old male presents with chronic back pain that has progressively worsened over the past few months. He also reports fever, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. On examination, there is localized tenderness over the lower thoracic and lumbar spine. MRI spine is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Characterized by chronic back pain, fever, night sweats, and weight loss . MRI often shows involvement of two or more adjacent vertebral bodies , typically affecting the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spine in adults. A hallmark feature is the destruction of the intervertebral disc space and adjacent vertebrae with potential abscess formation . The patient's symptoms of systemic infection (fever, night sweats, weight loss) combined with localized spinal tenderness and the typical MRI findings strongly suggest Pott's spine. Explanation of other options: Osteoporotic Vertebral Fracture (Option B): Common in older adults or those with osteoporosis, presenting typically as a sudden onset of back pain after minimal trauma or even no apparent cause. The patient's systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss are not typical of osteoporotic fractures. Metastatic Spinal Tumor (Option C): Can cause back pain and may involve vertebral bodies, but is more likely to cause widespread or multifocal pain and neurological deficits. Lacks specific systemic symptoms such as fever and night sweats that are associated with an infection like tuberculosis. Ankylosing Spondylitis (Option D): A chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints, leading to pain and progressive spinal stiffness. Typically lacks systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss unless there is a concurrent secondary inflammation or infection. Key Takeaways: Pott's disease (spinal TB) should be suspected in patients with chronic back pain, systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), and MRI findings of vertebral destruction with possible abscess formation. Early diagnosis and anti-tubercular treatment are essential to prevent complications such as neurological deficits and spinal deformity.

text: All are true about Weber syndrome except?
expl: Weber syndrome is characterized by damage to the cerebral peduncle. This leads to damage to corticospinal pathway and oculomotor nerve. Hence the patient will develop ipsilateral third nerve palsy and contralateral hemiplegia. The blood vessels compromised are paramedian branches of upper basilar and proximal posterior cerebral arteries Dorsal midbrain syndrome is Parinaud syndrome/ Supranuclear vertical gaze disorder caused by damage to posterior commissure. It is characterized by: Loss of up-gaze Sun setting sign Convergence retraction nystagmus Lid retraction Skew deviation Pseudo-abducens palsy Light near dissociation of pupils Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, chapter 426 page number. 3333

text: A 44 year old man has severe episodes of dizziness with associated vomiting and pain in the right ear. This occurs once or twice a week. During these attacks he feels the surrounding environment spinning around. He also mentions a high pitched sound frequently being present. On examination, during an attack, he has right horizontal nystagmus. Audiological testing reveals right-sided sensorineural deafness. What is the diagnosis?
expl: Meniere's disease is caused by distension of the endolymphatic compartment of the inner ear. The symptoms of Meniere's disease include vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus . The dizziness is described as a spinning or whirling feeling and may cause problems with balance. Some people feel nauseated and vomit during an attack. Tinnitus refers to a ringing or roaring sound in the ear. Others may notice some hearing loss, especially with sounds that have a low frequency. Horizontal nystagmus is more commonly seen on examination, but vertical nystagmus may also occur. Option A: Vestibular neuritis presents with acute onset of vertigo with nausea, vomiting, and gait impairment. Option C: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) presents with recurrent episodes of vertigo lasting one minute or less that are provoked by specific types of head movements. BPPV does not cause prolonged or sustained vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus, or neurologic deficits; these suggest an alternative diagnosis Option D: The most common clinical manifestations of vestibular schwannomas are unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, often in association with tinnitus Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 22, Pg: 160

text: A 27-year-old female presents with drooping of the left side of her face and an inability to close her left eye. She had a viral illness in the preceding week. There is no past medical history.On examination, there is a left VIIth nerve palsy. The remaining cranial nerves are normal. Power, tone and reflexes are normal in the limbs. What is the best course of treatment?
expl: This is the classical history of a post-viral Bell's palsy . There is some evidence to support a short course of steroids in the acute stages of the illness (NEJM 2007;357:1598-1607). This study suggests improved recovery of facial function with early treatment. No benefit was seen in acyclovir added to prednisolone in this study. Oral valaciclovir has been evaluated with an RCT but consensus supports steroids (with some clinicians continuing to support the concomitant use of acyclovir). You need to be confident that there are no features of Guillain-Barré (test reflexes), or brain stem vascular disease or space occupying lesion. The neurological examination of the cranial nerves thus needs to be completed with care. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3441

text: A 4B-year-old civil servant attends the clinic stating that she has difficulty swallowing. She gives a two months history of difficulty with solids which has progressed to difficulty tolerating liquids in the previous two weeks. She has noticed some weakness in her right arm which has affected her ability to lift certain objects like the kettle. Previously, she has enjoyed good health with no hearing loss or facial weakness. She describes no visual symptoms.On examination, she has an absent gag reflex on the right, with reduced palatal movements. There is weakness on rotating the head to the left with flattening and weakness of elevation of the right shoulder. Eye movements, visual acuity, hearing and tongue movements are all normal. Where is the likely site of the lesion?
expl: The clinical scenario is that of a right sided pathology affecting the IX, X and XI cranial nerves. This produces the palatal weakness and the swallowing difficulties (IX/X), while the shoulder and sternocleidomastoid weakness are due to accessory nerve (XI) involvement. The absence of hearing loss or facial weakness makes a cerebello-pontine angle lesion unlikely. A lesion outside the skull may also involve the XII nerve (tongue). The most likely site, therefore is the jugular foramen. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 441 Pg: 3444

text: Which of the following is true regarding the action of clopidogrel?

options.B: It is a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor
options.C: It is a hydroxymethyl coenzyme A inhibitor
options.D: It is an ADP receptor antagonist

ansText: It is an ADP receptor antagonist
expl: Clopidogrel prevents platelet aggregation through antagonism of the adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor. It has been shown to reduce mortality from stroke and ischaemic heart disease (IHD) in primary prevention studies. Vorapaxar is an anti-platelet agent that reduces platelet aggregation through reversible antagonism of Protease Activated Receptor-1 (PAR 1), also known as thrombin receptor. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2060

text: A 35 year old male is evaluated for young stroke. He gives history of burning pains in both his feet since his late teenage. What can be seen on examining this patient?
expl: We have a patient with stroke presenting at a very young age along with symptoms of peripheral neuropathy. This should make us thing of Fabry's Disease. It is an X linked dominant disorder. The characteristic skin lesions that are seen in Fabry's disease are Angiokeratomas. They are dark red to blue black maculopapular lesions that are seen in the area between the umbilicus and knee most abundantly. Other features are hypohidrosis, vascular diseases of the heart, kidneys and brain. Lenticular and corneal opacities may also e seen. Xanthomas, Central obesity can also occur in familial dyslipidemias that can also cause stroke in young. But here there is history of burning parasthesias due to peripheral neuropathy which is seen in Fabry's disease. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 418, Pg: 3259

text: Amn 81 year old man is admitted with confusion over the last 3 days. He has a past medical history of hypertension and has had frequent falls in the past. Clinical examination is unremarkable. Which of these conditions needs to be excluded?

text: A patient presented with an 11-day history of fever and neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture revealed lymphocyte predominance, glucose of 50 mg/dL, and protein of 3000 mg/dL, along with the presence of a cobweb-like coagulum. Gram stain was negative. Chest X-ray demonstrated upper lobe disease with hilar lymphadenopathy.
expl: The combination of subacute fever with neck stiffness, typical CSF profile (lymphocyte predominance, reduced glucose, markedly elevated protein), cobweb-like clot formation, and chest X-ray revealing upper lobe disease with hilar lymph node enlargement are hallmark findings of tuberculous meningitis . A negative Gram stain favors a mycobacterial infection over c ommon bacterial causes. Explanations of other options: Bacterial meningitis (Option B): Bacterial meningitis usually has a rapid onset (within 24-48 hours), shows neutrophil predominance in the CSF, and often yields a positive Gram stain. The slower progression and lymphocyte-rich CSF in this case argue against bacterial meningitis. Fungal meningitis (Option C): Although fungal meningitis may show comparable CSF findings such as reduced glucose and elevated protein, it is more commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals and usually lacks the classic upper lobe changes on chest X-ray. Pulmonary involvement in this context strongly favors tuberculosis. Viral meningitis (Option D): Viral meningitis is generally characterized by normal or only slightly raised protein, normal glucose, and no cobweb coagulum. The very high protein level (3000 mg/dL) together with low glucose makes a viral cause unlikely.

text: A child presents with two weeks of poor feeding and marked irritability. The sibling has confirmed tuberculosis and is receiving antitubercular therapy. As part of the evaluation, a lumbar puncture is done. Which of the following findings is most likely in the CSF?

options.A: Lymphocytosis with low sugar and high protein
options.B: Lymphocytosis with high sugar and high protein
options.C: Neutrophils with low sugar and low protein
options.D: Neutrophils with low sugar and high protein

ansText: Lymphocytosis with low sugar and high protein
expl: Explanation: The history of two weeks of poor feeding and irritability, along with close contact with a tuberculosis case, points toward a diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis . In tuberculous meningitis, cerebrospinal fluid usually demonstrates lymphocytic pleocytosis (up to 1000/μL), increased protein levels (100-800 mg/dL), and reduced glucose. This classic combination of findings represents the chronic inflammatory reaction seen in CNS tuberculosis. Explanations of other options: Lymphocytosis with high sugar and high protein (Option B): Although lymphocytosis and elevated protein are consistent with CNS infections, increased glucose (hyperglycorrhachia) is not characteristic of tuberculous meningitis. In TB meningitis, *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* typically lowers CSF glucose through heightened utilization. Therefore, elevated glucose would argue against this diagnosis. Neutrophils with low sugar and low protein (Option C): A pattern of low glucose together with low protein is unusual in CNS infections, since infections generally cause protein to rise as part of the inflammatory process. In addition, neutrophilic predominance is more indicative of acute bacterial meningitis. Neutrophils with low sugar and high protein (Option D): Although neutrophils may appear in the CSF during acute bacterial meningitis, their predominance is not typical of tuberculous meningitis, which is usually characterized by a lymphocytic response.

text: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimen of a patient is shown below, along with microscopy. The report reveals mononuclear cytosis, raised protein levels, and reduced glucose. What is the most probable etiology?
expl: Explanation: The combination of clinical details with CSF findings - lymphocytic predominance, elevated proteins, hypoglycorrhachia (low sugar), and the presence of a characteristic cobweb-like clot - points towards tuberculous meningitis (TBM) . Features of Tuberculous Meningitis (TBM): Etiology: Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis via hematogenous spread or rupture of subependymal tubercles into the subarachnoid space. Presentation: Subacute onset with fever, headache, meningismus, and cranial nerve palsies (especially ocular nerves from basal meningeal involvement). Complications: Hydrocephalus, elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), and ischemic infarcts. CSF Findings: Lymphocytic predominance Elevated protein (100-500 mg/dL) Decreased glucose ( Cobweb-like pellicle formation Diagnosis: Gold Standard: CSF culture for M ycobacterium tuberculosis. Supportive Tests: AFB staining, CSF ADA levels, or PCR for TB DNA. Management: Early initiation of antitubercular therapy (ATT) . Corticosteroids to minimize inflammation and reduce complications. CSF Findings in Different Types of Meningitis: Explanation of Other Options: Aseptic meningitis (Option B): Typically viral, presents with lymphocytic predominance but normal glucose and near-normal protein levels. Bacterial meningitis (Option C): Usually shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, very high protein, and markedly reduced glucose, with turbid CSF. Chemical meningitis (Option D): Results from rupture of intracranial tumor contents (e.g., dermoid, glioma) into CSF. Shows variable inflammatory response, elevated protein, but absence of microbial organisms. text: Factor VII deficiency should be considered with which of the following coagulation abnormalities?

options.C: Prolongation of both PT and aPTT

expl: Commonly used tests of hemostasis provide the initial screening for clotting factor activity, and disease phenotype often correlates with the level of clotting activity. An isolated abnormal prothrombin time (PT)suggests factor VII deficiency, whereas a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) indicates most commonly hemophilia or factor XI deficiency. The prolongation of both PT and aPTT suggests deficiency of factors V, X, and II, or fibrinogen abnormalities. The addition of the missing factor at a range of doses to the subject's plasma will correct the abnormal clotting times; the result is expressed as a percentage of the activity observed in normal subjects. Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 116 pg. 911

text: A 21-year old woman living in rural Indonesia is in her third trimester of pregnancy and is found to have severe microcytic anemia with a hematocrit of only 19%. She denies vaginal bleeding but consistently has darkened stools, which are positive when tested for occult blood. Blood laboratory testing is also remarkable for eosinophilia and low serum albumin concentration. Which of the following parasitic infections is the most likely to result in this syndrome?
expl: Intestinal blood loss is the principal clinical manifestation of hookworm infection, which can lead to iron deficiency and microcytic anemia. Pregnant women and children are at greater risk because of their higher iron needs. Diphyllobothrium latum infection is associated with development of megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency and is thus associated with an elevated,rather than low, red blood cell mean corpuscular volume. Infection with Enterobius vermicularis and Entamoeba histolytica, is not usually associated with intestinal blood loss or iron deficiency. Reference : Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st Ed , Ch: 232, pg.1775

text: A 16 year old boy with known sickle-cell disease is brought to the emergency department profoundly unwell. expl: Patients with sickle-cell disease have compromised splenic function resulting from microvascular occlusion. text: A 38-year-old man is referred after his first myocardial infarction for your opinion. He has a total cholesterol level of 370 mg/dl, with normal triglycerides. You note the presence of corneal arcus and tendon xanthomas. Which of the following genetic factors is not likely to be a cause of the hypercholesterolemia?

options.C: Failure of the LDL receptors to move to the cell surface

expl: Familial hypercholesterolemia is associated with an autosomal-dominant mutation on the short arm of chromosome 19, thereby reducing the number of high-affinity, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptors by up to 50%. Over 300 mutations have been described so far Patients present with premature coronary heart disease (CHD) and have a standardized mortality ratio of up to nine times that of age- and sex-matched controls. Homozygotes present with CHD in childhood, heterozygotes present with CHD at the age of 30+ years. Other mutations that can lead to FH include PCSK9 gain of function, APOB and LDLRAP1. text: A 51-year-old male laborer presents with a haematemesis. Which of the following features confers the greatest risk of a poor outcome?

options.B: A history of ischaemic heart disease (IHD)
options.D: A pulse of 90 beats per minute

ansText: A history of ischaemic heart disease (IHD)
expl: Among the options given, history of ischemic heart disease confers the greatest risk of a poorer outcome. There are a number of available scoring systems which stratify subjects with GI bleed into high and low risk groups. The Rockall scoring system is based on: Age (the higher the age the worse the prognosis) Comorbidities (like IHD) Presence of shock Endoscopic abnormalities. The Canadian Consensus Conference Statement utilizes a similar system, incorporating endoscopic factors including: Active bleeding Major stigmata of recent haemorrhage Ulcers greater than 2 cm in diameter The location of ulcers in proximity to large arteries. The Blatchford score is based on clinical parameters alone: Elevated blood urea nitrogen Reduced haemoglobin A drop in systolic blood pressure Raised pulse rate The presence of melaena or syncope Evidence of hepatic or cardiac disease. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 48, Pg: 313

ansText: Replacement of glutamate by valine in n-chain of HbA
expl: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Replacement of glutamate by valine in 13 chain of HBA Sickle cell anemia Sickle cell anemia is a hereditary hemoglobinopathy, i.e., the type of disease characterized by production of defective hemoglobin. Sickle cell anemia results from mutation in 13-globin gene. It is caused by a point mutation at the sixth position of the f3-globin chain leading to subsitution of a valine residue for a glutamic acid residue resulting in sickle hemoglobin (HbS). text: Elective splenectomy is preferred in which of the given conditions?
expl: Explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis is a genetic condition where red blood cells are sphere-shaped rather than biconcave, and the main treatment is elective splenectomy. In hereditary spherocytosis , splenectomy is highly beneficial since the spleen is chiefly responsible for destroying spherocytes. The timing depends on disease severity: In severe cases it is done electively at 4-6 years, in moderate cases, it may be postponed until adolescence , while mild cases are usually managed with folic acid supplementation alone. Explanations of other options: G6PD deficiency (Option A): In G6PD deficiency, splenectomy can aggravate anaemia since the spleen plays a key role in clearing damaged red blood cells. Management mainly focuses on preventing exposure to oxidative triggers and treating acute hemolytic crises. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (Option B): In paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), hemolysis results from a complement system defect, making stem cell transplantation the only curative option. Splenectomy is not useful since the red cell destruction is complement-driven and occurs in the entire circulation. Hairy cell leukaemia (Option D): In hairy cell leukaemia, the primary treatment is chemotherapy , while splenectomy is reserved for patients with significant splenomegaly or those who do not respond to standard therapy, rather than being the first-line approach.

text: Which cell is primarily involved in causing structural damage to joints in RA?
expl: Osteoclasts are the cells that are ultimately responsible for the structural damage in RA. The chief pathology of RA is bone not only bone destruction, but also decreased bone formation. The first cells that are activated are CD4 + T cells. Macrophages are the chief inflammatory cells involved. But the bone damage is mediated by activated osteoclasts. Bone erosions: The damage is typically located at the regions where the synovium is inserted to the periosteal surface at the edge of bone, at the rim of the articular cartilage. This also explains the development of bone erosions at the radial aspect of the MCP. Juxtra-articular osteopenia is another pathology that is seen in the adjacent bone due to inflammation of marrow. It results in substantial thinning of bone trabeculae. TNFα inhibits bone formation by inhibiting osteoblasts. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 358, Pg: 2756-2757

text: A 65 year old man has been confirmed to have lung cancer. Which form of cancer has the worst prognosis?
expl: Small cell lung cancer has the worst prognosis out of all lung cancers and is rarely suitable for surgical resection. Even when diagnosed early the 2-year survival is in the order of 20-25%. The main form of therapy is chemotherapy. Small cell cancer is associated with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and squamous cell cancer is associated with paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia through increased parathyroid-related hormone. 75% of small cell cancers arise in the proximal airways. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:78 Pg 599

text: A 39-year-old woman gives an eight month history of bloody diarrhoea. On average she has six bowel motions per day with associated urgency. She also reports weight loss of approximately 3 kg. On examination she is dehydrated and tachycardic. There is evidence of pallor and abdominal examination reveals left-sided tenderness. Which of the following pathological features would you expect to find given the likely underlying diagnosis?
expl: Chronic bloody diarrhoea in a young patient is very suggestive of a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis (UC) . The time course is too long for an infective cause and whilst Crohn's disease (CD) may cause a colitis, this is less frequent. CD often presents watery diarrhoea. The predominant left sided symptoms (urgency and anatomical distribution of the tendency) should also point towards UC. The answer here therefore is diffuse mucosal inflammation . All the remaining options are histological features of Crohn's disease . Transmural inflammation is seen in CD. Sub serosal lymphoid aggregates are seen in CD Normal crypt architecture is found in CD while crypt abscesses and goblet cell depletion are seen in UC. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg:2474-2475

text: A 60 year old man is investigated for weight loss and dyspepsia. Endoscopic examination reveals an ulcerated lesion in stomach. Biopsy shows the presence of a low grade mucosa associated lymphoma and Helicobacter pylori. CT of chest & abdomen shows no metastases. What is the best treatment option for this patient?
expl: Helicobacter pylori colonization of the Upper GIT is associated with the following outcomes: Peptic Ulcer disease. It is more commonly associated with duodenal ulcer than gastric ulcer. Non cardio gastric adenocarcinoma Low grade gastric B cell MALT lymphoma H Pylori provides protection against Reflux esophagitis and its sequelae like Barret esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma. The diagnosis here is a gastric MALT (Mucosa Associated Lymphoid Tissue) tumour . These are usually marginal zone B cell lymphomas associated an excellent prognosis. MALT lymphoma is the third most common type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma . MALT lymphomas are most commonly found in the gastrointestinal tract ( stomach is the commonest). But they can be found in any extranodal site. Low grade gastric MALT tumours are associated with Helicobacter Pylori infection and respond in over 80% of cases to helicobacter eradication. A proportion of patients will not respond to eradication therapy alone and will go on to more conventional anti-lymphoma therapies such as cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, nucleoside analogues or radiotherapy. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 163, Pg: 1280-1283

text: Which microorganism causes cat scratch disease?
expl: Explanation: Cat scratch disease (CSD) is an infection caused by Bartonella henselae , a Gram-negative, facultative intracellular bacterium. It is transmitted by the bite or scratch of cats (especially kittens) or via fleas carrying infected feces. In immunocompetent patients, it causes localized lymphadenopathy and fever, while in immunocompromised individuals, it can lead to bacillary angiomatosis, peliosis hepatis, and endocarditis. Transmission: Primarily from cats; via scratches, bites, or fleas (Ctenocephalides felis). Clinical presentations: Cat scratch disease (immunocompetent): Papule/pustule at site, tender lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise. Bacillary angiomatosis (immunocompromised): Vascular skin lesions resembling Kaposi sarcoma, systemic symptoms. Peliosis hepatis: Blood-filled cavities in liver/spleen, hepatomegaly. Endocarditis: Culture-negative, seen in immunocompromised patients. Diagnosis: Serology (IgM/IgG via ELISA/IFA), PCR, Warthin-Starry silver stain, culture (difficult). Treatment: CSD: Often self-limiting. Severe → azithromycin or doxycycline. Bacillary angiomatosis/peliosis: Doxycycline or erythromycin for months. Endocarditis: Doxycycline + rifampin. Explanation of other options: B. quintana (Option B): Causes trench fever, spread by lice. B. bacilliformis (Option C): Causes Carrion's disease, transmitted by sandflies. Borrelia burgdorferi (Option D): Causes Lyme disease via tick bites. Key Takeaways: Bartonella henselae is the causative agent of cat scratch disease. In immunocompromised hosts, the infection manifests as bacillary angiomatosis or peliosis hepatis .

text: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Emergency department very agitated, complaining of abdominal pain. This has been her third attendance over the past six months, and each time there have been no significant findings. Her only medication of note is the oral contraceptive pill. On this occasion her BP is elevated 155/90 mmHg, her pulse is 92, and her temperature is 37.8°C. Her abdomen is generally tender but soft, and she has active bowel sounds. She complains of lower limb weakness, and she appears to have 4/5 power weakness below the knee.Investigations show: Hb 13.4 g/dl(13.5-18) WCC 10.2 x 10^9/L (4-10) PLT 194 x 10^9/L (150-400) Na 132 mmol/l (134-143) K 4.4 mmol/l (3.5-5) Creatinine 1.1 mg/dl Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is associated with: Hypertension A mild increase in temperature Non-specific abdominal pain Patients feel normal between attacks , and the disease itself is due to accumulation of both porphobilinogen and amino-levulinic acid. In general, drugs that lead to increased activity of the hepatic P450 system, such as phenobarbital, sulfonamides, oestrogens, and alcohol, are associated with increased risk of acute attacks. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 416, Pg: 3238

text: A 34 year old lady presents with a long history of abdominal pain and diarrhoea. She also gives a history of recurrent mouth ulcers. Recently the pain has become more intense, she has begun to lose weight and has developed fever with night sweats and she also complains of a rash over her legs. On examination she is thin, she has clubbing and erythema nodosum. On examination of the abdomen a firm tender mass can be palpated in the right iliac fossa. In this patient, which of the following investigations is most appropriate?
expl: The clinical features in this patient points towards a diagnosis of Crohn's disease . However, the features of increased pain, fever, sweats and a mass suggest the patient may have developed an abscess in the right iliac fossa . Hence, imaging this area with CT scan to detect and treat the collection is the investigation of choice. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 326, Pg: 2477

text: A 27-year-old shop worker is referred with a three month history of recurrent episodes of disorientation and confusion. Her friend has found her wandering around the house on several occasions, apparently with no idea of where she is or how she got there. Her mood has been very low, with frequent emotional outbursts, and she has considered leaving her job because of problems with working the computer and managing customers' queries. Her friend feels her condition is significantly worsening. Physical examination is normal, apart from recurrent, asymetrical, jerks in all four limbs. Which of the following investigations is likely to be most useful in reaching a diagnosis?
expl: This kind of rapid cognitive decline in a young person with myoclonus is strongly suggestive of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). A definitive diagnosis of any form of CJD requires pathological examination of brain tissue, which is usually only done post-mortem. During life, investigations are undertaken for two reasons: to exclude other possible diagnoses, and to support the diagnosis of CJD. Supportive investigations are EEG, CSF examination and MRI. The EEG in sporadic CJD may show significant abnormalities involving deep brain areas such as the thalami. The normal rhythms are gradually lost. Initially the changes are diffuse, and non-specific, developing into generalised bi- or triphasic periodic sharp wave complexes with a frequency of 1-2 per second. High voltage sharp waves may be synchronous with myoclonic jerks. In an appropriate clinical context, this EEG pattern is strongly suggestive of a diagnosis of CJD. Neither CSF examination nor MRI are options here, but both can also give supportive information. The CSF typically contains no inflammatory cells, but the total protein content may be raised. Analysis for brain specific proteins, particularly 14-3-3, is supportive in the right clinical context. In a proportion of cases, abnormalities of signal in the anterior basal ganglia (caudate/putamen, and sometimes the cortex) can be seen on MRI, which can also support the diagnosis. Chest x ray and liver function tests may help to exclude other diagnoses, but do not give supportive information for CJD. Visual evoked potentials may be altered in CJD, but no specific pattern has yet been identified to support the diagnosis. CT head generally demonstrates brain atrophy in CJD, but this is not a specific finding and is therefore less useful than an EEG. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 438, Pg: 3420 20th edition Chapter:430 Page number:3152-3153

text: Which of the following is not an evidence-based measure for preventing the transmission of COVID-19?
expl: Explanation: While several proven public health measures including vaccination, masking, and respiratory hygiene significantly reduce the transmission of COVID-19, ivermectin has not been shown to be effective for either prevention or treatment of the disease. Initial small-scale studies suggested a possible antiviral effect, but subsequent large randomized trials and meta-analyses failed to confirm any clear clinical benefit. Consequently, major health authorities such as the WHO, CDC, and NIH do not recommend ivermectin for COVID-19 prophylaxis or therapy outside of approved clinical trials. Measures to Prevent the Spread of COVID-19: Cough Etiquette (Option A ruled out) Always cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or your elbow when coughing or sneezing. Dispose of tissues immediately. Wear Masks (Option B ruled out) Practice Physical Distancing Wash Hands Regularly Use Hand Sanitizer Avoid Touching Face Get Vaccinated (Option D ruled out) Follow Local Guidelines Avoid Large Gatherings Monitor Symptoms and Get Tested Reference: WHO - COVID-19 Vaccines Advice https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/covid-19-vaccines/advice WHO - Advice for the Public https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public WHO - The Race for a COVID-19 Vaccine https://www.who.int/news-room/feature-stories/detail/the-race-for-a-covid-19-vaccine-explained CDC - Prevention and Treatment https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/about/prevention-treatment.html

text: SARS-CoV-2 is
expl: SARS-CoV-2 is the cause of a respiratory disease called COVID-19. The virus is a member of lineage B of the Betacoronavirus genus that not only includes the highly pathogenic viruses SARS-CoV-1 (which caused a smaller epidemic in 2002-2003) and MERS-CoV (a lineage C virus that caused small epidemics in 2012, 2015, and 2018), but also contains the lineage A common cold viruses CoV-OC43 and CoV-HKU1 and MERS-CoV. These are enveloped, positive-sense RNA viruses encoded by a viral RNA genome that is quite large, a single linear RNA segment that encodes four structural proteins, designated the S (spike), E (envelope), M (membrane), and N (nucleocapsid) proteins, and a large polyprotein that is cleaved into 16 nonstructural proteins in infected cells. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition page Ch: 199 Pg 1507
